The integral over the stabilizer uses the ordinary Frobenius norm F = ‖g‖F. The preceding bound uses logarithms of singular values. Here is the conversion, with the constants later spent in the restricted period integral.

Lowest-type coefficient estimate. Suppose m ≥ 3 and the opposite-sign parameters of π are separated by at least h = 1000m³. For any unit vector v₀ in its lowest K-type and any g in the signed unitary group,

|⟨v₀,π(g)v₀⟩| ≤ exp(100m³) F−40m².

First take q ≥ 1. The stated h exceeds 120m q3/2 since q ≤ m. Set M = min{t², t/√(2q)}. The estimate on the compact average gives log of the upper bound equal to −125m³M. Each singular value is at most exp(t), hence F² = Σ sj² ≤ m exp(2t). Also t ≤ 1 + mM. This is immediate when t ≤ 1. For t ≥ 1 both mt² and mt/√(2q) are at least t. Using log m ≤ m, we obtain

40m² log F ≤ 20m³ + 40m² + 40m³M ≤ 100m³ + 125m³M.

Rearranging and exponentiating proves the estimate. If q = 0 the group is compact and all singular values are 1. Then F = √m, and the right-hand side is at least 1 by log m ≤ m. Unitarity bounds the coefficient by 1. This argument uses one representation. The choice of a translate with a large projection needs a second representation on the stabilizer.

Where can the smaller representation be seen inside the larger one?

Keep the signed unitary groups H ⊂ G, the positive unit vector z fixed by H, and the real branching assumptions. Write m = n + 1 for the larger dimension and X = 8mB. Fix a lowest compact-type unit vector v₀ for π on G and a lowest compact-type unit vector w₀ for σ on H. The signed interlacing theorem and its coefficient projection supply an isometric intertwiner i from the space of σ to that of π. Set P = i∗. Then P takes values in the smaller space, while iP is the orthogonal projection onto its copy inside the larger space.

The task is to choose a translate π(g₀)v₀ whose projection has a quantitative lower bound. Consider the nonnegative function F(g) = |⟨iw₀,π(g)v₀⟩|² and the squared column length Y(g) = ‖g−1z‖₂². For Haar measures μ on G and ν on H let dπ, dσ be the corresponding formal degrees. Schur orthogonality says that the squared matrix coefficient of two vectors integrates to the product of their squared norms divided by the formal degree. For our unit vectors this gives ∫F dμ = 1/dπ. The model uses its fixed ambient Haar measure for the estimates below. M. Duflo and C. C. Moore, orthogonality relations for square-integrable representations[5].

Mixed coefficient moment. The branching construction gives the following bound on the average of Y with density dπF.

∫G Y(g)F(g) dμ(g) ≤ X8m/dπ.

Here is how a column of g−1 enters. Tensor π with the dual of the defining representation. Acting on a tensor supported in coordinate l and reading its z-coordinate inserts the matrix entry (g−1)l,z. The discrete-series decomposition of this tensor on smooth vectors writes the resulting coefficient as ∑s al,s(g) over at most m summands, each with one parameter lowered by 1. In each summand, Schur orthogonality gives ∫|al,s|² ≤ X6m/dπ. Three bounds multiply here. The scalar obtained by applying the tensor projection and taking the distinguished coordinate costs at most Xm, the squared projected input with its form normalization costs X4m, and the reciprocal shifted formal degree costs at most Xm/dπ. These are the tensor decomposition, projection and formal-degree estimates used at this step.

For each l, the square of the sum costs at most the number of summands times ∑s|al,s|² by Cauchy–Schwarz. Summing over l recovers the whole squared column. The three factors from Cauchy–Schwarz, the sum over s and the sum over l are each ≤ m ≤ X. Thus the exponent is at most 6m + 3 ≤ 8m. This moment controls the mass with a large distinguished column even when left multiplication by the stabilizer makes the full matrix arbitrarily large.

Such a matrix is obtained by rotations in the positive and negative subspaces and a two-dimensional signed-unitary block, as in the column decomposition. Then gb fixes z, so gb = ι(h₀) for some h₀ ∈ H. If h = h₀u with u ∈ U, then ι(h)−1g = ι(u)−1b−1 belongs to C. Indeed ‖ι(u)‖F² ≤ 4m, and inverse signed-unitary matrices have the same Frobenius norm. Each g ∈ S therefore contributes at least ν(U) to the integral of the indicator of C over these h. Multiply by F(g), integrate and change variables by left translation. Tonelli's theorem gives

ν(U) ∫S F dμ ≤ ∫C ∫H F(ι(h)k) dν(h) dμ(k).

Equivariance of i and Schur orthogonality on H make the inner integral exactly ‖Pπ(k)v₀‖²/dσ. Two quantitative comparisons fix the scale. Integrating the decaying subgroup coefficient of w₀ gives 1/dσ ≤ Dν(U), with D = X67m². Covering the ambient ball by translates of the identity neighbourhood of radius (100m(B + 1))−2 gives dπμ(C) ≤ K, with K = 4X24m³. The formal degree times the measure of that small neighbourhood is at most 4. T. Tao, An Epsilon of Room, I, Theorem 1.1.23 (Tonelli)[6].

If ‖Pπ(k)v₀‖² were smaller than 1/(4DK) throughout C, multiplying the displayed double integral by dπ would give at most ν(U)/4 on the right and at least ν(U)/2 on the left. Since 0 < ν(U) < ∞, one g₀ in C has projected squared norm at least 1/(4DK). The parameter gap implies X ≥ 16. The numerical inequalities 64m(m + 2X8m)² ≤ X20m and 4DK = 16X67m²+24m³ ≤ X200m³ give the asserted bounds after taking square roots. For the first inequality use m + 2X8m ≤ 3X8m and 576m ≤ X4m. In particular ℬ(100)‖Pπ(g₀)v₀‖ ≥ 1 for ℬ(100) = X100m⁴, the common scale of the period estimates.

For m = 4 the moment calculation costs 27 powers of X and allows 32. The coefficient before the squared projection is 16X2608, since 67·16 + 24·64 = 2608. The bound 16 ≤ X then gives 4DK ≤ X2609, within the allowed X12800.

Why does the projected vector yield a positive diagonal period?

Set v = π(g₀)v₀, p = Pv ≠ 0 and ρ = π restricted to H. Inner products are linear in their second argument. The preceding absolute-integral estimate at the identity makes h ↦ ⟨v,ρ(h)v⟩ integrable. On the smaller Hilbert space define the coefficient operator

⟨a,Tb⟩ = ∫H conj(⟨v,ρ(h)v⟩) ⟨a,σ(h)b⟩ dν(h).

Inversion of Haar measure on this unimodular group gives T = T∗. The coefficient of v is bounded and integrable, hence square-integrable. In an orthonormal basis of the smaller space, Schur orthogonality makes the matrix coefficients of σ an orthonormal family of functions after multiplication by √dσ. For every finite part of this family, subtract the orthogonal projection of the coefficient onto its span. The squared norm of the remainder is nonnegative. This gives Bessel’s inequality and bounds the sum of squares of all entries of T by the squared L² norm of the coefficient divided by dσ. Keeping finitely many of these entries gives a finite-rank operator. By Cauchy–Schwarz the squared operator norm of the discarded part is at most the sum of its squared entries, which tends to zero. Thus T is compact.

The lower estimate is Re⟨a,Ta⟩ ≥ |⟨p,a⟩|²/dσ. One way to see why the projection appears is to average ρ against the conjugate coefficient of w₀, multiplied by dσ. This is an orthogonal projection by Schur convolution, and fixes iw₀. Its quadratic form therefore dominates |⟨·,iw₀⟩|². For a in the span of translates of w₀, a change of variables in the two coefficient integrals transfers this inequality to T. That span is dense by irreducibility, so continuity gives the lower estimate for every a.

In an eigenbasis of the compact self-adjoint T, the quadratic form at p is the sum of the eigenvalues weighted by the squared coordinates of p. If all eigenvalues were smaller than ‖p‖²/(2dσ), this sum would be at most ‖p‖⁴/(2dσ). The preceding lower estimate gives at least ‖p‖⁴/dσ. Thus there is a unit eigenvector w with eigenvalue c₁ ≥ ‖p‖²/(2dσ) > 0. Inserting b = w into the defining integral gives c₁⟨a,w⟩, the diagonal term of the period. MIT 18.102, Lecture 22, Theorem 232 (compact self-adjoint spectral theorem)[7].

The construction also gives a smooth w. The form ∫⟨y,ρ(h)v⟩⟨σ(h)w,a⟩ dν represents ⟨Ay,a⟩ for a bounded operator from the larger space to the smaller one. Its norm bound is ‖w‖(∫|⟨v,ρ(h)v⟩| dν/dσ)1/2 by the coefficient Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and Schur orthogonality. Left invariance makes A equivariant. At y = v the eigenvector identity, conjugated, says Av = c₁w. Dividing the intertwiner by c₁ maps the smooth vector v to w, which is therefore smooth.

Check on a circle. To test this last operator identity, take normalized Haar measure on the unit circle, σ trivial, ρ(t) = diag(1,t) and v = (3/5,4/5). Embed σ as the first coordinate. Then Pv = 3/5 and dσ = 1. The coefficient of v is 9/25 + (16/25)t. Its conjugate integrates to 9/25, so the eigenvalue is 9/25 and the guaranteed lower bound is 9/50. This example checks the normalization of the diagonal integral independently of the large-gap estimates.

How is the size of the identity term used as the unit of comparison?

Diagonal normalization. The bounded-translate argument supplies an isometric embedding of the σ-model into the π-model, its adjoint P, and a choice of the bounded translate above with ℬ(100)‖Pv‖ ≥ 1. The branching eigenvector theorem, for the formal degree d′ > 0 of σ with respect to μ₀, supplies a smooth unit vector w and a scalar c₁ ≥ ‖Pv‖²/(2d′). For every vector a in σ the diagonal integral has the value

∫H conj(Φ(ι(h))) ⟨a,σ(h)w⟩ dμ₀(h) = c₁ ⟨a,w⟩.

In particular, setting a = w measures the positive diagonal scalar c₁ itself. The subgroup formal-degree estimate gives V₀ ≤ ℬ(11)/d′. Now 1 ≤ ℬ(100)²‖Pv‖² and 2 ≤ ℬ(1), so V₀ ≤ c₁ℬ(212). Multiplying by ℬ(1000) from the local integral gives c₁ℬ(1212). The simultaneous estimates also allow ℬ(600) for the derivative integral relative to V₀. A single exponent chosen for the full collection is C = 1000 + 600 + 11 + 201 = 1812. At scale b the construction takes B = b² and assumes log(8mb²) ≤ 6 log b. Thus ℬ(C) ≤ exp(q) with q = 6Cm⁴ log b.

Return to an arithmetic frame. At a real place τ choose an adapted frame Dτ that changes the arithmetic Gram matrix to signed coordinates, with Dτz equal to the distinguished coordinate vector. Then the distinguished column of DτgDτ−1 is exactly Dτgz. On the stabilizer the conjugate model reverses the coordinate order in both rows and columns. This is a continuous group isomorphism ρ with continuous inverse. The image of the arithmetic-coordinate Haar measure μτ is another Haar measure on the model group. Haar uniqueness gives ρ∗μτ = λτμ₀ for a finite λτ > 0. Consequently absolute integrability transfers in both directions. The integral of the norm gains λτ, as does the diagonal scalar after conjugating the smaller model's coefficient. Write cτ = λτc₁. If Iτ(g) is the absolute integral in these coordinates, then

Iτ(g) ‖Dτgz‖₂2m+5 ≤ exp(q) |cτ|,   2m + 5 = 2n + 7.

For example, multiplying μτ by 3 triples both Iτ and cτ. Their ratio still obeys the same bound. A. Sutherland, Number Theory I, Lecture 13, Theorem 13.3 (Haar uniqueness)[8].

What measure and weight does a single rational class contribute?

Write f for the number of real places, and fix a Haar measure on the product of their stabilizers. In the chosen frames this measure is κ times the product of the local Haar measures, for one κ > 0. The translated coefficient is a product of local functions, each absolutely integrable by the preceding result. Fubini gives an absolute integral of κ∏τIτ. Applied to the diagonal pairing it gives c∞ = κ∏τcτ. The product of the bounds therefore has exponent Q = fq and diagonal factor |c∞|. Haar uniqueness, Theorem 13.3[8] · T. Tao, An Epsilon of Room, I, Theorem 1.1.23 (Fubini–Tonelli)[6].

At finite places take a self-dual lattice Λ containing z and a nonzero level ideal 𝔪. Let K be the subgroup preserving Λ and acting trivially modulo 𝔪, and K′ its preimage in the finite stabilizer. Its finite-place Haar measure μf(K′) is positive and finite. The subgroup is open and contains the identity, and is compact because the stabilizer is closed and K is compact. For a translate g, the finite coefficient is the indicator of Sg = {hf : gfι(hf) ∈ K}. If h₀ belongs to this set, cancel gfι(h₀) inside K. Membership then says exactly h₀−1hf ∈ K′. Thus its measure is zero when it is empty and μf(K′) otherwise. For the identity term it equals μf(K′).

Given the adelic Haar measure, choose real and finite Haar factors whose product pushes forward to it. Indeed, multiplication identifies the two factors with the adelic group. Push forward any product of Haar measures and absorb the positive scalar from Haar uniqueness into the real factor. Let x be the chosen point in the stabilizer and γ a rational representative, set g = ι(x−1)γ, and write zγ = γz. The integral of the absolute coefficient factors as μf(Sg) times its real absolute integral. Denoting this adelic integral by Iγ(x), the estimate actually used in the sum is

Iγ(x) · (∏τ ‖Dτι(xτ−1)zγ,τ‖₂)2m+5 ≤ exp(Q) |c|,   c = μf(K′) c∞.

This c multiplies the value of the cusp form in the identity contribution. For every other class, multiplying the absolute coefficient integral by the supremum bound for the cusp form gives an upper bound on its weighted contribution. The congruence test and the lattice estimate for the sum then decide whether the identity term dominates. A simultaneous rescaling of the integrals and of the identity contribution preserves the comparison.

Fix the row input and pass through the grid

Suppose the reader prescribes a different smooth vector w ≠ 0. If the initial pairing vanished on every real translate of t(w), the real-translate vanishing theorem would make it vanish on t(w′) as well. Choose a successful translate h. Right invariance of the quotient integral moves h to ι(h⁻¹) in the core factor, where equivariance expresses it as a change of vector. Testing on vectors whose maximal-compact translates span finite-dimensional spaces suffices by the compact-finite vanishing theorem. This gives a vector v of that kind with P₀(y(v),t(w)) ≠ 0. Core surjectivity puts y(v) in the span of the bottom values Ψ₀ of allowed descending column chains. Rapid decrease makes the period linear on this span. At least one such Ψ₀ still pairs nontrivially. From now on keep that column chain and u = t(w) fixed.

At each stage the column function Ψi is a downward theta integral of Ψi+1. On the row side, apply the first i upward lifts to u, using real polynomials and finite test data chosen for those steps. At an odd stage the resulting period is a Fourier–Jacobi period, which also uses an auxiliary theta function on a line. At an even positive stage it is a Bessel period, tested along a unipotent subgroup against its character and paired on the smaller group. The grid comparison uses the conjugates of both the column and row functions. At the first stage, conjugating the initial period keeps it nonzero. A seesaw identity, which interchanges the two theta integrations, then produces a nonzero Fourier–Jacobi test.

Why can one insist on the prescribed tests at the next lift? Suppose all candidate Bessel periods vanish. Unfolding gives a Fourier–Jacobi functional vanishing on the images of all the allowed data under the transform taking test functions to the smaller pair of spaces. These images contain a nonzero lattice vacuum vector (fixed by the specified lattice translations) and its allowed Heisenberg translates. The vacuum irreducibility theorem for this functional forces vanishing on the whole vacuum space. Evaluating on the product datum from the preceding nonzero Fourier–Jacobi period contradicts this. Thus some Bessel test works. The Fock spanning theorem for the same class of functionals then gives a polynomial and a finite coset label at this step. Updating only these two entries leaves the earlier partial row lift fixed. The reverse transition similarly gives a Fourier–Jacobi test at the next odd stage.

Trace four steps. For m = 4 the sequence of nonzero tests is P₀ → Fourier–Jacobi at 1 → Bessel at 2 → Fourier–Jacobi at 3 → Bessel at 4. Each arrow asserts that a choice succeeds. The four complex values can differ. For any allowed even m ≥ 2, induction ends with a Bessel period at m, because the last index of the form 2k + 2 is attained at k = m/2 − 1. The partial row lift there is the full row lift.

Why one archimedean pair can serve every row

The preceding choices can depend on the row. At the final vertex the smaller Hermitian space is positive definite and the distinguished middle vector has negative norm. With the prescribed Harish–Chandra parameter and weight gap at least 120 times the cube of the terminal row rank, the space of compatible local Bessel bilinear forms at each real place τ has dimension at most one. Fix a generator bτ there, taking zero for a zero space. On pure tensors, fixing all coordinates except τ makes the terminal period a scalar multiple of bτ in that pair of local variables.

Here is the small algebraic step that joins the places. Write β(p) for this period on tuples, grouping the two inputs at each place as pτ. If any bτ vanishes identically, so does β. Otherwise choose p⁰ with every bτ(p⁰τ) ≠ 0. Replace the coordinates of p⁰ by those of p one at a time. At each replacement, cross multiplication cancels the unknown scalar for that slice. This gives

β(p) ∏τ bτ(p⁰τ) = β(p⁰) ∏τ bτ(pτ).

Only the product at the reference tuple needs to be inverted. Pure tensors span both spaces, so bilinearity extends proportionality to every pair of inputs. Composing the resulting common bilinear form with the real row-vector map for w gives Aw(ρ,ξ). Every tested period now equals Aw(ρ,ξ) times a scalar depending on the row, column and finite datum. A successful first test fixes a pair with Aw ≠ 0. Each further nonzero row has its own successful column and finite datum and hence a nonzero scalar. The fixed pair detects that row. The argument uses the real branching and decay estimates, core surjectivity, the two unfolding identities, Fock spanning and local Bessel uniqueness with its weight-gap hypothesis.

The base-coordinate contradiction

Let Pq be the base quotient map and iℂ its injective realization on the quotient coordinates. The coefficient identity says that a root of unity times a nonzero product of local constants times ψb(iℂ(emb(Pqy))) equals κ times a matrix coefficient for every input y and every reading b. Why the jets at 2 and 3 stay integral

A theta entry is obtained by differentiating the normalized series at zero. A Taylor coefficient can have a denominator at a small prime even when its derivative is integral. For a series F(z) and a tuple m of nonnegative orders, its jet is ∂mF(0) = (∏j mj!)[zm]F. The estimate says these derivatives have p-adic norm at most 1 in every integral frame admitted by the construction. This gives valuation at least zero for the entries formed from them.

Fix a word u, its auxiliary tuple μ and a finite place w of residue characteristic p. The place is level-free when p differs from the word’s level prime T and the two auxiliary primes g₀, g₁, and lies outside the tuple’s excluded set Qp(μ). For each such place with p ≠ d, the entry bound covers every step i < m with even product of adjacent ranks NiNi+1 and every pair of lattice classes at that step. Level freeness supplies the admissible combination of translates. A separate test classifies primes of the host. The first class consists of the primes dividing the host modulus QS, including 2. The construction assumes a splitting bound of at least 3. It gives (−d/3) = 1, so d ≡ 2 mod 3. Also q ≠ 3. Thus 3 belongs to the first class if it divides QS, and to the split class otherwise. The integrality proof uses the congruence in both cases. The global proof obtains its inert Frobenius estimate separately.

The factor that cancels the denominator at 3

Work over the completed algebraic closure of the 3-adic numbers. A discriminant-normalized period lattice has invariants g₂³ − 27g₃² = 1. Complex multiplication gives an algebraic integer j = 1728g₂³. The proof chooses a curve W with equation y² = x(x − A)(x − B) matching these invariants. Its discriminant is 16[AB(A − B)]² = 1. The bound on j gives |A² − AB + B²|₃ ≤ 1. These two conditions imply |A|₃, |B|₃ ≤ 1, so the curve has integral coefficients.

Write b₂ = a₁² + 4a₂ for the standard invariant of this integral Weierstrass equation. The formal theta calculation contains b₂/12. To see how the factor 3 disappears, take the CM endomorphism β = −1 + 2ω, where ω = (1 + √(−d))/2. Its conjugate is −β, so β² = −d and ββ̄ = d. The kernel has order d prime to 3 and its nonzero points have integral curve coordinates. Both β and β − β̄ = 2β are 3-adic units. The endomorphism identity uses the following combination.

(β² − 1)b₂/12 = −((d + 1)/3) · b₂/4.

The integer (d + 1)/3 and the 3-adic unit 4 give an integral right side. For the example with CM discriminant −23 this reads (−23 − 1)b₂/12 = −2b₂. It works for every integral b₂. The formal curve theorem combines this bound, the integral kernel coordinates and the unit β − β̄ to bound every positive derivative of the correction series φ in the additive coordinate.

Here φ is the zero-constant correction that appears on passing from the local curve parameter to the theta expansion. The scalar theta theorem starts with a lattice period whose half-period images under ω and ω̄ lie outside the lattice. Each shift is killed modulo the lattice by a positive integer N prime to 3. The half-period and the shifted half-period have orders dividing 2 and 2N. The torsion translation formula then gives integral coefficients for each translate multiplied by exp(+φ) in the curve parameter. The formal change to additive variables supplies the inverse correction exp(−φ), using the positive-derivative bounds just proved. Multiplying the two exponentials cancels the correction. The argument passes to finite sums with integral weights and to the permitted integral frames.

How many factors of √p can a determinant lose?

At the discriminant prime p = d, a derivative can pick up one factor of a scalar S with |S|p ≤ √p each time it differentiates a matched pair from the exponential. Alternation in the determinant limits the number of such pairs. Fix a step of the lift with input and output ranks N₀ and N₁. For each label t there are two sets of coordinates, denoted by − and +. Write y±tab for the theta variables, where a indexes an input coordinate and b an output coordinate. The kernel already constructed has the form Θ = exp(−S∑t,a,buty−taby+tab)H. Here |ut|p ≤ 1, and every derivative of H at zero has norm at most 1.

Encode the differential operator by a polynomial G in two kinds of variables. The entries X±tra specify a frame row r. The symbol Z±tab stands for ∂/∂y±tab. A Young diagram is a left-aligned array of boxes with weakly decreasing row lengths. For each column of height h in a diagram, choose h distinct output coordinates in increasing order. Take the determinant of the matrix XZ on the first h frame rows and those output columns. Multiply these determinants over all diagram columns, signs and labels to obtain G. Substituting the derivatives for Z and evaluating the result at y = 0 leaves a polynomial in X. The entry theorem bounds every coefficient of that polynomial for every permitted column choice.

For a fixed label let α and β be the − and + diagrams. Write |α| for the number of boxes and α₀, β₀ for their top-row lengths, hence also their numbers of columns. One paired contraction on the symbols is the operator Δt = ∑a,b ∂Z−tab∂Z+tab. The contraction bound is

ΔtnG = 0   if   n > Ct = |α| − α₀ + min(α₀, β₀).

Expand each − determinant by permutations. Every term contains one factor from the top row per diagram column and |α| − α₀ factors from other rows. Differentiating a − factor from row r and output coordinate b leaves the operator ∑aX−tra∂Z+tab on the + side. For r = 0 it replaces column b of a + minor, when present, by the same vector with entries ∑aX−t0aX+tia in row i. A second top-row replacement in that minor differentiates a constant column or produces two identical columns. Both determinants vanish. Thus a surviving term uses at most β₀ top-row replacements on the + side and at most α₀ on the − side. Ordinary derivatives commute, so the other row operations can be moved past the top-row operations. Each contraction consumes either one of the |α| − α₀ other factors or one of those common top-row slots. This proves the cap.

Compute both contractions in a two-by-two example

Take one label, two input and two output coordinates. Let α have one row of two boxes and β two rows of one box each. Choose separate output coordinates for the two height-one − minors and both coordinates for the height-two + minor. Specialize the − frame’s top row to (1,1) and the + frame to the identity. From formal contractions to a valuation of the lift

Why does Δ control an actual Taylor coefficient? For a fixed frame monomial Xm, assign a multi-index κ of derivatives to H in the product rule. The rest must differentiate matching − and + coordinates, with h derivatives of each sign at a coordinate that occurs h times in the exponential. Its coefficient has a denominator h!, while the two derivative factorials give (h!)². One h! remains in the numerator. Let nt count the matched pairs at label t. After extracting the derivative of H and the factor ∏t(−Sut)nt, the remaining coefficient A is an integer, a signed sum of binomial choices and the surviving factorials. In the symbol polynomial its exact identity is

(∏t nt!) A = [XmZκ] (∏t Δtnt) G.

The brackets extract a monomial coefficient. The factorial on the left counts the possible orders of the paired differentiations at each label. If one nt exceeds its cap, commuting the operators brings that power next to G. The right side vanishes, so A is zero in ℤ. For every surviving term |A|p ≤ 1, the derivative of H is integral, and the absolute value of the remaining scalar is at most p(∑t Ct)/2. The ultrametric triangle inequality gives the same bound on the finite sum. With vp(p) = 1, every nonzero coefficient has valuation at least −½∑t Ct.

The family uses a common bound for prescribed diagram rows. At step j = i + 1, write cj,t for this count at the chosen word. At an unmarked label it equals |α|. At a marked label it is |α| − α₀ + α₁ + β₀, where α₁ is the second-row length, or zero if that row is empty. Both values majorize Ct. In the example they are respectively 2 and 1. Thus all pairs of source and target lattice classes satisfy the entry bound −½∑t cj,t. The selected theorem uses it at each place above the distinguished discriminant prime that is free of the word’s level prime, the two auxiliary type primes and the primes excluded by the tuple.

For the bound on the whole map, let Mj be the maximum of ∑t cj,t over the finite set of words. At p = d the prescribed main term is Fram(j) and the error allowance is Fram(j) + Mj/2. Their difference is −Mj/2. There is a separate denominator valuation δ = vp(DΓ) for the chosen word’s integer DΓ. The entry-to-lattice comparison subtracts δ at each lift, with a credit ηδ at the first lift, where η denotes the comparison parameter. For a tuple used by the chain and a ramified source vector in the specified lattice, composition gives the column bound ∑j(−Mj/2 − δ) + ηδ. The comparison of jet entries with lattice maps and the kernel shape at d are the two arithmetic inputs to this transfer.

5Lattices and the arithmetic main term

A local valuation gain becomes a positive multiple of log p after taking a lattice height. Each word in the theta construction carries an auxiliary prime level. A lower bound on the logarithm of that prime enters the lattice comparison. Expanding the bound cancels the period and auxiliary-prime terms and identifies the main term to subtract from the arithmetic prime sum.

5.1The lattices that carry the comparison

Over a number field K, an arithmetic lattice in a finite-dimensional K-vector space V is a finitely generated module over the ring of integers of K spanning V. To measure it one also needs norms at the infinite places. A basis of V and a matrix Xv at each such place give these frames. Each frame must have nonzero determinant. For such a lattice A of positive rank r over a totally complex number field, its mean slope is −(2/[K : ℚ]) log(ht(A))/r. Here ht is the lattice height in the chosen metric. The factor 2/[K : ℚ] averages over the complex places. A smaller height at fixed rank raises the mean slope. The proof obtains positivity of ht and uses [K : ℚ] = 2 times the number of infinite places.

For each choice of translation and each word u in a finite nonempty set W, the construction has a lattice Nu, a height allowance hu, and a linear map from the ambient space of Nu to the dual of the ambient space of a common lattice R. This dual consists of linear forms on that space. Its integral lattice consists of the forms taking integral values on R. The global hypotheses include an upper bound by hu for the height of each nonzero map.

Write μ for the mean slope, μmax for the maximum sublattice slope, and μmin for the minimum quotient slope. The comparison takes a mean weighted by the positive ranks ru of the word lattices. Set

s = ∑u ru(μ(Nu) − hu)/∑u ru,   bF = maxu(μmax(Nu) − hu) − s.

The latter quantity is nonnegative. For each word, its adjusted mean slope is bounded above by that word's adjusted maximum and hence by their common maximum. Averaging gives the assertion. The symbols s and bF in this chapter are real quantities at a fixed translation.

5.2What the counting bound contributes

Each stage j and place ρ has positive weight wjρ. Let v > 0 be the host normalization, and ℓg the logarithm of the product of the two auxiliary primes used for the host. Ec = CcLa(1 + m²/k),   λ = ∑j (1/f) ∑ρ log(wjρv/π) + mℓg − Ec.

For every word u, the word count gives λ ≤ log Tu ≤ CcmL. It also gives |log Tu − log Tu′| ≤ Cc log k between any two words at this translation. The first inequality supplies the counting floor used in the main term. The other two control fluctuations in the slope estimate. Scalar La is log of the product of the master scale a and the root discriminant of the field E.

5.3The cancellation in the main term

Write γ for Euler's constant and d for the real logarithmic derivative at 1 of the distinguished quadratic character in this comparison. Set Ωlog = γ + log(π/v) − d. The local divisibility inequality contributes the term SD − A log Tu, where

SD = m∑t[at log at − at − atΩlog].

At zero we interpret a log a by its continuous value zero. Since A ≥ 0, subtracting A log Tu is bounded above by subtracting Aλ. The local exponent comparison contributes mAℓg with an explicit error bound. We can now calculate exactly which deterministic quantity lies under those bounds.

First expand the logarithm inside λ. Each place contributes log wjρ + log(v/π). The second summand is independent of ρ, so the mean over f places reproduces it once per stage. Thus −Aλ contributes −mA log(v/π), −mAℓg, and +AEc, as well as the weighted logarithms of w. The period term inside SD contributes +mA log(v/π), exactly cancelling the first of those terms. Adding the exponent main term +mAℓg cancels the second. Distributing A = ∑tat in the remaining place sum yields

SD − Aλ + mAℓg = M + AEc,
M = ∑j,t at[log at − 1 − γ + d − (1/f) ∑ρ log wjρ].

The plus sign of d comes from subtracting Ωlog. At m = f = 1 with a single top index and w = 1, the main term reduces to a(log a − 1 − γ + d). Doubling v adds a log 2 to SD and subtracts the same amount through −Aλ. This illustrates why a change of metric normalization in only one term would leave a linear error.

A check with two different place weights. Specialize the displayed identity to one stage, top weights 1 and 3, and place weights 2 and 8. Then A = 4 and the mean of the place logarithms is log 4. To track the cancellations, set v = 2π and write ℓg = log 15. These are values for checking the algebra. The formula for λ gives log 8 + log 15 − Ec. The period in SD contributes +4 log 2. Substitution gives

SD − 4λ + 4 log 15 = 3 log 3 − 4 − 4γ + 4d − 4 log 4 + 4Ec.

The coefficient of log 15 is zero. The surviving −4 log 4 comes from the geometric mean √(2·8) of the place weights. The count error enters with a plus sign, scaled by the total top weight 4. These three features persist for arbitrary finite sets of places and top weights.

The identification with the prime-sum expression uses specific bijections and equalities. The top indices correspond to the finite arithmetic sample, the f place indices to the chosen half of the finite group, the respective weights agree, γ agrees, and d equals the real part of the coefficient of the distinguished sign character. With these correspondences, reindex the two finite sums and take real parts. The final identification equates the weighted arithmetic prime sum to the sum over the sampled top indices and stages. Subtracting the matched main term M on both sides identifies the residual in the balance calculation.

5.6Why the slope bound contains a logarithm

Think of a lattice through its finite list of Harder–Narasimhan slopes, each repeated according to rank. A step in its filtration contains the directions whose slopes meet a given threshold. For a slope λ of the underlying real lattice the arithmetic normalization is 2λ + cK, with the same field constant for all words and the target. The resulting list has arithmetic mean equal to the lattice's mean slope. For the source lattices subtract each height allowance and concatenate the lists over all words. Their mean is s and every entry is at most s + bF. If a fraction p lies below s − τ, for τ ≥ 0, then the mean is at most p(s − τ) + (1 − p)(s + bF). Rearranging gives p ≤ bF/(bF + τ) when the denominator is positive. If both quantities vanish, all slopes equal s and the strict lower tail is empty. This bounds the rank lost when we discard low-slope steps in the source.

What happens to the remaining directions under the word maps? At threshold s − τ, take the sum of the images of the retained steps in R∨. A slope inequality for the maps, together with their height bounds, places this sum in the target filtration step. Bound its codimension using a matrix calculation at one infinite place. With p bounded as above, the resulting fraction of target slopes below the threshold is at most

ω(τ) = [η + 4bF/(bF + τ) + 4√e]/(1 − δ).

The matrix calculation uses bounds on traces and on Hilbert–Schmidt deviations after restriction to the selected columns. These estimates connect the dimensions of the source steps to the dimension of their combined image. Counting the target slopes below threshold now amounts to counting the dimensions missing from its filtration step.

Let ν run through the normalized target slopes with multiplicity. The lower-slope bound says ν ≥ s − H. Consequently the interval of τ in [0, H] for which ν < s − τ has length max(s − ν, 0). Average these lengths over the finite list. Their integral representation, followed by the bound above, gives

s − mean(ν) ≤ mean[max(s − ν, 0)] = ∫0H fraction{ν < s − τ} dτ ≤ ∫0H ω(τ) dτ.

For example, set s = 4 and take the three numbers 1, 3, 5 with H = 3. Two lie below 4 − τ for 0 ≤ τ < 1, and one lies below it for 1 ≤ τ < 3. The integral of the fraction is (2/3)·1 + (1/3)·2 = 4/3. This equals the average of the positive deficits 3, 1, 0. The signed mean deficit is only 1, since the last value exceeds 4. This finite list illustrates the integration step.

For bF > 0, integrating bF/(bF + τ) gives bF log(1 + H/bF). For bF = 0 this contribution vanishes. The two constant terms in ω integrate to (η + 4√e)H/(1 − δ). Since mean(ν) = μ(R∨), the calculation actually proves the bound without subtracting log |W|. The later theorem uses the displayed weaker version by subtracting the nonnegative logarithm of the number of words.

5.9Why each orbit is a product of residue groups

At each selected place the residue field has T elements. Its unit group H has T − 1 elements. The level-zero forms admit a model as complex functions on a finite set X. An element of H in one coordinate acts by a local dilation, also called a diamond operator. The operator Nv sums all these dilations in the coordinate v. Under the model, its kernel consists of functions whose sum along that coordinate is zero at every point. The ramified subspace is the intersection of these kernels.

Freeness uses arithmetic. Suppose a tuple of local multipliers fixes a level class. Represent it by an adelic element δ, whose components at the two auxiliary type primes are the identity. The power δT−1 belongs to the level subgroup, since the residues of all its multipliers have that power equal to 1. The diamond operator normalizes the level, so the same power of δκ belongs to the level for every level element κ. Fixing the class supplies a rational element γ from the double-coset relation. The admissible stabilizer gives γT−1 = 1. At each of the two distinct auxiliary primes p, the local reduction calculation kills every power of γ of order coprime to p. To see the force of having two primes, write T − 1 = pam with p ∤ m. The first condition kills γpa, whose order divides m. Now γ has order dividing pa, which is coprime to the second prime. Hence γ = 1 and δ itself lies in the level subgroup. Each local multiplier fixes a nonzero level functional killed by T. A multiplier c must therefore satisfy c ≡ 1 mod T. The tuple is the identity.

Choosing orbit representatives now identifies X with Q × Hf, where Q indexes the orbits of the function model. Its size includes the multiplicity of the value space. On each orbit a function has (T − 1)f entries before imposing any sums.

5.10Counting the independent values

Keep only the entries indexed by tuples with every coordinate different from the identity. They determine a function with vanishing line sums uniquely. To recover an entry with an identity coordinate, it must be the negative of the sum of the other entries on that line. Each of those entries has one fewer identity coordinate, so induction recovers the full table. Conversely, to extend a unit value at such a tuple a, use the product over coordinates v of (1hv=av − 1hv=1). It sums to zero along every coordinate and restricts to the unit value at a and zero at every other retained tuple. Taking linear combinations extends arbitrary data. Thus there are (T − 2)f independent values on each orbit.

dfull = |Q| (T − 1)f,   dram = |Q| (T − 2)f.

A four-by-four check. Take one orbit, T = 5 and f = 2. Order the four residues in both coordinates as 2, 3, 4, 1. Put ones on the diagonal of the first three-by-three block, zeros in its other six entries. Zero row sums force the first three entries of the last column to be −1. Zero column sums force the first three entries of the last row to be −1. Both conditions put 3 in the final corner. The nine free entries determine all sixteen. The eight row and column equations have one redundancy because summing all rows also sums all columns. The lost fraction is 7/16.

5.11From an exact count to a uniform error

For a nonzero full space and T ≥ 3, Bernoulli’s inequality gives

1 − dram/dfull = 1 − (1 − 1/(T − 1))f ≤ f/(T − 1) ≤ 2f/T.

The scale conditions give T ≥ bm/2 ≥ b, with b = exp(xε), b ≥ 3 and m ≥ 2. Thus dfull − dram ≤ de dfull for de = 2f/b. The undivided inequality also holds if the full space is zero. For each fixed family with ε > 0, one threshold works for every later x and every family index. The number f can depend on that index, but the same de works for all its words. Eventually f ≤ k ≤ x5, 2f ≤ exp(xε/2), and xε ≥ 4xε/8. Consequently √de ≤ exp(−xε/4) ≤ exp(−xε/8). Put Ex = exp(−xε/8). To obtain a bound common to all indices at this x, the proof enlarges the rank-loss cap to Ex² and the separate matrix-error cap to 2Ex². The rank term in the frame error 5σ + 3Ex now has the same value at every index. The common frame calculation supplies the diagonal and off-diagonal bounds on the full period matrices.

5.12What controls the variation of the prime level?

The comparison of two word counts uses a Vandermonde product V(z) = ∏a<b(za − zb) in the decreasing real parameters at a place. Its logarithm is a sum over pairs. For the first row a = 0 the two compared gaps are each at least 4kΔ and change by at most Δ. The variation of each logarithm is at most 1/(4k). For a ≥ 1 the gaps are at least 3(b − a)Δ and change by at most 2Δ, giving 2/[3(b − a)] per pair. Both bounds follow by integrating 1/t between the gaps. A harmonic sum over b bounds the logarithmic variation at a place by 1/4 + (2/3)k(1 + log k). Summing over f places and applying the factor 1/(fk) in the level parameter leaves variation of order log k. The shared auxiliary factor cancels when the two word windows are compared. The absolute bounds for each word also use a torus-pair estimate involving the mass, volume and formal degree.

5.13How close are the period operators to a common orthonormal frame?

Two periods can each preserve lengths and still take their values on the same line. A slope estimate that uses many words therefore needs two measurements. For a fixed family member let Pu carry the full complex space of word u, of dimension du, into one Hilbert space. Normalize by the real number cu, the product of its two unfolding volumes divided by the product of its column representation dimensions over the infinite places. The operator from the space of v to the space of u is

Kuv = (cucv)−1/2 Pu∗Pv,   Q(A) = ∑j ‖Aej‖².

Here the ej run through an orthonormal basis of the domain. For u = v we measure Q(Kuu − I). For distinct words we measure Q(Kuv), which adds the squared absolute values of all correlations between the two normalized families of columns. The estimates are for the full word dimension. The arithmetic lattice retained at the ramified level can have fewer columns. To see why correlations influence rank, collect any set of nonzero retained columns in a matrix A and put G = A*A. If its positive eigenvalues are λ₁,…,λᵣ, then (∑λᵢ)² ≤ r∑λᵢ² by Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus rank(A) ≥ (tr G)²/tr(G²). For two unit columns the numerator is 4. Identical columns give denominator 4 and rank one. Orthogonal columns give denominator 2 and rank two. The estimates below control the corresponding diagonal and cross terms for the selected arithmetic spaces.

5.14Separating the nonidentity terms with zero Gram label

The geometric expansion of Kuv converges absolutely. Write Buv for its subseries of terms with Gram label zero and with the identity excluded. Set D∗ equal to the positive reference size for the target dimension and ξ = exp(−kf log k). The proof uses four estimates. On different words the subseries vanishes, and the remaining squared norm is at most (1 + b−6)dudv/D∗. On the diagonal it gives

Q(Buu) ≤ ξdu,   Q(Kuu − Buu − I) ≤ Γdu²/D∗.

The four estimates have different suppliers. Local types kill the unwanted off-diagonal terms. A positive-kernel estimate controls their diagonal subseries. The selected different-word estimate controls the rest off the diagonal. On the diagonal a geometric row estimate controls what is left after subtracting the identity. Absolute convergence permits these subtractions.

Why can a pair of words have a zero orbital term?

Fix two distinct words u and v in the selected family. Their local unitary representations have different weight parameters at every infinite place. Examine a single nonidentity term with Gram label zero in Buv. It compares a flag with a translate of the other flag. Call the pair relevant when the differentials of their two characters agree on every common infinitesimal unipotent direction. There are two ways for its orbital integral P to vanish.

If relevance fails, one direction gives unequal phases. In fact the proof rescales that direction so that, with N infinite places, the difference in the two character exponents is πi/N at each place. The product of the first character with the conjugate of the second therefore takes the value exp(πi) = −1. This character is trivial on the rational lattice. Averaging over its compact quotient in the common unipotent group gives zero, since translating the character average by that element changes its sign. The orbital integrand transforms by exactly this character, so the orbital integral vanishes.

For a relevant pair with Gram label zero, the geometric normal form gives a positive orthonormal frame perpendicular to both flag subspaces at each infinite place. Write its columns as W and the ambient Hermitian form as J, so W∗JW = I. Every M ∈ U(k) extends to a symmetry fixing those subspaces pointwise. Indeed, put

H = I + W(M − I)W∗J.   HW = WM,   Hy = y whenever W∗Jy = 0.

On the frame this map preserves the inner product because M is unitary, and on its orthogonal complement it is the identity. The other flag sees the action as CMC∗ for a fixed unitary matrix C at that place. Invariance of the orbital integral under the pointwise stabilizer gives covariance between these two actions. This uses the existence of the fundamental domain and integrability of the orbital kernel.

Choose one infinite place and let M vary only there. Fix arbitrary vectors in every other tensor factor on each side. Let Su and Sv insert a local vector into those fixed tensors. For A = Su∗PSv, covariance reads

πu(M)A = Aπv(CMC∗),   πu(M)R = Rπv(M),   R = Aπv(C).

A nonzero R would be an isomorphism. Its kernel and image are invariant, and the two finite-dimensional representations are irreducible. An isomorphism preserves the weights of the diagonal torus, including the distinguished extremal weight that determines each type. The unequal parameters rule this out. Hence R = 0 and A = 0. Varying the fixed tensors shows that every matrix coefficient of P between pure tensors vanishes. They span both spaces.

Can a scalar unitary distinguish these two types of U(2)?

On the determinant line and on Sym²(ℂ²), the scalar zI acts by z². Suppose an intertwiner sends a generator of the determinant line to a quadratic tensor w. Every diag(z,z−1) with |z| = 1 fixes w. In the basis e₁², e₁e₂, e₂², the three eigenvalues are z², 1 and z−2. Thus w is a multiple of e₁e₂. Swapping the basis vectors fixes that monomial and multiplies the determinant by −1. Equivariance gives w = −w, so w = 0.

Both cases kill each selected term individually, so their sum Buv is zero. The other terms still contribute to Kuv. The separate different-word estimate bounds the squared norm of Kuv − Buv, and substituting zero gives the bound for the full block.

How large can the surviving part of a different-word block be?

Fix distinct words u and v and put Δ = dudv/D∗. The preceding argument removes the nonidentity terms whose geometric Gram label is zero. The remaining sum, called K₀, contains the identity part and two groups of terms with nonzero label. The identity part also vanishes for this calculation. The two groups can point in the same direction in the Hilbert space of operators. The proof bounds the squared norm of each group before adding them.

Call the two groups G (generic) and N (nongeneric). Genericity tests a pair of lattice flags. Their integral span has a saturation, obtained by intersecting its field span with the ambient lattice. At primes away from the level, genericity requires that the original span already give the saturation locally. At primes dividing the level, one admissible matrix must supply the saturation using the corrected frame differences divided by the level. A term is generic when a representative passes these tests.

Each term t contributes a vector vt supported on one pair of lattices. Its row records those lattices and a finite index i. For either group S, form ai by summing its vectors with index i. In the square of that sum, terms with the same index but different lattice pairs have disjoint support. Absolute convergence permits regrouping, so only ordered pairs in the same row contribute. With Γ₁ the positive Gram normalization, the resulting energy is

Φ(S) = Γ₁ ∑i ‖ai‖² = Γ₁ ∑s,t ∈ S, same row Re ⟨vs, vt⟩.

Individual inner products can have either sign. To bound the sum, the proof groups pairs by their corank s₀ = k − dim Θ, where Θ consists of first components of vector pairs compatible with the two flags and their comparison map. On a common row with both Gram labels nonzero, s₀ ≥ 1. Among generic pairs of corank one, the scalar pairs preserve the two coefficients of the distinguished flag vectors under comparison.

The large-corank estimate bounds the sum of absolute inner products over all same-row pairs of nonzero-label terms of corank at least two by εΔ, including the factor Γ₁. Thus each group can use this bound on its own subset. In G, the nonscalar corank-one pairs cost at most another εΔ in absolute value. The signed sum of the scalar pairs is at most AΔ. In N, one signed bound ε′Δ covers all corank-one pairs. These are the only cases, giving

Φ(G) ≤ (A + 2ε)Δ,   Φ(N) ≤ (ε + ε′)Δ.

The common Gram matrix converts each energy to an upper bound on the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of its operator sum, with a factor P. The triangle inequality then gives the retained block bound

‖K₀‖² ≤ (√[P(A + 2ε)] + √[P(ε + ε′)])² Δ ≤ (1 + b−6)Δ.

Why take the square roots? Consider two contributions along one unit vector, with coefficients 1 and 1/10. Their squared norms are 1 and 1/100, but their sum has squared norm 121/100. That example illustrates only the last addition. On the selected route the kernel expansion identifies the surviving block with the full block after the zero subseries is removed. Its Hilbert–Schmidt squared norm therefore obeys the same bound used in the frame estimate.

Why does the Gram matrix cost only P, and where does b−6 come from?

For each group the squared norm is Re ∑ij Mij⟨ai, aj⟩. The supplied matrix bound says that PΓ₁I − M is positive semidefinite. Factor it as a sum of outer products wℓwℓ∗. Substituting in the difference between PΦ(S) and the squared norm gives ∑ℓ ‖∑i wℓi ai‖² ≥ 0.

Set h = b−7. Under the selected size hypotheses, b ≥ 16, the two level primes satisfy gi ≥ (kb)⁸, and k ≥ 70 log b. The full rank and density inequalities give ε, ε′ ≤ h² and A ≤ (1 + h)exp(h²). For f infinite places, the Gram factor P = (1 + 3/g₁)f(1 + 3/g₂)f is at most exp(6h). Using h ≤ 1/1000, the two radicands are at most 1 + 11h and 3h². Their square roots sum to at most 1 + 11h/2 + 7h/4. Its square is at most 1 + 16h ≤ 1 + b−6. The remaining arithmetic inputs are the absolute bounds from counting loops, the nongeneric corank-one estimate, and the main scalar-row estimate from the lattice and mass calculation.

How many flags can have the same Gram data?

Fix a row in the common frame and one Gram class Z. To count generic flags in this row, keep the part of a flag visible in the definite orthogonal space. It is a sublattice P of a fixed lattice L₀ of ambient dimension k. Its rank is k − 1. The frame determinant formula gives a bound G depending on the prescribed data. Write B for the fixed-witness bound on the number of flag classes supported by any one such P. Each contributing flag has a witness P. Summing over possible witnesses gives an upper bound even when two witnesses count the same class.

The difficulty is that P can have large index in the integral points of its own span. Set M = L₀ ∩ spanK(P), where K is the CM field. This saturation has the same field span and rank as P. It is primitive in L₀, meaning it contains every point of L₀ in that span. With the normalized determinant (the square root of the order of the dual quotient in the span), write d = det(M) and j = #(M/P). The integral, positive definite lattice and the standing CM norm hypotheses give an integer d ≥ 1. The index formula gives det(P) = j d. Hence the determinant budget G leaves room for indices only up to G/d.

For a fixed saturation let α = k + log₂[K ∶ ℚ]. The projective-module counting bound supplies at most jα submodules of index j. For x ≥ 1 there are at most ⌊x⌋ indices through x, each contributing at most xα. This accounts for the extra power in the estimate. If Cprim(L₀,n,d) counts primitive sublattices of rank n and determinant d, the total number of eligible witnesses satisfies

#{P ⊆ L₀ ∣ rank P = n, det(P) ≤ G} ≤ ∑1 ≤ d ≤ ⌊G⌋ Cprim(L₀,n,d) (G/d)α + 1.

For G < 1 there are no witnesses. For the single generic flag take n = k − 1 and multiply by B. The row weights are nonnegative, so summing first over rows or first over d yields the same upper bound. The remaining arithmetic estimate concerns the mean of the primitive counts.

Count the eight rank-one sublattices of determinant at most two by hand

Take the standard Hermitian lattice ℤ[i]². A nonzero rank-one submodule has a generator (a,b), unique up to the four units, because ℤ[i] is a principal ideal domain. The Gram entry is h = |a|² + |b|². Its dual in its own line is obtained by dividing the generator by h. The quotient has h² elements, hence the normalized determinant is h. At h = 1 the two coordinate axes are the only possibilities. At h = 2 both coordinates can be units, giving the four primitive lines generated by (1,u), u ∈ {1,−1,i,−i}. Otherwise one coordinate vanishes and the other is a unit times 1 + i. These last two submodules have index two in the coordinate axes. This lists 2 + 4 + 2 = 8 submodules. In this concrete model the primitive counts are 2 and 4, and α + 1 = 4. The general counting expression gives 2·2⁴ + 4·1⁴ = 36. Its slack comes from bounding every index by the same power.

Why a pair costs two flag counts. A loop term carries two flags and a comparison isometry. For fixed Gram classes, positive corank s and a determinant cutoff, the two flags admit a common witness P of rank k − s. Under the level and admissibility hypotheses, moving each flag by its allowed integral unipotent transformation carries the comparison isometry to the one for the new pair, by uniqueness on the orthogonal quotient. Thus the two flag classes determine the triple class. If each flag set at P has at most J classes, the ordered pair has at most J² choices. Multiply the displayed witness bound by J² and average the primitive counts in the relevant genus. The fixed-witness estimates and the primitive genus estimates enter separately in the uniform row bounds.

How many flag classes can one fixed sublattice support?

Fix a base flag, a row lattice Λ and a Gram class Z in the common frame. Let r be its isotropic rank, k the dimension of its definite complement, f the number of conjugate pairs of embeddings of the CM field E, and N = T(u)f for the base word u. Fix P inside the definite row lattice L₀, of rank k−s over E after taking its span, with 1 ≤ s ≤ k. A term flag belongs to this count if it satisfies the row and frame conditions, its cross-Gram matrix is equivalent to Z by integral triangular changes with diagonal one, and its visible lattice contains P. Count classes under the integral unipotent transformations and allowed frame changes.

The uniform theorem assumes the standing and numerical conditions on the two words, a standard base flag, an admissible row, a relevant Gram cell and Cℓ ≥ 1. For a sufficiently large height parameter C, write HZ for the prescribed height of Z. Choose Δ ≥ 1 and H with det P ≤ Δ, HZ ≤ H and Δ ≤ H³. Saturation in L₀ gives [sat(P)∶P] ≤ Δ since the saturated lattice has determinant at least one. If the flag set is nonempty, an actual term proves the Gram invariant is nonzero. The cell supplies a nonzero maximal minor of the first r rows. The proof uses Z itself as its bounded representative. The common budget Q = HZ² bounds the absolute norm of that minor, the product of the absolute values of the Gram invariant over the selected complex embeddings, and the specified different-ideal norm.

How many ways can P lift? An isometry fixing the base frame puts the row in split form and preserves the definite lattice. Every original class has a representative with exact cross-Gram matrix Z in the split calculation. A lift of P there has the form p ↦ p + φ(p), with φ valued in the isotropic lattice and the graph orthogonal to the moving frame. In one isotropic coordinate a linear form on P costs at most [sat(P)∶P] representatives beyond the restrictions of forms on its saturation. Forms on the primitive saturation contribute at most N² modulo pairings with L₀. Taking all r coordinates gives at most (N²Δ)r lift representatives. Frame-fixing integral unipotents move each graph into this list. Summing over the list gives an upper bound even if a class admits more than one graph.

What remains once the lift is fixed? Put S₀ = L₀ ∩ P⊥, a definite lattice of rank s. A nonzero ideal I of norm at most M = Δ²N² satisfies I S₀∨ ⊆ S₀, where the dual is taken in its span. Let Y be the top r rows of the exact Gram matrix and let a be its chosen nonzero maximal minor. The moving frame gives a tuple of perpendicular components w₀,…,wᵣ in S₀∨. Write y for their linear combination with the signed maximal minors of Y as coefficients. Its squared length satisfies T(u)〈y,y〉 = G, the fixed nonzero Gram invariant. For a nonzero difference in the dual lattice, integrality after multiplication by I bounds the product of its embedded squared lengths below by 1/N(I). Packing points separated in this way gives at most 9sf(MQ)s possible y. For a fixed y, the difference of two tuples has cofactor combination zero. The adjugate of the chosen submatrix expresses this difference as a combination of the rows of Y with coefficients in ((a)I)−1S₀. Reducing those r coefficients modulo S₀ costs at most (MQ)sr. The integral changes are realized by unipotents preserving the lifted graph.

With the perpendicular tuple fixed, the remaining difference is an r × (r+1) matrix x in the isotropic coordinates satisfying x*Y + Y*x = 0, where * denotes conjugate transpose. The centre acts by x ↦ x + cY for integral skew-Hermitian c. Clearing denominators with the minor a and the r-th power of the extended different bounds the number of residual representatives by Q2r². Every flag class occurs in the image of the perpendicular and isotropic representative sets. Multiplying their sizes is therefore sufficient.

A rank-one coordinate calculation over the Gaussian integers

Take S₀ = ℤ[i] with its usual norm, r = s = 1, Y = (t,0) for an integer t ≥ 1, and impose |t w₁|² = t². There are four choices for w₁, the Gaussian units. Row translations add tv to w₀, so its real and imaginary parts each give one residue modulo t. This yields exactly 4t² perpendicular classes. For integral isotropic corrections the skew equation forces x = (ij,0) with j ∈ ℤ. Integral skew scalars act by adding (itℓ,0), leaving t classes. At t = 2 this gives 16 perpendicular representatives and 2 isotropic representatives. The 32 ordered pairs describe the two coordinate equations in this model. To obtain an admissible flag one would also have to realize the pair in a single integral row with the prescribed base, Gram matrix and level.

The bound used in the row sum. Combining the graph count and the two residual counts first gives the following upper bound on the number of classes over P.

(N²Δ)r · 9sf(Δ²N²Q)s+sr · Q2r².

The standing height estimate gives N² ≤ HZ ≤ H. Since Δ ≤ H³ and Q ≤ H², the middle base is at most H6+1+2 = H⁹. The last factor is at most H4r². With H ≥ 1 one may enlarge this last exponent to 16r², obtaining

Bₛ = N2r Δr 9sf H9s + 9sr + 16r².

The generic row uses s = 1, Δ = max(G,1) for its determinant cutoff G, and H = HZ. The paired row uses a common determinant allowance and height for the two Gram classes. It applies Bₛ to each flag at the same P, then uses Bₛ² before summing over witnesses. The primitive genus mean then counts candidate witnesses of corank one. The ordered-pair estimate uses a mean allowing higher corank.

How often does a primitive hyperplane occur across the rows?

The fixed-witness estimate bounds the number of flags once their witness lattice is given. To average this bound we also need to count witnesses. After saturation the arithmetic input for one generic flag concerns primitive hyperplanes of exact determinant. Fix the frame and the word in the standing unramified CM datum. Its prime Tu is at least three and splits completely in the CM field E. The definite complement has dimension k ≥ 3. Write j = k−1 and f = [E∶ℚ]/2. For a row lattice L and an integer d ≥ 1, count the E-hyperplanes U for which the restriction to P = L ∩ U has |P∨/P| = d². Call this count Nd(L). Intersecting with the whole field hyperplane is what makes P primitive. Submodules of finite index in P have already been accounted for at saturation.

Why average over a genus? A genus collects lattices that are isometric at every completion. The count above is invariant under isometries. For a nonempty set of row representatives choose one complement lattice L₀. In its genus take one representative L per isometry class, and write a(L) = 1/|Aut(L)| and m = ∑ a(L). Apply the row-to-genus comparison first with the observable Nd, then with the constant observable one. The common row multiplicity cancels. With wΛ the row weights, the exact identity is

m ∑Λ wΛNd(LΛ) = (∑Λ wΛ) ∑[L] a(L)Nd(L).

Count the marked pairs in the other order. For a fixed lattice its finite automorphism group permutes the marked hyperplanes. Each orbit contributes its size divided by |Aut(L)|, which is the reciprocal order of the subgroup fixing the pair. This lets us first choose a rational isometry class of hyperplanes and then count the lattices meeting that hyperplane with the prescribed discriminant. The proof covers all possible marked pairs by its subspace representatives, so this second operation yields an upper bound.

Check both counts in one Gaussian lattice

Take the identity Hermitian form on ℤ[i]³. A primitive normal vector v determines U = v⊥, and four unit multiples give the same hyperplane. Put d = ⟨v,v⟩. Primitivity gives a vector w pairing to one with v. A basis of P followed by w is a basis of the full lattice. The squared length of the projection of w onto the normal line is 1/d. Factoring the Gram determinant of that basis thus gives 1 = det Gram(P)/d. The Gaussian index of the dual quotient, counted as a finite abelian group, is the absolute norm of this determinant, namely d².

At d = 3 the three coordinate norms are 1,1,1 or 0,1,2 up to permutation. In the first case the four phases per coordinate give 4³/4 = 16 hyperplanes. In the second there are 6 orders, four phases for the norm-one entry and four for the norm-two entry, giving 6·4²/4 = 24. Every integral isometry permutes the three coordinate axes and assigns a Gaussian unit to each, so the group has order 6·4³ = 384. The two stabilizers have orders 24 and 16. Counting marks at the lattice gives 40/384. Counting by orbits gives 1/24 + 1/16, the same 5/48. This example checks the change of order for one ambient lattice.

Use the identity Hermitian form on ℤ[i]⁴. A saturated plane has a Gaussian basis u, v. Put pab = uavb − ubva. A single nonzero minor forces the field plane to be the corresponding coordinate plane, whose saturated lattice has determinant 1. There are six such planes. At determinant 2, precisely two minors must therefore be units. Their index pairs share an index, since expanding the definitions gives p₁₂p₃₄ − p₁₃p₂₄ + p₁₄p₂₃ = 0. Disjoint pairs would leave a single nonzero product. With common index a, the plane is spanned by ea and eb + εec with b < c and ε one of the four Gaussian units. The two coefficients of value one along a and b show that these vectors already generate the whole intersection. There are 4 choices of a, 3 unordered pairs {b,c}, and 4 phases, or 48 planes. They form a single orbit under the 4!·4⁴ = 6,144 coordinate isometries, so their contribution for this lattice is 48/6,144 = 1/128. This calculation illustrates the marked mass for one lattice. All the word maps take values in the same target. Its dimension D counts the independent ways the chosen archimedean representation occurs in automorphic L² after applying the finite-place projector e. The main term M for this integer is a real number. If dv is the formal degree at the real place v and V is the Haar volume of a fundamental domain F, then M = c0V, where c0 = (∏v dv) Re e(1). Why should this expression approximate a dimension? Both arise from one kernel.

Let φ be the product of the normalized archimedean matrix coefficients, their formal degrees and the finite-place function e, with the archimedean coefficients conjugated. Summing φ(x⁻¹γz) over rational group elements γ gives a kernel K(x,z). It represents an orthogonal projection of rank D. Choose continuous representatives F1, …, FD of an orthonormal basis of the range. The geometric kernel and the basis expansion give the same action on compactly supported test functions. Continuity and uniqueness of the automorphic representatives identify the two kernels pointwise. In particular,

Re K(x,x) = ∑j |Fj(x)|² ≥ 0,   ∫F Re K(x,x) dμ = D.

Each basis vector contributes one to the integral. On the geometric side the identity γ = 1 gives the constant c0 on the diagonal. Its integral is M. The real parts of the remaining summands can have either sign.

Which parameters enter the dimension comparison?

Fix a positive level-growth exponent Cg. The theorem chooses a lower bound for the ambient dimension n before varying the field and level. At each of the f infinite places the discrete series has the prescribed signature (p, q), with p + q = n and q² ≤ n. The CM field has root discriminant d with log d ≤ exp(n), and log f ≤ √n. The scale b ≥ 2 satisfies log b ≤ exp(nf log n/16). The congruence level g lies between 1 and bCg. The auxiliary rational prime exceeds 4n and splits completely in the CM field.

The absolute values of the archimedean weight entries are ≤ b². Whenever two entries at the same place have opposite signature signs, their distance is at least 8·10¹⁴(Cg + 4)n¹⁹f⁵ log(bd). This gap supplies rapid decay for the far terms. The threshold for a point to lie in the deep cusp uses the same field and level data and equals τ∗ = (nf d g b)−11q.

What does a short sublattice measure?

Let Λ be the lattice at the point and let B be a nonzero sublattice of rank s over the CM field E. Embed B at the f conjugate pairs using the positive metrics at that point. Its real covolume is taken in its own span, of real dimension 2fs. Multiply the covolume by 2fs|disc E|−s/2 and take the (2fs)th root. This is its normalized size. The least size is the infimum over all such B. The root makes it meaningful to compare different ranks. The canonical lattice filtration has a nonzero step strictly below t precisely when the least size is < t. Its step at or below t is already nonzero at equality.

For example, give the two coordinate directions of ℤ[i]² lengths ½ and 2, respectively. Here f = 1 and |disc E| = 4, so the prefactor is one in every rank. The fundamental square of the first Gaussian line has area ¼ and its normalized size is ½. The full lattice has four-dimensional covolume one. To find the least size, project a line sublattice onto a nonzero coordinate. This identifies it with a Gaussian ideal. An element of least nonzero norm generates that ideal. Round the real and imaginary parts of each quotient to integers. The remainder has smaller norm than the divisor and belongs to the ideal, so it must be zero. Thus the line has a generator (a,b) with squared length |a|²/4 + 4|b|² ≥ ¼. Every full-rank sublattice has positive integer index, hence covolume at least one. The least size is exactly ½. The strict test used in the short-flag bound therefore excludes this example at the boundary.

How many distant terms can survive at a point?

In the trace estimate, the variable x describes a lattice and γ runs over rational group elements. Fix x for now. At a real place v, take the polar decomposition of the matrix of x⁻¹γx as k exp(X), with k unitary and X Hermitian. Write zv(γ) = ‖X‖HS. This is the square root of the sum of the squared logarithms of its singular values. A nonzero summand is far when some zv exceeds the chosen radius ε. Equality with ε belongs to the inner interval. Zero summands may be dropped throughout.

Rational point count. Write tx = min(½, least(x)), where least(x) is the smallest normalized sublattice size, interpreted as an infimum. Among rational elements whose finite component after conjugation lies in the supporting compact subgroup, the number with zv(γ) ≤ Rv at every place, for prescribed nonnegative radii, satisfies

# {γ in the box} ≤ P(x) exp(κ ∑v Rv),   P(x) = (3√n/tx²)2n²f,   κ = 2n².

Here n is the matrix size and f is the number of real places. To see the lattice in this count, subtract two distinct rational elements from the box. Their finite support condition makes the difference a nonzero map from the lattice at x into itself. The lattice size inequality, using self-duality, gives a lower bound for the geometric mean of the operator norms of this difference across all places, namely tx². Thus the matrices form a separated set, even though two of them may approach one another at an individual place.

Why does the exponent contain 2n²f?

At place v the matrices lie in a ball of operator radius exp(Rv), since the largest log singular value is at most zv. Put R̄ = (∑ Rv)/f. Rescale that space of matrices by exp(R̄ − Rv). The product of the rescalings is one, so geometric-mean separation persists, while every coordinate ball now has radius exp(R̄). In the maximum norm on the product, distinct centers are therefore at least tx² apart. Open balls of radius tx²/2 around them are disjoint and fit in the concentric ball of radius exp(R̄) + tx²/2. The product space has real dimension 2n²f. Scaling its Lebesgue volume bounds the count by (1 + 2 exp(R̄)/tx²)2n²f. Since n ≥ 1, tx ≤ ½ and R̄ ≥ 0, the base is at most 3√n exp(R̄)/tx². Raising this to the indicated power yields the box bound.

How much of the fundamental domain can lie in the deep region?

Choose a point x using Haar measure on the fundamental domain divided by its volume V. The question is now about the point itself. Thus the event is covered by measurable sets indexed by ordered compositions of these ranks. This cover lets us bound its volume with the same flag density that appeared in the near orbital integral.

The flag-measure theorem bounds that probability by κj times the integral of the size density over the ordered simplex. How does marking a flag change the volume being counted?

Fix the positive rank jumps j₁,…,jₐ and let B be a measurable region of admissible ordered sizes. A point whose canonical flag has those ranks and sizes supplies one saturated isotropic flag. If we count all such flags over the point, the indicator of the event is bounded above by the number of markings. For instance, if three points have probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4 and carry respectively zero, one and two eligible markings, the points with a marking have probability 3/4. Counting all markings gives 1/2 + 2(1/4) = 1. This inequality permits the geometric proof to use arithmetic stabilizers.

Choose a basis adapted to a marked flag. Its data include one full lattice class for each successive quotient, of rank jᵢ, and a finite-adelic double class in the fixed residual Hermitian model supplied by the volume-ratio theorem, of signature (p−J, q−J), where J = ∑ jᵢ. On that space two finite representatives are equivalent when a rational isometry on the left and an element of the compact lattice stabilizer on the right identify them. The construction of an integral frame and the comparison of two markings put any marking with the same data into the chosen representative by these changes of basis. The archimedean flag sizes are preserved under the corresponding simultaneous change of frame. For each realized tuple of data it therefore suffices to integrate on the quotient by the subgroup preserving its marked flag. These slices cover the original event. Counting an overlap twice gives an upper bound.

The sum is countable. Each block lattice has finitely many generators in a countable number field, and the open compact subgroup at the finite places has at most countably many cosets in a second-countable group. The residual double quotient is a further quotient of that countable set.

For the fixed marked flag the sizes at umk equal those at m, with the unipotent element u on the left and the compact element k on the right. The block diagonal coordinate gives the size variable τ and its density, whose integral on B we denote by I(B). The mass of a single marked slice is at most the product of this integral, a common factor from the unipotent covolume and the real Haar measures, one lattice weight for each block, and a stabilizer covolume on the residual Hermitian space. All these quantities are nonnegative.

We can now sum over every tuple of block classes and residual class, including tuples for which no marked flag was found. The sum of products separates. The sum over coefficient-lattice classes evaluates the weight of each block. At rank jᵢ this gives 2f jᵢ² times the normalized general linear volume of that rank. H M(B) ≤ Aj V₀ I(B),   H V = V₀ RJ.

The second equality is the Hermitian volume-ratio theorem, with V the full fundamental-domain volume and RJ the product of its rank factors from n−2J+1 through n. Both volumes and the gauge are positive and finite. Dividing gives Pr(event) = M(B)/V ≤ (Aj/RJ) I(B). The quotient of these constants is precisely κj. What must an adapted frame remember?

A rational basis that follows a flag identifies its vector spaces. The volume calculation also needs to know which coefficients give integral vectors. Let E/F be the CM extension, unramified at every finite place. Write O for the integers of E, h for the nonsingular Hermitian form (linear in the second entry), and L for the self-dual lattice belonging to the chosen finite point. Self-duality means that x lies in L exactly when h(y,x) lies in O for all y in L. Fix a saturated flag 0 = S₀ ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ Sₐ whose last space is totally isotropic. Total isotropy means that every two vectors in it pair to zero. Put jᵢ = rank(Sᵢ/Sᵢ₋₁), d = ∑jᵢ, and suppose each real signature is (p,q) with d ≤ min(p,q).

Saturation says Sᵢ = L ∩ spanE(Sᵢ). If x ∈ Sᵢ and ax ∈ Sᵢ₋₁ for some nonzero a ∈ O, then x already lies in Sᵢ₋₁. Thus the quotient is torsion-free. It is finitely generated as an O-module. Over the Dedekind domain O it is projective, so the quotient map admits a section. Its image Aᵢ gives Sᵢ = Sᵢ₋₁ ⊕ Aᵢ. Choose a basis over E for the span of each Aᵢ, and let Λᵢ ⊂ Ejᵢ be the coefficient vectors of its integral elements. This construction also works when Aᵢ is a nonprincipal ideal and has no one-element integral basis.

Set W = spanE(Sₐ). We need a second isotropic space pairing perfectly with W and a decomposition that preserves L. Apply the same projectivity argument to L/Sₐ. If π is the quotient map and s a section, then 1 − sπ projects L onto Sₐ. Extend it by scalars to a projector P on the full rational space, with image W and P(L) ⊆ L.

For an integral vector z take y = Tz and x = P(z − y). The remainder r = z − x − y lies in both ker P and ker Q. It is orthogonal to W = im P and to W′ = im T, because T†r = 0. All three summands remain in L. The perfect pairing makes their sum direct.

Why are the residual lattices equivalent at a finite place?

At an inert finite place, work first over the completed unramified quadratic extension. A self-dual lattice has an integral Gram matrix with unit determinant in an integral basis. Its reduction is a nonsingular Hermitian space over a quadratic extension of finite fields. In positive dimension it has a vector whose Hermitian value is nonzero. Otherwise, expanding the value on x + ay would give Tr(a h(x,y)) = 0 for every residue scalar a. The trace pairing of finite fields is nondegenerate, so every pairing would vanish. Lift such a vector. Its value is a unit of the base ring. Every unit is a norm in an unramified quadratic local extension, so scaling the vector gives Hermitian value one. At a split place the two integral components pair perfectly and one can take an arbitrary basis on the first and its dual on the second. For a finite place v of the real base field, a rational vector belongs to the localized lattice when some base integer outside v takes it into the original lattice. At a split place this condition retains both primes above v. The genus comparison uses a rational isometry that matches these localized lattices. The condition on the completed lattices is open because their stabilizers are open. To see why rational isometries meet this open set, take a local isometry U. Multiply by a rational scalar λ of norm one so that 1 + λU is invertible. Only finitely many λ are excluded by the determinant polynomial, and the ratios (1 + kθ)/(1 − kθ) for integers k give infinitely many choices when θ is a nonzero purely imaginary element. Set

X = (1 − λU)(1 + λU)−1,   X† = −X,   λU = (1 − X)(1 + X)−1.

Approximate X by rational matrices Y and replace each by (Y − Y†)/2. They are exactly skew-adjoint and still approximate X. At a place above two the denominator costs a fixed precision, which can be supplied by a closer initial approximation. At a split place use simultaneous approximation in the two completions. The inverse displayed transformation is continuous on its domain and sends these rational skew-adjoint matrices to rational isometries. Undo the scalar λ. A sufficiently close choice lies in the same open lattice coset as U, so it takes the first localized lattice into the second. Duality reverses this inclusion, and both lattices are self-dual, giving equality. The rational choice here may depend on the finite place.

Can one choose the block representatives at every scale at once?

Its elements act by left multiplication on tuples g of invertible complex j × j matrices, one matrix per embedding pair. We want one representative of each Γ-orbit. This lets a single unit interval of logarithmic determinants measure every other interval.

First minimize the largest absolute value of an entry, taken over all matrices in the tuple, as the tuple varies over its orbit. A minimum exists because only finitely many translates can have size bounded by any fixed number. Indeed, choose nonzero integers a, b in O with aOj ⊂ Λ ⊂ b−1Oj. For γ ∈ Γ the entries of abγ are integral. A bound on γg bounds γ after multiplication by the fixed inverse g−1. At every embedding these integral entries now lie in a bounded set. The simultaneous embedding of O is a lattice, so only finitely many entries, and hence matrices, occur.

Break a tie by dividing each matrix tuple by its size and assigning the normalized tuple a real number in a fixed, injective, measurable way. For instance, enumerate the open balls with rational centers and radii in its coordinate space and use ternary digit 2 for membership in a ball, 0 otherwise. These balls distinguish points. On the finite set of minimizers, choose the least such number. Conditions of the form “its size and tie breaker precede those of γg” are Borel, and Γ is countable, so the selected points form a measurable set D. Positive scaling multiplies all sizes by the same number and preserves all normalized coordinates. Hence D is stable under positive scalars. Left multiplication on invertible matrices is free, so the translates of D partition the matrix group.
