Which ideal does a marked vector remember?

To compare ranks, mark one nonzero vector x of a rank-j coefficient lattice Λ. The saturated line through x consists of the multiples c x that still lie in Λ. Its coefficients form a fractional ideal I containing 1. Thus I = 𝔞−1 for a unique nonzero integral ideal 𝔞. For a primitive vector I = 𝒪E. For x = 2e₁ in the standard lattice, the coefficient 1/2 is allowed, so I = ½𝒪E and 𝔞 = 2𝒪E.

Use x as the first rational basis vector, and project to the other k = j−1 coordinates. The image Λ′ is a full torsion-free module over the integer ring. Every finitely generated torsion-free module over this Dedekind domain is projective, so the projection admits an integral linear section on Λ′. Its first coordinate extends to an E-linear functional ℓ on Ek. The shear (c,y) ↦ (c−ℓ(y),y) sends this section to the last k coordinates and fixes the marked vector. The pair now has the form

(Λ,x) ≃ (𝔞−1 ⊕ Λ′, e₁).

Every displayed pair exists, since 1 belongs to 𝔞−1. A change of basis fixing e₁ fixes its scalar multiples pointwise and induces a rational change of basis on the quotient. It therefore preserves the actual ideal 𝔞 and the class of Λ′. Conversely, a change between two quotient lattices extends by the identity on the marked line. This proves that the labels are exact. In rank one without a marking we summed over ideal classes. Marking a vector fixes the scale on its line, so here even two distinct principal ideals can supply different terms.

In each coefficient class integrate over the real matrix quotient, now allowing every determinant, and sum these integrals. Write ⟨·⟩ for this sum of integrals. A Gaussian lets us evaluate both kinds of integral in a single identity.

For a moved lattice L, let A(L) be ∑0≠x∈L exp(−π‖x‖²). The Gaussian has integral one. Write L∨ for the dual under the pairing ∑v,a Re(xᵥₐyᵥₐ). The two ones are the zero vectors on the two sides. The dual has covolume 1/t. Dualizing the arithmetic lattice sends full classes bijectively to full classes. The pairing of embedded field vectors is half the rational trace of their dot product, and taking the integral dual twice returns the original lattice. On moving matrices the change is inverse transpose, which preserves matrix Haar measure. Thus integrating a function of L∨ over all classes gives the same value as integrating it on L.

Its covolume u = 1/t satisfies 0 < u < 1, so its marked integral is Cⱼ∫₀¹ u² du/u² = Cⱼ. Consequently

Vⱼ/2 + Cⱼ/2 = Cⱼ,   Vⱼ = Cⱼ.

The previous rank has finite mass by induction from V₁, and ζE(j) is finite for j ≥ 2. The right side is therefore already finite when the identity is used to determine Vⱼ.

Conversely, if a rational element takes a point in one rectangle to another, the finite coordinates force the same double class. Within that rectangle the real coordinates force γ∞ = 1, so γ = 1. Why is there just one finite orbit for the unit vector?

Fix a rational vector x of Hermitian norm σ = +1 or −1, a reference finite representative xf whose lattice contains it, and the full finite stabilizer K of the reference lattice. Let H be the group of isometries fixing x. If a second finite representative g gives a lattice containing x, the assertion needed for unfolding is

g ∈ H(𝔸fin) xf K.

Work first over the local integer ring at one finite place. On a self-dual lattice L containing x, the coefficient of the projection of y onto its line is ⟨x,y⟩/σ. It is integral, since σ is a unit. Subtracting that multiple of x gives the integral decomposition L = 𝒪x ⊕ B, where B is the orthogonal complement in L. A vector in the rational complement that pairs integrally with B pairs integrally with the whole lattice, hence belongs to B by self-duality. Thus B is itself self-dual. The local classification of self-dual lattices identifies the complements for g and xf by an integral isometry between them. Extend it by the identity on x. Outside finitely many places the two original lattices already agree, so these maps can be chosen to be the identity there. Their product h is an adelic isometry fixing x and taking one local lattice family to the other. Then (hxf)−1g belongs to K, as claimed. Conversely, multiplying on the right by K fixes the lattice, and multiplying on the left by h preserves the condition that it contains x.

This argument also identifies the level. An isometry fixing x preserves L exactly when it preserves B. For an integral modulus c, the image of h−1 on L is just its image on B. As this lies in the perpendicular space, containment in cL is equivalent to containment in cB. This identifies the subgroup induced on the complement by a congruence condition. The double coset above uses the full lattice stabilizer. For example, −1 preserves the reference lattice. At principal level 3 it takes a primitive unit vector to a different residue class, so one may have more than one finite orbit at that finer level. The same calculation applies over the two factors at a split place and over an unramified extension in residue characteristic two.

One residue calculation illustrates the dyadic case. Over 𝔽₄ with conjugation z ↦ z², take the standard Hermitian form in three coordinates and x = (1,1,1). Its norm is 1. Its complement has basis b₁ = (1,1,0), b₂ = (1,0,1). Each basis vector has norm zero and their pairing is 1. For ω²+ω+1 = 0, the norm of b₁+ωb₂ is ω+ω² = 1. The projection along x and this choice of a nonsingular direction both make sense in characteristic two.

How many vectors represent a unit at a finite place?

Fix a finite place of F. Write O for its valuation ring, π for a uniformizer and k for its residue field of size Q. The quadratic algebra is unramified. Its residue algebra is either k × k (put η = +1) or the field of Q² elements (put η = −1). Normalize additive Haar measure to give volume one to Λ and to O. The density at β is the mass of vectors with norm in β + πjO, divided by the volume Q−j of that target ball, as j increases.

Start with one coordinate. At a split place its norm is uv. There are Q−1 ways to make any prescribed nonzero value and 2Q−1 ways to make zero. At an inert place the norm is zQ+1. On the cyclic multiplicative group of order Q²−1 it has image of order Q−1 and kernel of order Q+1. Only zero has norm zero. In both cases the number for a prescribed value b is Q−η, with an extra ηQ when b = 0. Keith Conrad, Finite Fields, Theorem 5.7 (trace and norm)[15].

The reduction of Λ is nondegenerate by self-duality. In the split case it is a pair of spaces in perfect duality, so dual bases give the sum of M products. In the field case it has a vector with nonzero norm. Indeed, if all norms vanished, expanding the norm of x + az for every scalar a would give Tr(a h(x,z)) = 0 for every a. The nondegenerate field trace pairing would then force h = 0. Scale a vector of nonzero norm to norm one by surjectivity of the field norm, split off its orthogonal complement, and repeat. In either case the reduced form is a sum of M copies of the one-coordinate norm.

Let ZM count the vectors of norm zero, including the origin. With the first M coordinates fixed, the last norm has to cancel their sum. Each choice gives Q−η possibilities for the last coordinate, plus the correction ηQ on ZM choices. Hence Z₀ = 1 and ZM+1 = Q2M(Q−η) + ηQZM. Substitution gives QZM = Q2M + (Q−1)(ηQ)M. Multiplying all coordinates by a scalar of prescribed nonzero norm permutes the nonzero fibres. Dividing the remaining Q2M−ZM vectors by Q−1 therefore gives the count for one nonzero target.

BM = Q2M−1 − ηMQM−1.   Density at β = BM/Q2M−1 = 1 − ηMQ−M.

Why does the first residue digit suffice? Given a solution x modulo πj, write a lift as x + πjz. For j ≥ 1 the next digit of its norm changes by the linear functional Tr h(x,z) on the 2M residue coordinates. Here the next digit means the coefficient of πj, viewed in k. The quadratic term in z vanishes modulo πj+1. At an inert place x is nonzero modulo π, so nondegeneracy makes h(x,·) onto the residue extension, and the trace onto k is surjective even in characteristic two. At a split place the functional is u·δv + v·δu, which is nonzero at a unit value u·v. Thus exactly Q2M−1 lifts hit each prescribed next digit. The density ratio stays fixed at every level. This extends the good-place lifting calculation for one unit target to primes above 2. In rank one, successive lifting and completeness also give an integral scalar of any prescribed unit norm. Scaling by this scalar preserves Λ and its Haar measure, so the unit fibres have equal density. This also recovers the answer by dividing the total mass of vectors of unit norm by the volume 1−1/Q of the units.

Take the base field ℚ₂ and M = 3. In the split case, each of the seven nonzero triples u admits four triples v with u·v = 1 over 𝔽₂. In the inert case every nonzero element of 𝔽₄ has norm one. An odd number of the three coordinates must be nonzero, giving 3·3 + 3³ = 36 possibilities. Thus the counts modulo 2 are 28 and 36 among 64, respectively. Modulo 4, a prescribed lift of 1 has 28·32 = 896 or 36·32 = 1152 representations among 4096 vectors. Dividing those proportions by the target mass 1/4 gives 7/8 and 9/8 again. The inert density exceeds one because the mass is measured per unit of target volume.

How do the local densities give the discriminant in the mean?

In rank M ≥ 3 the one-vector mean identity expresses the normalized average for the target ±1 as a product of densities. Its global proportionality constant is fixed to one by the genus-mass argument. It initially applies to smooth compactly supported archimedean tests. The rank comparison uses nonnegative tests and then exhausts the Gaussian. Each local density uses Fourier self-dual measures for the same additive character on both the vector space and the scalar target. To use the count above, we need the volume of each of the two integral lattices in these measures. At a finite place u, define the integer tᵤ by declaring the annihilator of Oᵤ under the character pairing to be π−tᵤOᵤ. Put Dᵤ = Qᵤtᵤ. The integral trace pairing of an unramified quadratic algebra is perfect, so Hermitian self-duality gives the vector annihilator π−tᵤΛ. For a compact open additive subgroup A, the Fourier transform of its indicator equals vol(A) on its annihilator and zero elsewhere, by translation invariance. Fourier inversion at zero gives vol(A) vol(A⊥) = 1. Enlarging or shrinking by π−tᵤ scales the volume by Dᵤ in one base dimension. The vector lattice has 2M base dimensions, the scalar lattice one. Their respective volumes are therefore Dᵤ−M and Dᵤ−1/2. Dividing the vector volume by the scalar volume gives the corrected density.

αu(β) = Dᵤ1/2−M(1 − ηuMQᵤ−M).

At a real place v, let λv be the nonzero frequency of the character relative to exp(2πit). In the signed diagonal frame the trace pairing on ℂM has real diagonal entries ±2λv, each complex coordinate supplying two real entries. Fourier inversion gives the square root of the absolute determinant as the self-dual volume multiplier, namely 2M|λv|M. The real scalar line contributes |λv|1/2. The local factor for the test function is thus 2M|λv|M−1/2 times its ordinary real density dᵥ at the chosen sign.

All these characters are components of one character trivial on the diagonal copy of F. The adelic character theorem expresses it as the standard trace character scaled by some b ∈ F×. The real frequencies are the real embeddings of b. At finite places the trace-dual of the integers is the inverse different. Thus tᵤ is the valuation of the fractional ideal (b)𝔇 at u, where 𝔇 is the different of F/ℚ. Taking ideal norms gives ∏uDᵤ = |disc(F)| ∏v|λv|, with only finitely many Dᵤ different from one. The finite Euler factors left in αu multiply to 1/LM for M ≥ 2 by the split and inert Euler product. Thus every frequency cancels. Since the relative different of the unramified quadratic extension E/F is the unit ideal, the discriminant tower formula gives |disc(E)| = |disc(F)|². Equivalently |disc(F)| = (2νE)f. How can small ideals bound a regulator?

The flag coefficient contains one copy of the residue of ζE at 1 for each block of the flag. We first estimate this residue for any totally complex number field E of degree 2f. Write D for its absolute discriminant, Y = √D, h for its class number and R for its regulator. We will prove that for every real s > 1,

Use one embedding σv from each complex conjugate pair, and write ℓv(x) = 2 log |σv(x)|. Their sum is log |NE/ℚ(x)|. On units the sum is zero. Delete the last coordinate. The unit logarithms then form a lattice Λ in ℝf−1 with covolume R, in the same normalization as the coefficient-line mass. We will cover its quotient torus once for each ideal class. Fix a class C and a nonzero integral ideal 𝔟 in its inverse class. For any point t of ℝf−1, append a last coordinate so that the full vector b has sum log(N𝔟 · Y). In ℂf take the product of open discs with radii exp(bᵥ/2). Its Euclidean volume is πfN𝔟 · Y. The lattice 𝔟 has covolume 2−fN𝔟 · Y. Thus the disc product has volume strictly greater than 22f times the covolume. It is convex and symmetric, so Minkowski’s lattice point theorem supplies a nonzero x ∈ 𝔟 with ℓv(x) < bᵥ for every v. The ideal 𝔞 = (x)𝔟−1 is integral and lies in C. The sum of the coordinate gaps is log(Y/N𝔞), so N𝔞 ≤ Y. Sutherland, Theorem 14.13, Minkowski’s lattice point theorem[22].

For each such 𝔞 fix a generator y of 𝔟𝔞. Since y/x is a unit, translating t by its unit logarithm and subtracting the first f−1 coordinates of ℓ(y) leaves the first f−1 gaps bᵥ−ℓv(x). They are nonnegative and their sum is at most log(Y/N𝔞). Thus one translated simplex per small ideal covers the torus. A simplex in k = f−1 coordinates given by uᵢ ≥ 0 and ∑uᵢ ≤ L has volume Lk/k!, by successive integration. In dimension zero its volume is one. Projecting a measurable simplex to the torus can only decrease its volume, as one sees by cutting it along translates of a fundamental domain. Hence R is at most the sum of these simplex volumes over the small ideals in C.

Sum over the h classes. Each nonzero integral ideal of norm at most Y enters once. For u = Y/N𝔞 ≥ 1 the exponential series gives (log u)k/k! ≤ u ≤ us. Extending the sum to all nonzero integral ideals therefore bounds hR by YsζE(s). Above a rational prime p there are at most 2f prime ideals, each of norm at least p. Indeed, the integer ring modulo p has p2f elements and maps onto the product of their residue fields by the Chinese remainder theorem. Unique factorization of ideals now bounds the Euler product by ζ(s)2f. Finally ζ(s) ≤ 1 + ∫1∞t−s dt = s/(s−1), proving the estimate.

Why is there a canonical flag below ½?

At the point x the data are a self-dual Hermitian lattice Λ in an n-dimensional space over the CM field, and a positive definite metric at each real place. A lattice size is a normalized covolume. Its rank enters the exponent so that scaling lengths by a factor c scales the size by c. For a nonzero lattice M, its largest size is the supremum of the sizes of its nonzero quotients M/K, where K is saturated and the quotient carries the quotient metric. Saturation means that the quotient has no torsion. The least size τ of Λ is the infimum of the sizes of its nonzero sublattices.

For t > 0, let F≤t be the sum of all nonzero sublattices whose largest size is at most t, and define F<t using a strict inequality. The Harder–Narasimhan filtration theorem for Hermitian lattices supplies the following size properties. Both sums are saturated. When nonzero, the closed step has largest size at most t and the open step has largest size strictly below t. Every nonzero lattice in Λ/F≤t has size strictly greater than t, and every nonzero lattice in Λ/F<t has size at least t. In positive rank the closed step is zero precisely when t < τ and the open step precisely when t ≤ τ.

A jump is a size t for which F<t ⊊ F≤t. Its quotient has size exactly t. Indeed the open-step inequality bounds its size below by t, and the largest size of the closed step bounds it above by t. Every nonzero closed step occurs at a jump. To see this, take s equal to its largest size. The lattice is included among the generators at s and s ≤ t, so F≤s = F≤t. Its largest size equals s, while a nonzero open step at s must have largest size strictly below s. The two steps at s are therefore distinct. The same argument at the largest size of a nonzero open step locates its last jump strictly below its endpoint.

At each jump the rank increases because the quotient of the two saturated steps is nonzero and torsion-free. If s < t, then F≤s ⊆ F<t. Thus distinct jumps have distinct resulting ranks in {1,…,n}. Listing the jumps below ½ in increasing order gives the finite flag. When τ < ½ the first jump is τ, since its open step is zero and its closed step is nonzero. The last lattice is exactly S = F<½. Any jump at ½ itself falls outside this list.

(F<t)⊥Λ = F≤1/t,   (F≤t)⊥Λ = F<1/t.

Indeed the jumps remaining after the strict step have sizes at least t, so the corresponding dual jumps have sizes at most 1/t. At t = ½ this gives S⊥Λ = F≤2. For positive ranks, the integral maps form a full lattice of real dimension D = 2fab. To find an integral map near a prescribed point, use Euclidean lattice transference. In dimension D, a full lattice of dual minimum λ has covering radius at most D/(2λ). Thus it is enough to show λ ≥ 2√f · L/(d H).

What does an integral covector measure? It assigns to each integral map Φ the integer TrE/ℚ(tr(ΨΦ)) for a reverse matrix Ψ. The field trace pairing is nondegenerate, so every integral covector has this form after rational extension. If 𝔇 is the different, then δΨ sends the target lattice into the source for every δ in 𝔇. Indeed, evaluating on rank-one maps tests each scalar pairing of Ψ with a target vector and a source covector. Their traces remain integers after multiplication by every element of 𝒪E. By definition these pairings belong to the inverse different 𝔇−1. The lattice is recovered from its integral dual, giving the assertion.

Suppose Ψ ≠ 0. Its image of the target lattice is nonzero. Multiplying any nonzero sublattice of that image by 𝔇 puts it in the source and multiplies its normalized size by d. For the target lattice B, put K = B ∩ ker Ψ and I = ΨB, of rank r > 0. The kernel is saturated, and B/K maps isomorphically onto I as an arithmetic lattice. In orthonormal coordinates for the quotient metric and the image metric, the real volume factor at a complex place is the square of the absolute determinant, at most ‖Ψv‖2rop. Multiplying over the places and taking the (2fr)th root bounds size(I)/size(B/K) above by the geometric mean of the operator norms. The numerator is at least L/d and the denominator at most H. This proves the lower bound L/(d H) for that geometric mean. The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and the bound of operator norm by Hilbert–Schmidt norm now give ∑v ‖Ψv‖²HS ≥ f(L/(d H))².

The field trace sums twice the real part at each complex place. In Euclidean coordinates the real dual vector therefore has norm 2(∑ ‖Ψv‖²HS)1/2. Substitution into D/(2λ) gives the displayed bound. For example, over ℚ(i), multiplication by 1/2 already has integral field trace on every Gaussian integer. Its real dual vector has length one. The factor two recovers the ordinary Euclidean dual of the square lattice.

How does the map act on a quotient of the original lattice?

Let S be saturated in A, meaning that A/S has no torsion. Write a for the rank of A/S. Let the target be a sublattice R of rank b. Give the quotient its quotient metric and R its induced metric. An integral matrix on these two lattices lifts to a rational matrix on the ambient space by composing projection to the quotient, the rounded map, and inclusion of R. It kills S and sends A into R. At a real place choose orthonormal bases adapted to the source quotient and target subspace. The lifted error can be taken zero on the orthogonal complement and hence has the same sum of squared entries as its rectangular block. The bound holds for this extension of the error from the span of A. In the central application that span is the whole space. In the first layer only the error on the middle quotient is controlled at this stage.

How do we round a map on the middle quotient?

Keep the isotropic lattice R from the gap in the flag. Let W be its rational span, let Λ be the self-dual Hermitian lattice at x, and put P = Λ ∩ W⊥. Write j = dim W and n = dim V. A nilpotent infinitesimal displacement T kills W and takes W⊥ into W. Restriction to W⊥ therefore gives a map W⊥/W → W. Adding a central displacement leaves that map unchanged. The first rounding takes place in the lattice of integral maps P/R → R.

Covering estimate for maps between lattices. If R has largest normalized size at most h and every lattice M with R ⊊ M ⊆ P has quotient M/R of normalized size at least l > 0, then the restrictions of any family T as above admit one rational approximation Φ. It takes P into R and kills R. At each real place choose an extension Dᵥ of the difference (Tᵥ−Φv)|Wᵥ⊥ to the whole space. The extensions can be chosen so that

‖D‖x ≤ j(n−2j) √f d h/(2l).

This is the matrix covering bound for a quotient and a sublattice. Its dimension factor is the product of the two ranks. Nondegeneracy gives dim W⊥ = n−j, so the source has rank n−2j and the target rank j. The theorem realizes both lattices isometrically in their spans, applies a covering estimate for the pair, and carries the approximating map back by the quotient and inclusion. There is one complex place of the CM field above each real place of its totally real subfield. Thus the summed norm uses f places and the discriminant factor is the CM root discriminant d. The covering estimate for the pair of Hermitian lattices is the geometry-of-numbers input here.

Lifting the integral map. We need a skew-Hermitian matrix on all of Λ that still agrees with Φ on P. Since P is the intersection of Λ with a rational subspace, Λ/P is torsion-free. It is finitely generated over the ring of integers, a Dedekind domain, and hence projective. The quotient map therefore splits. Subtracting its splitting composed with the quotient map from the identity gives a projection π from Λ onto P which fixes P. Extend π to the rational vector space and set Ψ = Φπ. Then Ψ(Λ) ⊆ R, Ψ agrees with Φ on P, and Ψ kills W. Torsion-free finite modules over a Dedekind domain[9] · Finite locally free and projective modules[25].

Write Ψ† for the adjoint relative to the original Hermitian form. Self-duality of Λ makes Ψ† integral. Indeed ⟨z,Ψ†y⟩ = ⟨Ψz,y⟩ is integral for all y,z ∈ Λ. Moreover Ψ† kills W⊥, since Ψ has image in W. Its image lies in W⊥, since Ψ kills W. It follows that Y₀ = Ψ − Ψ† is skew-Hermitian and lowers every step of 0 ⊂ W ⊂ W⊥ ⊂ V. On P it is exactly Φ. This construction preserves integrality even at primes above two.

Isotropy makes W and JW orthogonal for the positive definite product. Let H be their joint orthogonal complement. Then JH = H and the original form has W⊥ = W ⊕ H. Let B* be the adjoint for the positive definite product. The matrix A = B − J B*J is skew-Hermitian for the original form and agrees with D on W⊥. Its second block goes from JW to H. These two blocks occupy disjoint entries in an adapted orthonormal basis, and conjugation by the unitary J preserves their Hilbert–Schmidt norms. Therefore ‖A‖HS² = 2‖B‖HS². Let J exchange the first and fourth standard basis vectors and fix the middle two. Take W spanned by the first vector and choose B with its sole unit entry in row 1, column 2. Here j = 1 and n = 4, so the rank factor 1·(4−2) = 2 attains the bound n²/8.

Passing to a finite-index sublattice can only increase that size. The ratio used in the matrix covering bound is thus h/(1/h) = h².

Why can a rational correction put the finite component in the level?

The level allows an open neighborhood of the given finite component. To find a rational point in that neighborhood, use the same nilpotent coordinates as in the rounding argument. Exponential and logarithm are inverse polynomials, exp(T) = 1 + T + T²/2 and log(1 + T) = T − T²/2. They preserve rationality and are continuous over the finite adèles. A basis of the Lie algebra over the base field F thus reduces the question to approximating one finite adèle by a number in F, independently in each coordinate.

An open condition on a finite adèle prescribes precision at finitely many primes and integrality elsewhere. Multiply by a common nonzero integer d clearing all denominators. At the selected primes prescribe the required residue of the integral numerator modulo a sufficiently high prime-ideal power. At any further prime dividing d, prescribe divisibility by the local factor of (d) to preserve integrality after division. The Chinese remainder theorem gives a single numerator in the integers of F. Dividing by d gives the required rational coordinate. Applied to all coordinates and followed by exponentiation, this supplies δ in the desired open set.

In particular n ≥ 8, the representations are unitary discrete series, and each coordinate of the Harish-Chandra parameter λ at each real place satisfies |λᵢ| ≤ b².

‖∂Xw‖ ≤ ‖X‖HS βP ‖w‖,   βP = √n b² + (3/2)n3/2 + 3P.

Here is why the dependence on P is linear. At one place write Eij for the operators representing the matrix units in the complexified Lie algebra. The compact roots eᵢ−eⱼ join two coordinates with the same signature sign. The noncompact roots join opposite signs. Let ρc and ρn be the half sums of the respective positive roots (i < j). The starting compact highest weight is Λ = λ + ρn − ρc. The counting hypotheses separate opposite-sign parameter coordinates by a common gap h ≥ 120nq3/2, where q is the real Witt index. The lowest-type multiplicity and infinitesimal-character theorems identify this compact type and give the scalar of the full quadratic Casimir operator on its generated module. Moving a compact generator past a noncompact one adds their commutator, which is again a sum of noncompact generators. Thus words of length at most P lie in the compact-stable space obtained by applying at most P noncompact generators to the starting compact type. In one such step, the tensor-product rule with the off-diagonal block permits the old compact highest weight or a shift by a root joining opposite signs. The root eᵢ−eⱼ has Euclidean norm √2. By compact-type decomposition and induction, every highest weight μ seen by order P satisfies ‖μ−Λ‖ ≤ √2P. This bound on possible compact types holds for the entire span of words.

Any two matrices in S differ multiplicatively by a matrix of operator norm at most 2 at each place. The factor ef allows a Jacobian loss of at most e at each place.

The lattice separation inequality gives a lower bound t(y)² for the geometric mean over the real places of the operator-norm distances between two distinct such matrices. To see the two factors, take the difference of the corresponding rational transformations. It sends the lattice at y into itself and has nonzero image. For such a map between lattices, the geometric mean of its local operator norms is at least the least size of the target divided by the largest size of the source. Here the target has least size τ(y). The Hermitian lattice is self-dual, so duality reverses the filtration and replaces each size by its reciprocal. The largest size of the source is 1/τ(y). Their quotient is τ(y)², which is at least t(y)² after truncation. At least one local distance is therefore ≥ t(y)². In the maximum of the local norms, the open balls of radius t(y)²/2 about the matrices are disjoint. They lie in the ball of radius 2 + t(y)²/2. Enlarging 4 to 4√n gives the bound used in the count. Dividing by the finite volume introduced above gives the cube constant

5.16Putting the words in the same row coordinates

Choose one orthonormal basis of the target, adapted to the common arithmetic row subspace, and one orthonormal basis for each full word space. Let Mu record the coordinates of Pu in those bases. In Mu∗Mv the sum over the shared row index gives exactly the inner products between the two sets of images, by Parseval. This is why the previous bounds apply simultaneously to the matrices. The unfolding volumes and dimensions give cu ≥ 0. The lower dimension proviso gives du > 0, and the scale bound gives e0 < 1. Together they force strict positivity. Indeed, when the normalizer vanishes the normalized block is defined to be zero. Its squared distance from the identity would then equal the full positive dimension.

For each word an isometric inclusion Vu selects the ramified columns, with Vu∗Vu = I. The top rows of the resulting matrix represent the rational arithmetic map after a common invertible row change and a word-dependent invertible column change. At the chosen complex place a single simultaneous conjugation may be necessary. It preserves absolute squares. Invertibility explains how to recognize the arithmetic map. Isometry explains how the selected columns sit inside the full space. The rank computation separately measures how many columns are retained.

How many independent directions do the period maps detect?

Start with one word u. Its normalized period map Au = cu−1/2Pu takes du columns into the common row space. Its Gram matrix is Kuu = Au∗Au. Choose an orthonormal basis of the kernel and extend it to the source. For each unit vector x in the kernel basis, Aux = 0 gives (Kuu − I)x = −x. It contributes exactly 1 to the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm Q(Kuu − I). The remaining basis vectors contribute nonnegative terms. By the dimension formula for a linear map,

dim ker Au ≤ Q(Kuu − I),   rank Au ≥ (1 − e0)du   if   Q(Kuu − I) ≤ e0du.

The sum over lists of minors enters the first part of this error. It gives the diagonal subseries bound Q(Buu) ≤ ξdu, where ξ = exp(−kf log k). Write D∗ for the positive reference mass of the whole row space and Γ for the family scale with log Γ = CΓm⁵fL. The complementary estimate gives Q(Kuu − Buu − I) ≤ Γdu²/D∗. The chosen word sizes satisfy duΓ²/D∗ ≤ C0. Applying ‖X + Y‖² ≤ 2‖X‖² + 2‖Y‖² gives e0 = 2ξ + 2C0/Γ. For example, the coordinate map from ℂ⁸ to ℂ⁷ that drops the last coordinate has squared error exactly 1 and rank 7. Appending zero rows leaves its Gram matrix unchanged. An upper bound for the number of available rows therefore needs additional information.

What happens when all the words share the same rows?

Write D = Dall for the dimension of the entire common row space, including the rows later discarded when the lattice map takes its top block. Let R = ∑u du count all the columns. The automorphic projection trace gives D ≤ (1 + η₁)D∗. Independently, for u ≠ v the period correlation estimate gives Q(Kuv) ≤ (1 + η₀)dudv/D∗, with Kuv = Au∗Av. To measure how many rows the columns span together, form the positive operator F = ∑u AuAu∗. Its kernel is the orthogonal complement of their span, since ⟨Fy, y⟩ = ∑u ‖Au∗y‖².

For example, take two one-column maps from ℂ to ℂ², both sending z to (z, 0). Both diagonal Gram matrices equal 1, yet the columns span just one line. Their mixed Gram entry is 1, and F has diagonal entries 2 and 0. Move the second column to (0, 1). The two diagonal Gram matrices still equal 1, but the mixed Gram entry vanishes, F becomes the identity, and the span has dimension two. In both cases tr F = 2. The second trace moment tr(F²) falls from 4 to 2 as the repeated direction is replaced by an independent one.

Cycling the factors under the trace gives tr F = ∑u tr Kuu and tr(F²) = ∑u,v Q(Kuv). Put a = √e0. On the diagonal, Cauchy–Schwarz gives |tr(Kuu − I)| ≤ √du ‖Kuu − I‖ ≤ a du, with the Hilbert–Schmidt norm throughout. The triangle inequality gives ‖Kuu‖ ≤ (1 + a)√du. Adding the distinct-word terms gives

tr F ≥ (1 − a)R,   tr(F²) ≤ (1 + η₀)R²/D∗ + (1 + a)²R.

Dimension bound. Suppose 0 < σ ≤ 1/4, D∗ > 0, R ≥ D∗/σ, −1 ≤ η₀, and η₀, η₁, a ≤ σ/2. Then the period columns span at least D/(1 + 5σ) dimensions. To see this, the lower bound for R absorbs the last summand of tr(F²) into a multiple of R²/D∗. The independent row count then gives

D tr(F²)/(tr F)² ≤ (1 + η₁)[1 + η₀ + σ(1 + a)²]/(1 − a)² ≤ 1 + 5σ.

For the last inequality, replace η₀, η₁ and a by σ/2 and multiply by (1 − σ/2)². Expanding, the right side exceeds the left by σ(16 − 52σ + 4σ² − σ³)/8, which is positive for 0 < σ ≤ 1/4. Finally let h be the rank of F. Its h positive eigenvalues sum to tr F and their squares sum to tr(F²). Cauchy–Schwarz gives (tr F)² ≤ h tr(F²), proving the claim.

This function has positive second derivative, so it lies below the chord joining its values at 0 and 1/2. Those values are 1 and (26/19)² < 2. The chord is therefore at most 1+2t. Finally 1+5σ ≤ 5/4 gives (1+5σ)(1+2t) ≤ 1+5σ+3t. Applying the same eigenvalue inequality to F′ gives the displayed rank.

For example, suppose the trace hypotheses hold with D = 100, σ = 1/100 and ρ = 1/10,000. The full span has dimension at least 100/1.05, hence at least 96. For the retained columns the denominator rises to 1.08. Their images still span at least 93 of the same 100 directions.

Put t = √ρ and L = 1 + 5σ + 3t. For the numerator, take the bound for tr(F²) before division by the first trace. Multiplying it by D, absorbing the term linear in R and using the same numerical inequality as above gives D tr((F′)²) ≤ (1 + 5σ)(1 − a)²R². Multiply this by t(1 − a) and expand the square to obtain (1 + 5σ)(1 − a)² ≤ L[1 − a − t(t + a)]². Applying the eigenvalue inequality to F′ gives the stated rank.

Restricting the columns changes the domain of the period map. Both ranks above are still measured in the space of all D rows. The map to the dual arithmetic lattice keeps only its Dar arithmetic rows. This projection has kernel of dimension D − Dar, so it can remove at most that many independent directions from any span. For example, let π project ℂ³ onto its first two coordinates. The planes spanned by (e₁, e₃) and by (e₁, e₂) both have dimension two before projection. Their images have dimensions one and two, respectively. In either case the exact loss for a plane W is dim(W ∩ ker π), by the dimension formula applied to π restricted to W.

Thus the number of missing directions among the arithmetic rows is at most the number missing among all rows. If the latter number is at most ωD and Dar ≥ (1 − δ)D with δ < 1, the missing fraction among the arithmetic rows is at most ω/(1 − δ). This is the denominator in the slope argument, where one makes a further selection of columns by slope.

5.18Counting matrices at one prime

Let q be either auxiliary prime. The number of invertible n-by-n matrices over the field of q elements is qn²Πn(q), where Πn(q) = ∏j=1n(1 − q−j). Choose the columns in order. Once i independent columns have been chosen, their span excludes precisely qi out of the qn choices for the next column. An index divides this count by the number of allowed level matrices. On the column side, these are upper triangular with diagonal entries 1. The strictly upper triangle has k(k − 1)/2 free entries.

The row has a central block of size k + 1 flanked by (m/2 − 1) singleton blocks on each side. Between different blocks all entries above the diagonal are free. Within the central block the first k positions have a free strictly upper triangle. Its final column has zeros in all k positions above its diagonal within that block. Thus the whole row matrix has r(r − 1)/2 − k free entries. Every choice has determinant one. Subtract the exponents of q in the two indices. The difference is r(r + 1)/2 + k − k(k + 1)/2 = A, where A = mk + m(m − 1)/2. The first k factors of Π cancel.

row index / column index = qA P(q),   P(q) = ∏j=k+1r(1 − q−j).

Check at q = 2, k = m = 2. The two invertible groups have orders (4 − 1)(4 − 2) = 6 and (8 − 1)(8 − 2)(8 − 4) = 168. Each level subgroup has one free binary entry, so its order is 2. The quotient of indices is 84/3 = 28, exactly 25(1 − 2−3). This checks the local identity in small ranks. The estimates for the full family use m ≥ 44.

5.20How a volume becomes a sum over lattice classes

The formula for the word scale uses the volume of a unitary group on the row side and a Hermitian genus mass on the column side. To compare ranks, we need both in the same units. A genus consists of lattices isometric at every finite place. Its mass is the sum of 1/|Aut(Λ)| over its global isometry classes. The proof starts in positive definite rank two, where the automorphism groups are finite.

Let Γ be the rational unitary group, G its adelic group and K the subgroup preserving the completed lattice at finite places and unrestricted at infinity. In the definite case the prescribed archimedean measures are probabilities. Applying the product normalization to the whole compact group at each infinite place gives μ(K) = 1. Pick representatives gi of the finite double quotient Γ∖G/K. In the class of gi, exactly |Γ ∩ giKgi−1| translates of a point by Γ land in giK. Weight that coset’s indicator by the reciprocal. Its sum over Γ is one on that class. Integrating the weighted indicators over G now gives the volume of a fundamental domain. The stabilizers are the lattice automorphism groups, so the result is the genus mass.

A finite model. Take G = S₃ and Γ = K = {1, (12)}. The two double cosets have representatives 1 and (13), with stabilizer orders 2 and 1. Their weights add to 3/2. Directly, μ(K) = 1 gives mass 1/2 to each element and a Γ-fundamental domain has three elements. This explains the inverse stabilizer in the formula. A deeper finite level K′ ⊂ K has measure 1/[K:K′]. Renormalizing that subgroup to measure one therefore multiplies the covolume by its index. In the word count the row uses its own index and the column uses its own, so their quotient is row index divided by column index.

5.21Why adjacent ranks have a predictable mass ratio

Write M for the new rank, f for the number of conjugate pairs of complex embeddings of the CM field, and v for half its root discriminant. The quadratic extension of its totally real subfield is unramified at every finite prime. For a totally positive definite integral Hermitian lattice Λ, count vectors whose squared lengths are at most j² at every embedding. Sum these counts over the genus using the reciprocal automorphism weights above. The zero vector contributes the mass μΛ. Grouping the other vectors by their represented value gives the same sum, now expressed through representation counts. Divide by j2fM and let j grow. The two ways of counting give

μΛ (πM/M!)f / (vfM δ) = (cM−1 λΛ/δ) M−f Lη(M) / √((2v)f).

On the left, πM/M! is the volume of a unit ball in ℂM, and δ is the positive square root of the absolute norm of the lattice discriminant ideal. On the right, cM−1 is the mass constant for the preceding rank, λΛ is a product of local lattice corrections, and Lη(M) is the Euler product of the CM field. This second limit uses the representation-density formula and the asymptotic sum of its local factors. The zero vector’s separate contribution tends to zero after division. Cancel δ and use M!/M = (M − 1)!. For a lattice with an orthonormal integral basis every local lattice correction is one. The two standard masses consequently satisfy the following identity for the ranks M ≥ 3 used here.

massM / massM−1 = [((M − 1)!)(v/π)M]f Lη(M) / √((2v)f).

For instance, take M = 3 and a finite prime of the totally real subfield of residue size 2. If it is inert, the unique prime above it has norm 4 and its Euler factor is (1 + 2−3)−1 = 8/9. If it splits, its two primes of norm 2 each contribute (1 − 2−3)−1/2, giving 8/7 together. These are factors at a single prime. Across the rank increments, the same positive rank-one constant occurs in both standard masses and cancels in their ratio.

To reach the indefinite row, the normalized unit-vector unfolding supplies the same ratio for a space and the orthogonal complement of a vector of norm +1 or −1. From definite rank two, use +1 to compare successive positive definite ranks. For a constant signature (P, Q) with P ≥ 2, induction on Q uses a −1 vector, whose complement has signature (P, Q − 1). The two inductions identify the row volume with the standard mass of its rank r. In the word-scale formula the column mass then cancels the common ranks, leaving exactly the increments M = k + 1, …, r. These are the factors estimated in the lower bound for each word.

The mass identity tells us the scale Xu for each word u. How small can that scale be, even for the least favorable word? Put G = log(g0g1) and L = xε. There are f infinite places ρ and m positive weights wjρ at each. Their contribution is S = (1/f)∑ρ∑j log(wjρv/π), where v is half the root discriminant. 5.23What survives in the quotient of dimensions?

Fix a place. Write its row as λ = (c0, …, ck−2, −b0, …, −bm−1) of length r = k + m − 1. Its first block is nonnegative and decreases in steps of at least one. The bj are positive and increase in steps of at least one. The column u0 > ⋯ > uk−1 belonging to the word interlaces the first block, with ui > ci > ui+1. Write V(y) = ∏i<j(yi − yj). Each cross-block gap ci + bj is at least bj, and each gap within the negative block is at least one. This proves the first inequality below.

V(λ) ≥ V(c)∏j bjk−1,   V(u) ≤ D2k−3V(c),   D = 8xeL.

For the second inequality, the column has k − 1 gaps touching its first entry and another k − 2 touching its last. Each is at most D. Each remaining gap ui − uj is bounded by the distinct gap ci−1 − cj. The unused adjacent gaps of c are at least one. Dividing the inequalities now cancels the factor V(c). For a small check take c = (4, 0), u = (6, 2, −1) and b = (3, 5). The row has gap product 7,560, the column has gap product 84, and their ratio is 90. This example illustrates the interlacing calculation alone.

The local factor in the mass identity is dρFr/V(u), with formal degree dρ and Fr = ∏h=0r−1h!. At the required separation between parameters of opposite signature, the discrete-series estimate with tolerance 1/3 gives dρ ≥ (2/3)V(λ)/Fr by Weyl’s dimension formula. Thus the row factorials cancel as well. The source allows a logarithmic loss of 2k log D + 2k(1 + log k) in the Vandermonde comparison. At the family threshold, 2(log 8 + 1 + log x) ≤ L and log(2k) ≤ L, so this loss is at most 5kL.

5.24Adding the losses in the mass identity

The geometric weights satisfy 0 < bj < wjρ ≤ (1 + 1/x)bj and wjρ ≤ 2eL. Then k log w − (k − 1) log b = log w + (k − 1) log(w/b) ≤ 2L + k/x. Each rank increment M = k + 1, …, r contributes a positive mass Euler product Lη(M). Group its local logarithms by the rational prime p. A prime ideal of residue degree d above p contributes at most (d/2)[−log(1 − p−M)] in absolute value. The residue degrees above p sum to at most the field degree 2f. Summing over p gives |log Lη(M)| ≤ f log ζ(M) ≤ f, since M ≥ 2. Averaging over the f places leaves a total cost at most m − 1 for the r − k rank increments.

Subtract S + mG from log Xu and multiply by k. In the mass identity the surplus m(m − 1)[log(v/π) + G]/2 is nonnegative. The two remaining discriminant terms cost at most kL + (m − 1)L/2, using 0 ≤ log(v/π) ≤ L and log(2v) ≤ L. The two auxiliary primes together cost at most 2. Add these amounts to the place and Euler losses.

8kL + (m − 1)L/2 + m + 2 + k ≤ 11kL,   log Xu ≥ S + mG − 11L.

Indeed, (m − 1)L/2 ≤ kL/2 and m + 2 + k ≤ 5kL/2 because 44 ≤ m ≤ k and L ≥ 1. For fixed family and constants ε > 0, C0, CY, a single threshold works for every admissible scale above it, every family index, every choice of spacing and weights satisfying the stated data, and every word. 5.25Why a real-place degree has the size of a Vandermonde product

The placewise mass estimate compares a row with the column belonging to a word. The row supplies a discrete series of the real unitary group U(p, q), an irreducible unitary representation σ with square-integrable matrix coefficients. For a nonzero vector w, its formal degree is ‖w‖4 divided by the integral of |⟨w, σ(g)w⟩|2. Multiplying the Haar measure by a positive number divides the degree by that number. The numerical comparison therefore requires a specific measure.

Let N = p + q with both signs present. The parameter λ has strictly decreasing entries indexed from 0, with λi − (N−1)/2 integral. Each index carries a sign, with p positive and q negative. Write Fn = ∏0≤a<na! and V(λ) = ∏i<j(λi − λj). On the normalized measure one has the following equality for the large-gap parameters used here.

d(λ) = V(λ)/FN,   FN = ∏i<j(j−i).

5.26How an integral fixes the missing constant

Imagine moving λ by integer steps. When an admissible step raises one coordinate by one, the degree and the Vandermonde change by exactly the same ratio. Along λi(t) = λi + t(N−1−i), for integers t ≥ 0, the steps can be ordered so that decreasing order and the gap survive. Thus d(λ(t))/V(λ(t)) stays constant. To find its value, let Tt be the lowest compact type, the finite-dimensional representation of U(p) × U(q) selected by the weight λ(t). Form Yt = tpq dim(Tt)/d(λ(t)).

Put A = ∏(j−i) over opposite-sign pairs i<j. On the algebraic side the compact Weyl dimension formula cancels the same-sign factors of the moving Vandermonde up to ratios tending to one. Indeed, if the moving gap is g, its ratio is (g+b)/g, where b counts opposite signs strictly between the indices. Each opposite-sign pair leaves t/[λi−λj+t(j−i)], tending to 1/(j−i).

On the analytic side, polar coordinates use probability measure on the compact group and one complex coordinate per opposite-sign pair. The Haar density includes the constant c = FN/(πpqFpFq). Rescaling each complex coordinate by 1/√t absorbs tpq. The limiting squared coefficient has a Gaussian factor exp(−(j−i)|z|²) in each coordinate, whose plane integral is π/(j−i). The coefficient supplies a lower limit and an integrable upper bound supplies the matching upper limit. Comparing the two values of the same limit gives the stated degree.

V(λ)/[d(λ)FpFqA] = lim Yt = cπpq/A = FN/(FpFqA).

5.28An upper bound for the scale of every word

Relative variation alone can leave all the words equally large. To bound their absolute scale, start again from the mass identity used for the lower bound. It gives fk log Xu as a sum of six terms. For an upper bound, a term of known negative sign can be discarded. The remaining positive contributions must be estimated even when the word and the family member vary. Assume 44 ≤ m ≤ k, r = k + m − 1, L ≥ 9 and log(2k) ≤ L. Write CY for the bound log gi ≤ CYL on each of the two auxiliary primes. The following budget is divided throughout by fkmL, so its sum bounds log Xu/(mL).

  • The coefficient of log(v/π) is f[(m − 1)k + m(m − 1)/2]. Since 0 ≤ log(v/π) ≤ L and m ≤ k, the normalized contribution is at most 3/2. The term in −log(2v) is nonpositive.
  • At most m Euler values enter. Each logarithm is at most f by the comparison with ζ(M) at integers M ≥ 2. Together they cost at most 1/(kL). The finite corrections log(1 − gi−j) are nonpositive.
  • The positive prime term has coefficient fm(2k + m − 1)/2. Since log(g0g1) ≤ 2CYL, it costs at most 3CY.
  • At each infinite place, separate the logarithm of the ratio of representation dimensions from the factorial products in Weyl’s formula. The gap estimate for the real-place degree and the column estimate bound the first by km(log 3 + 5 log(2k) + 5L + 10). For the factorials there are r − k additional factors j!. Each is at most rr. Since r ≤ 2k, their logarithms total at most 2kmL. Summing over f places costs at most 12/L + 12 after normalization.

These four bounds imply

log Xu/(mL) ≤ 3/2 + 1/(kL) + 3CY + 12/L + 12 ≤ 15 + 3CY.

For the last inequality even the looser k ≥ 5 suffices. The constants independent of CY sum to at most 3/2 + 1/45 + 4/3 + 12 = 1337/90, strictly below 15. Take the maximum of the thresholds for this estimate, the lower estimate, the real-place gap and the mass inputs. Thus the same threshold works for all words. To pass to the chosen prime Tu, its window has center XuΓ−2/(fk) and upper multiplicative allowance 1 + 1/(fk). With Γ ≥ 1 this gives log Tu ≤ log Xu + 1. The construction absorbs the additive allowance into its common counting constant. The existence of a prime in the window is a separate arithmetic input.

The term Ωlog in the main-term calculation has a geometric meaning. At a single complex embedding, the norm of a generator of a differential line depends on the generator and the elliptic lattice. 5.30Which changes of scale cancel?

Let K0 be the imaginary quadratic host field of discriminant −dK, and E the extension used in the host. Take a nonzero integral ideal 𝔠 of K0 with norm prime to 2dK. If Δ is the discriminant of its embedded elliptic lattice and δ12 = Δ, the rescaled lattice Λ = δ·φ0(𝔠) has discriminant one. Take any number field M inside ℂ containing the specified images of E and the Weierstrass invariants g2(Λ), g3(Λ). For each embedding ρ of M, transport those two invariants and let Aρ > 0 be the area of the corresponding period lattice.

Fix a host embedding label τ. The source spans the vectors of conjugates of elements of the host fractional ideal and intersects the resulting module with the τ-coordinate line. Write ℓτ for the resulting module inside M and DM = [M : ℚ]. For a nonzero s in ℓτ, put I(s) = [ℓτ : 𝒪Ms]. The measured quantity is

mρ(s) = log(π |ρ(s)|² / Aρ),   Ω̄τ = (2 log I(s) − ∑ρ mρ(s)) / DM.

When ℓτ has generator a, every such s has form ca with 0 ≠ c ∈ 𝒪M. The index is |NM/ℚ(c)|. Meanwhile each local logarithm increases by 2 log |ρ(c)|. Their sum increases by twice the logarithm of precisely that index. Thus Ω̄τ equals the average of −mρ(a). For a small check, take the free line ℤ[i] and use the test element s = 1 + i. Its multiples form a sublattice of index 2. Each of the two embeddings contributes an extra log 2, cancelling the finite contribution 2 log 2. This example checks the normalization in a free line.

5.31Why the root discriminant appears

Write n = [E : ℚ], h = [E : K0] = n/2. Let b be the absolute norm of the product of the host fractional ideal with the relative different of E/K0. The ideal-index calculation gives I(s)n bDM = |NM/ℚ(s)|n. Taking logarithms and summing the local metrics eliminates the norm of s. Hence

Ω̄τ = (1/DM) ∑ρ log(Aρ/π) − (2/n) log b.

Set B equal to the absolute norm of the relative different. Its half-different identity gives b² = B. The discriminant tower formula gives |disc(E)| = B(dK)h. Since rd(E) = |disc(E)|1/n, the correction (2/n) log b equals log rd(E) − log √dK.

For the area term the proof compares the conjugate lattices with a family indexed by ideal classes. Over a common extension their homotheties give 6 log Aoriginal = 6 log Afamily + log |ρ(u)|, with u a discriminant unit. The unit contributes zero to the sum over embeddings. Averaging over the extension gives the same mean as over M, because each embedding occurs with the same multiplicity. The Chowla–Selberg class-sum formula then evaluates the area mean as γ + log(2π/√dK) − dχ, where dχ = Re(L′(1,χ)/L(1,χ)) for the host quadratic character. This dχ is the scalar denoted d in the main-term calculation above. Subtracting the correction cancels log √dK. For every compatible M and every τ this gives

Ω̄τ = γ + log(2π/rd(E)) − dχ = Ωlog.

This identifies the scalar that occurs earlier with v = rd(E)/2. The calculation uses the CM family of period lattices, the Chowla–Selberg evaluation and the ideal-index formula as inputs.

6Theta lifts, local factors and the Galois input

How can a theorem attaching Galois representations in odd dimension give one in even dimension? Lift the same automorphic representation twice to a larger odd rank, adding different character lists each time. The shared part can then be recovered. Both global theta integrals must produce a nonzero form for this argument to start.

What is being lifted? · Two parallel lifts · Recovering the even-dimensional row · The iterated chain · Whittaker factors · Split and inert places · The finite test vector · Real places · Continuation · Split lattice calculation · Inert cell calculation

6.1What is being lifted?

A Hermitian form measures lengths using both a field and its conjugation. On two complex coordinates the example is ⟨x,y⟩ = x₁y₁ + x₂y₂. Its unitary group consists of the changes of coordinates preserving this pairing. For a number field we can make such a change at each place. An adelic group element collects these choices, integral at almost every finite place. A rational change of coordinates gives the same change simultaneously in all completions.

An automorphic form here is a function on the adelic group, invariant under those rational changes on the left and satisfying additional finiteness and regularity conditions. Translating its argument on the right produces a space of functions carrying a group action. The irreducible space being lifted is U, and φ is one vector in it. A theta kernel converts φ into a function on another group by integration. To show that this conversion retains some information, one proves that a resulting vector has positive squared norm. At a good finite prime the commuting Hecke operators then provide a list of spectral parameters, with multiplicities, which can be compared on the two sides.

6.2Two parallel lifts to odd rank

Let E be a CM field, a totally imaginary quadratic extension of its totally real subfield F. The version used here assumes that E/F is unramified at all finite places, that E contains a square root of a negative rational integer, and that [F : ℚ] is even. At every nonsplit finite place the underlying prime of F has odd residue characteristic, norm greater than three and does not divide the absolute different of F. Take an even rank n ≥ 1 and an automorphic representation U of the definite unitary group of rank n. Fix its highest weights λ at the complex embeddings and a finite split place w₀ of E.

For a Hermitian source with identity Gram matrix and signature (n, 0), the lifting theorem gives a rank threshold d₀. The proof chooses t = 2(d₀ + n) + 1. Both targets are definite skew-Hermitian models of rank D = n + t, an odd integer above the threshold. Each lift uses its own compatible pair of splitting Hecke characters. The proof takes a common lower bound b for the components of λ at the chosen complex embedding above each real place and chooses their target exponents so that mW,j(v) ≤ 2b − D. Thus every required archimedean inequality D + mW,j(v) ≤ 2λv,k holds. Applying the same rank theorem once for each pair produces U₁ and U₂.

There is one common algebraic Hecke character κ, and two lists ψj,h of t algebraic Hecke characters. No character from the first list equals any character from the second as a global character. At a split place w where κ and list j are unramified and U has a Satake multiset, write B(w) for its algebraically normalized eigenvalues. Unramified means the character is trivial on local units. Its value at a uniformizer is then well defined. The target eigenvalues obey the following multiset identity, with multiplicities retained.

Bj(w) = κ(w)−1B(w) ⊔ {ψj,h(w) ∣ 0 ≤ h < t}.

At infinity the target weight jumps are the union of the original jumps shifted by the weight of κ and the negatives of the weights of the added characters. At the chosen w₀ the construction specifically guarantees that κ and every member of list 1 are unramified. Distinct global characters can agree in value at an individual prime. The proof compares their associated global Galois characters.

6.3Why each global theta lift is nonzero

The lifting theorem first obtains a real threshold L for integrability of a height power against Haar measure. Taking an integer N > 2L and d₀ = max(N, 2n) gives both D ≥ 2n and L < D/2. For splitting characters with the prescribed restrictions and archimedean exponents, the real-place pairing supplies a nonzero vector f∞ in the Weil model and a nonzero automorphic form φ with matching type. The outstanding choice is the finite-place Schwartz vector ffin.

Let ω be the Weil representation of the source and target adelic unitary groups on test functions on adelic n-by-D matrices over F. For a source group element g and a target element h, its theta kernel sums the translated test function over rational matrices, diagonally embedded into the adeles. With DX the model’s source integration domain, the lift of φ is the function of h given by

Θ(Φ, φ)(h) = ∫DX (∑ξ∈Matn×D(F) [ω(g, h)Φ](ξ)) φ(g) dμ(g).

This convention conjugates the source form. The matrix coefficient used to test nonvanishing pairs ω(g, 1)Φ with Φ using additive Haar measure on the adelic matrix space. The source coefficient pairs the right translate of φ with φ on DX.

Set Φ = f∞ ⊗ ffin. Write cΦ(g) for the Weil matrix coefficient and mφ(g) for the source matrix coefficient. The Rallis input says the following integral converges and must vanish if the theta transform of (Φ, φ) is identically zero.

I(Φ, φ) = ∫ cΦ(g) mφ(g) dg.

Choose a finite set S containing enough places to control the level of φ, the ramification and the tail estimate. Use a local bump vector at each place of S and the model's vacuum vector elsewhere. The proof decomposes the integral into archimedean, finite-in-S and outside-S factors. The Schur calculation supplies a nonzero scalar and the chosen coefficient is nonzero at the identity. A compact open set of positive measure supplies the main contribution. A bound on the outside-S tail gives the strict estimate that prevents cancellation. This proves I(Φ, φ) ≠ 0 for the chosen data. The resulting theta transform is an automorphic form. An equivariant projection onto an automorphic constituent preserves a nonzero component, yielding a target representation to which the weight and local-parameter statements apply. Thus the contribution from K has absolute value rμ(K), strictly larger than the maximum possible contribution from its complement. The other factors are a positive Haar volume and a nonzero scalar.

6.4Recovering the even-dimensional representation

To see the danger in subtracting eigenvalues at just one prime, take the cyclic group of order four generated by g. The two characters taking g to 1 and −1 agree at g². A list of values at g² cannot tell which character was added. Once two semisimple representations have been identified as representations of the entire group, one can compare the multiplicities of each irreducible constituent and subtract known character lines. The argument below explains how the good primes supply that global comparison.

Apply the available odd-rank Galois theorem twice, each time in dimension D. It attaches continuous semisimple ℓ-adic representations ρ₁ and ρ₂ to U₁ and U₂. Let χj,h be the ℓ-adic character attached to ψj,h, and Pj(g, X) the characteristic polynomial of ρj(g). Injectivity of the Hecke-to-Galois character map preserves disjointness across the two lists. Comparing normalized Frobenius data at good split places and using density gives, for every Galois element g,

P₁(g, X) ∏h(X − χ2,h(g)) = P₂(g, X) ∏h(X − χ1,h(g)).

The representations ρ₁ ⊕ ⨁χ2,h and ρ₂ ⊕ ⨁χ1,h consequently have the same characteristic polynomials. The proof uses semisimplicity and a one-character splitting theorem to separate a line χ1,h from ρ₁ and retain a comparison identity for the complement. Induction removes all t lines, preserving continuity, semisimplicity and the required local conditions. The remaining dimension is D − t = n. Tensoring with the ℓ-adic character of κ restores the original normalization. Given a source Satake multiset at w₀, unramifiedness of the first list supplies the local conclusion there. Repeating the construction at each split place gives weakly compatible representations. Their isomorphism transports the local conclusions to a common representation.

The strong local–global statement attaches a continuous semisimple ℓ-adic representation of dimension a to regular algebraic polarized cuspidal data on GLa over a CM field. It includes comparisons away from ℓ and Hodge–Tate data above ℓ. Its closing proof supplies the global theta-lift theorem to the geometry construction. The intervening proof combines the two-lift input with odd-rank geometry, congruence and a limiting argument, then passes to the local–global statement.

A separate calculation in the long-chain application concerns a single row and its adjoint. It has its own rank variables and its own hypothesis ensuring that the lifted row survives.

6.5The row and its adjoint

An automorphic form is a function on an arithmetic quotient of a group with specified transformation and regularity properties. A theta lift uses an integral kernel to carry such functions between groups. In the part of the proof examined here, the relevant spaces of forms at fixed level and weight are presented as finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces. This allows a precise question about nonvanishing before any local representation is identified.

Fix an index i. It specifies a row number j and a tuple of character data μ. Suppress these two subscripts. Write M for the row space and V for the target space. There is a linear map P from V to M. Its adjoint T goes from M to V. The row space has designated subspaces Mσ for its types σ. A type here labels a component of the space of forms. The target has subspaces Vπ for target types π.

The required Gram hypothesis says that PT acts by a real scalar λσ on Mσ, strictly positive whenever Mσ is nonzero. For every f in that subspace the adjoint identity gives

‖Tf‖2 = Re ⟨f, PTf⟩ = λσ ‖f‖2.

Thus a nonzero row vector survives the upward map. Positive semidefiniteness, which is automatic for an operator times its adjoint, would only yield λσ ≥ 0. Strict positivity is a genuine arithmetic input. The point-condition construction gets the local scalars from its linked isotropy and scalar hypotheses before calling the pairing theorem.

6.6Locating one target type

Call σ and π paired if there are f ∈ Mσ and v ∈ Vπ with ⟨v, Tf⟩ ≠ 0. Assume that the target subspaces span V, are pairwise orthogonal, and that for each σ at most one π can pair with it. The uniqueness property is the upward form of Howe duality in this argument.

Choose nonzero f in Mσ. If every target component were orthogonal to Tf, their span would also be orthogonal to it. This would force ⟨Tf, Tf⟩ = 0, contrary to the Gram identity. Some π therefore pairs with σ. Now take any g in the same row subspace. A nonzero inner product of Tg with a different component would supply a second paired type, contrary to uniqueness. Since the orthogonal components span V, Tg lies in Vπ. The entire image T(Mσ) is a nonzero subspace of Vπ.

6.7Reading the parameter at a split place

Work with a CM field, a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real number field. At a finite place of the real field which splits into two places in the CM field, the relevant unitary groups have local descriptions by general linear groups. Write K for the local field at the chosen place. The source rank is r = k + m − 1 and the target rank is r + t. The rank data impose r + 5 ≤ t. In particular r < t, the inequality used in the local classification theorem. These are dimensions of underlying linear groups. The spaces of automorphic forms in the Gram calculation can have different dimensions.

A representation assigns an invertible linear action to each group element. A smooth representation of a group over K is one in which each vector is fixed by an open subgroup. An irreducible representation has no proper nonzero invariant subspace. Unitarisability asks for an invariant positive inner product. The classification step takes a smooth, irreducible, unitarisable representation τ of GLr(K), a smooth irreducible representation Π of GLr+t(K), and a smooth unitary character μ of K×. Its pairing hypothesis asks for a nonzero equivariant bilinear map on test functions and vectors. The test functions are locally constant and compactly supported on the space of (r + t)-by-r matrices. Equivariance says that acting on the function and the target vector is compatible with the source group action. The actual comparison applies this condition to a determinant twist of the target representation.

Given the stated inputs on finiteness and irreducibility of induced representations, the local theorem identifies Π with the parabolically induced product of τ and μ ∘ det on GLt(K). Parabolic induction here uses the subgroup of upper block triangular matrices, with diagonal blocks of sizes r and t. These blocks act on the tensor product of the two input representations. The construction extends this action to the full group by induction. In the application, Π is the twisted target and the comparison removes the twist afterward.

What information survives on the Galois side? A local parameter records the local representation in a form with well-defined direct sums and twists by characters. At each split place w, let Aw denote the source parameter and μw the parameter of the character. Write μw[b] for its real-power twist with exponent b. Let ηw−1 denote the final inverse character in this normalization. The paired target has parameter

(Aw ⊕ ⨁0≤h<t μw[(t − 1)/2 − h]) ⊗ ηw−1.

There are t one-dimensional terms. Their exponents decrease by one from (t − 1)/2 to −(t − 1)/2. They account for the entire increase in rank. The parameter-translation laws turn the induced product into a sum, identify the segment for μ ∘ det, and then remove the determinant twist to give η⁻¹ on the full sum.

A rank check. If k = 6, m = 2 and t = 13, the rank formula gives r = 7 and target rank 20. The extra block has 13 character terms with exponents 6, 5, …, −6. This is an example of the rank arithmetic. Choosing the three integers supplies none of the automorphic forms or nonzero pairings needed by the theorem.

The parallel arrows above recover a Galois representation. The following successive arrows serve a different purpose. One needs a downward map onto an entire space of functions. Nonvanishing on a basis alone is insufficient. For the map (x,y) ↦ x + y, both coordinate vectors survive and their difference dies. The proof must also distinguish the images of different labels. That distinction gives injectivity in the upward direction and hence surjectivity for its finite-dimensional adjoint.

The upward integral uses the conjugate theta kernel against F. A local zeta nonvanishing theorem supplies φ and v for which an integral I of Weil and source matrix coefficients, over elements integral outside S, is nonzero. This already forces F ≠ 0. Let L₀ be the holomorphic value at s = t/2 of the partial, twisted function LS(s + ½). The Hecke form of the doubling identity gives the Petersson square of the conjugate upward lift.

⟨ΘφF, ΘφF⟩ = vol(Yj+1) · L₀ · I / dS(t/2).

The volume of the target quotient is positive. The partial normalizing factor dS(t/2) is nonzero. Once L₀ ≠ 0, all factors on the right are nonzero. A zero lift would give a zero Petersson square.

Why L₀ is nonzero at this step. The proof starts from the parameter family at stage zero with the prescribed half-rank bound. It twists that family by a unitary character. Its Euler product converges and is nonzero at (t + 1)/2 because t ≥ r + 5. Each previous step also contributed a length-t segment. For its index a, with 1 ≤ a ≤ j, the corresponding quotient character is μa μj+1−1. The proof uses the distinct infinity exponents of these characters to obtain an entire partial L-function nonzero at every integer from 1 through t. At the desired point the segment arguments are

t/2 + ½ + (t − 1)/2 − h = t − h,   0 ≤ h < t.

Thus the last segment factor is evaluated at 1, where absolute Euler-product convergence alone would leave a gap. The quotient-character theorem covers that endpoint. Multiplying the twisted initial factor by the finite product of segment factors gives a holomorphic continuation near t/2 with nonzero value L₀. At stage zero the segment product is empty.

Finite-dimensionality and the positive Hermitian metric now give x ∈ Cj+1 satisfying ⟨y, x⟩j+1 = ⟨pjy, u⟩j for all y. The span of target evaluations and the adjoint pairing identify the nonzero lift above with an actual evaluation x(w₀). Consequently x ≠ 0. Local transfer identifies its parameter family outside S. With α and β the source and target character values at a place w, it multiplies each member of B(w) by α/β and appends the multiset of t terms α qw(t−1)/2−h. Here qw is the residue-field size. The induction applies the same argument to x with this new family.

For each chain of length at most m satisfying these hypotheses, the downward composite maps onto C₀. Write a possible kernel vector as a sum of simultaneous eigenvectors and group the terms whose parameters agree outside the excluded places. Inside one group the sum again has those eigenvalues. If that sum is nonzero, the nonvanishing theorem applies to the sum itself, even if its eigenspace has dimension greater than one. Across different groups the parameter update is injective and the resulting eigenspaces are linearly independent. Their images can add to zero only if every grouped component was zero. 6.11Where the quotient volume comes from

Doubling puts the two copies of the source in a single hyperbolic space. There is a test vector Δ(Φ₁, Φ₂) on the doubled space whose kernel on the embedded pair (g₁, g₂) recovers the product of the original kernels. Extending the section by the height contributes exactly h(g)s−s₀. The determinant character explains the inverse twist in the doubling integral.

Siegel–Weil identifies the normalized mean of the doubled theta kernel with an Eisenstein value at s₀. For b ≤ 2a the proof invokes the convergent-range theorem with a + w < b, where w is the dimension of a maximal totally isotropic subspace of B. For b > 2a, the series identity applies in the convergence region s₀ > a/2. When the two source integrals are paired, the squared norm of each kernel on the target grows at most polynomially. Cuspidal rapid decay makes the absolute triple integral finite, so the target pairing can be performed first. Converting the normalized target mean into the Petersson integral multiplies it by vol([H]). This produces a holomorphic continuation value of the full doubling integral. The proof first works at the frame lattice, then transfers it to the given self-dual lattice.

At the identity, let hγ be the positive height of a representative of a rational Siegel coset. The spherical section to be summed has magnitude hγT, with T = Re s + a/2. Arithmetic reduction assigns to each coset a tuple j of a nonnegative integers. For a base B > 1 and a constant C, its height is at most C B−∑j. For any fixed tuple the number of cosets in any finite sample with this label is at most C Ba∑j. Multiplying those bounds gives a bound for the whole label.

∑γ with label j hγT ≤ C1+T (Ba−T)∑j.

For T > a, summing over the tuple gives a product of a geometric series with common ratio Ba−T < 1. This bounds every finite subsum, establishing summability of the nonnegative spherical majorant. Iwasawa decomposition and the bound for the section on the compact subgroup transfer convergence to the flat section and its translates. The terms vary holomorphically in s through powers of positive heights. Choose a small vertical strip around the point, with both edges inside the half-plane. Each term is bounded in absolute value throughout the strip by the sum of its absolute values at the two endpoint real parts, since a positive height raised to a real exponent is monotone in that exponent. Both endpoint majorants are summable. The holomorphic terms therefore converge locally uniformly.

If the last nonzero orthogonal coordinate of a lattice vector x is its jth, then x lies outside the previous span. To allow for tied minima, let k be the first index with λk = λj. If x were shorter, it and the first k − 1 vectors would give k independent vectors shorter than λk. Thus ‖x‖ ≥ λj. Every nonzero coordinate of x is scaled by at least 1/λj. Thus ‖Tx‖ ≥ 1.

The inverse image of the open unit ball under T contains no nonzero lattice point. Its volume is vol(ball)·∏λj. By the symmetric convex body bound this is at most 2rcovol(L). To see the volume threshold, shrink the body by one half. If it had more volume than a fundamental cell of L, two of its translates into that cell would overlap. The difference of the two original points would be a nonzero lattice vector in the original body, by convexity and symmetry. The unit ball contains the open cube of side 2/√r, in orthonormal coordinates. For r ≥ 1 these observations give

λ₁ ⋯ λr ≤ rr/2 covol(L).

The covolume is taken in the real span of L. For an integral basis u with image under the row map φ, it is √det Gram(φu).

Take one row from each block of D minima. Suppose we have selected i rows independent over E. Their field span has dimension Di over ℚ. The ball of radius λDi+1 contains Di + 1 real-independent lattice vectors. Lift them through φ to integral combinations of the original rows. A rational relation between the lifts would, after clearing denominators, be an integral relation between the independent images. At least one lift therefore lies outside the previous field span. Choose it as the next row wi+1. Since the minima increase, the first radius in each block, raised to the power D, is bounded by the product of the D radii in that block. Consequently

∏i=1n ‖φwi‖D ≤ ∏k=0n−1 λDk+1D ≤ λ₁ ⋯ λr.

Here φ is only required to be additive and ℤ-linear. It sends a row to its archimedean coordinates after the given change of variables. The dimension argument takes place over E before applying φ.

Why are the inverses of the normalized blocks bounded?

Choose a dyadic scale ai with ‖φwi‖ ≤ ai < 2‖φwi‖. Dividing each row by its scale bounds every entry of the resulting matrix c. Take all D integral-basis multiples of each of the n selected rows. They span a full-rank sublattice of the original row lattice, of index m ≥ 1. Its squared volume is m² det Gram(φu). Each of the D real rows coming from wi carries the same scale ai. With G(c) the Gram determinant of all the rescaled rows, we get

(m covol(L))² = (∏ aiD)² G(c).

The product of the scales is bounded in the form ∏ aiD ≤ 2rrr/2 covol(L). Cancel the covolume. This bounds m² by a constant times G(c). Since m ≥ 1, it also bounds G(c) away from zero. On the bounded closed set of matrix entries this continuous determinant has a finite upper bound. Its positive lower bound keeps c in an invertible compact set, where inversion is bounded. The upper bound gives a uniform bound for the integer m. Taking the factorial of an integer upper bound makes one integer M divisible by every possible m. Multiplication by M therefore puts every original row in the module generated by the selected rows.
