Use the same rows at every finite place. Write Ō for the product of the local integer rings at finite places. Given the finite adelic block β, take Λ = {x ∈ En ∣ xβ ∈ Ōn}. An integer clearing the denominators of β shows that Λ contains a multiple of every coordinate row. Clearing the denominators of β−1 bounds Λ inside one fractional free module. As the ring of integers is Noetherian, Λ is finitely generated. Apply the argument at infinity to Λ and call the selected row matrix Δ. The entries of Δβ are integral by construction. For its inverse, choose positive integers d₁,d₂ clearing the denominators of β and Δ−1, respectively. Approximate a row of β−1 by a rational row x so that their difference belongs to d₁d₂Ōn. Multiplying by β shows that xβ is integral. Hence x belongs to Λ, and Mx is an integral combination of the rows of Δ. Multiplication by Δ−1 gives integral entries for MxΔ−1. The original approximation error still has integral entries after multiplication by MΔ−1. This proves that M(Δβ)−1 is integral at every finite place. Together with the compact real block this is the uniform reduction used for the height label.

Why the second row can require the third minimum

Use E = ℚ(i), n = 2, and the ordinary Euclidean norm on ℂ². Let the finite block be diag(1,1/3) above 3 and the identity elsewhere. Its rational row lattice is Λ = ℤ[i]e₁ ⊕ 3ℤ[i]e₂. The first two independent real vectors can be e₁ and ie₁. They span just one line over E. Every row outside that line has length at least 3, attained by 3e₂. The four real minima are 1,1,3,3. The two chosen field rows have squared lengths 1 and 9, whose product equals the covolume 9. The dyadic scales 1 and 4 give the real block diag(1,3/4). Its inverse is diag(1,4/3). With Δ = diag(1,3), the finite block Δβ is the identity above 3 and diag(1,3) elsewhere. Both matrices and their inverses have integral entries at the places where they occur.

Count the centres for a fixed label. At scalar depth k, subtract a rational element from an adele of F to put it in a fixed compact set. Bound its real components in absolute value by a nonnegative integer R. At each real place use the grid 2−kℤ between −R and R. Its integer numerators have exactly 2·2kR + 1 possibilities. Rounding leaves an error of size at most 2−k. The finite component stays in a fixed compact set. Across the d real places the number of scalar centres is bounded by C₀ bk, where b = 2d, C₀ = (2R + 1)d and B = b².

Choose δ in E with conjugate −δ so that (1,δ) is an F-basis. A skew-Hermitian matrix S can be described by n² scalar adelic coordinates tij. Its (i,j) entry is (tij−tji) + δ(tij+tji). On the diagonal this is 2δtii. Off the diagonal the two ordered entries share two scalar coordinates. Cover tij at depth μi+μj. Its error then carries the factor corresponding to the left and right diagonal scalings. Combining the coordinate choices writes S as a rational matrix plus a centre y plus DμωDμ, where Dμ = diag(sμᵢ) and the entries of ω lie in a fixed compact set. The finite set Yμ of centres is the image of the product of the scalar grids. Its size is at most the number of grid tuples.

|Yμ| ≤ ∏i,j C₀ bμᵢ+μⱼ = C₀n² b2n∑μᵢ = C₀n² Bn∑μᵢ.

A rank-two count. Take one real place, a scalar grid with R = 1 and label μ = (1,0). The four ordered depths are 2, 1, 1 and 0. The corresponding lists of integer numerators have 9, 5, 5 and 3 entries. Their product gives 675 tuples. The formula above permits 3⁴·4² = 1,296. These numbers count candidates and bound their image. Counting rational cosets still requires the multiplicity argument.

Why a centre has bounded multiplicity. Subtract the rational unipotent term and put the compact error into a matrix w(q). In the Cayley coordinates the proof obtains a rational invertible matrix Z(q) = z(μ,y)w(q), with w(q) in a fixed compact set. The map q ↦ Z(q) is injective. In fact, equality of two such matrices makes the original rational representatives differ on the left by an element stabilizing the diagonal subspace. They represent the same Siegel coset.

Fix μ and a centre y. For a nonempty finite collection of cosets using them, choose one member q₀. Multiplying by Z(q₀)−1 cancels the common left factor z(μ,y). The relative matrices w(q₀)−1w(q) are rational and belong to a fixed compact set, independent of μ, y and q₀. Each matrix entry belongs to a finite set of rational points, so there are at most N possible relative matrices. Left multiplication preserves injectivity. Each chosen centre can therefore account for at most N cosets. Summing over all available centres gives an upper bound even when some centres are unused and others occur for multiple cosets.

#{q ∈ A with label μ} ≤ N |Yμ| ≤ N C₀n² Bn∑μᵢ   for every finite sample A.

A uniform finite bound on all finite samples also bounds the full fibre, since a larger fibre would contain a finite sample exceeding it. The summability proof uses exactly the finite-sample statement. Multiplication by the height bound raised to the power T gives the geometric decay when T > n.

How do the Fourier coefficients recover the theta mean?

Consider the lower range of the Siegel–Weil formula. Write n for the source rank and m for the dimension of the target Hermitian space V over the quadratic extension E/F. Thus n < m ≤ 2n and n + w < m, where w is the Witt index of V. The evaluation point s₀ = (m − n)/2 can lie on the boundary of absolute convergence or to its left. Take a test function Φ in the global Fock subspace of the Schrödinger model. With this input we can compare one frequency of the two sides at a time. The frequencies are rational Hermitian n × n matrices β. A frequency is nondegenerate when det β ≠ 0.

For an automorphic function F, move g by the upper unipotent matrix u(b) with diagonal blocks 1 and upper right block b. Invariance under rational unipotent translations makes this function of b periodic. Its domain is the Hermitian adelic matrices modulo the rational ones. Use a fundamental region 𝒟 of volume one. Put ⟨β,b⟩ = ½ TrE/F(tr(βb)), with rational entries embedded in the adeles and the field trace extended to the adeles.

Cβ(F)(g) = ∫𝒟 F(u(b)g) ψ(−⟨β,b⟩) db.

On the theta side, a frequency selects a Gram matrix. Write φ = ω(g)Φ for the translated test function. A rational tuple x of n vectors of V contributes φ(h−1x) to the theta kernel. Translating by u(b) multiplies this summand by ψ(⟨Gram(x),b⟩). The target action of h preserves the Gram matrix. After weighting by the inverse β-character, integration gives 1 if Gram(x) = β and 0 otherwise. Absolute theta convergence justifies grouping tuples by Gram matrix, averaging over [U(V)] and integrating the resulting character series. When det β ≠ 0, every tuple in that fibre has rank n, since rank(x∗Gram(V)x) ≤ rank(x). Thus Cβ(I)(g) is the normalized average of the sum over precisely these full-rank tuples, where I is the theta mean.

On the Eisenstein side, the same frequency selects the open cell. For Re z > n/2 the coset sum has a summable bound on a compact set of representatives. This permits integration of the sum by cells. On each other cell, when det β ≠ 0, there is a translation preserving its contribution and multiplying its character by a scalar different from 1. Its integral is therefore zero. The open-cell cosets are indexed by rational Hermitian translations. Their translates of 𝒟 cover the full adelic Hermitian space, giving the integral below. Here w is the Weyl element interchanging the two isotropic coordinate spaces and fz is the flat section.

Cβ(E(·,z))(g) = ∫Hermn(𝔸) fz(w u(b)g) ψ(−⟨β,b⟩) db.

The Weyl action is a Fourier transform. Evaluating it at zero integrates the translated test function against the Gram character. Consequently the section in this integral is the Gram-character integral of φ times the height H(w u(b)g)z−s₀. This identifies the unfolded family on the right half-plane with the Whittaker integral for β. Its holomorphic value at s₀ is the same full-rank fibre average computed on the theta side. The input used here combines finite-place factors, the unramified Gram-density calculation, a real-place computation, global factorization and a low-rank density identity. Finite linear combination treats the compact argument, then the Iwasawa decomposition transports the identity to arbitrary g.

What can be invisible to all the nondegenerate coefficients?

Take the additive group of symmetric 2 × 2 matrices over the field of three elements. This finite example has 27 elements. Set ζ = exp(2πi/3), T = diag(1,0) and F(B) = ζB₁₁. The normalized β-coefficient is the average of ζtr((T−β)B). At β = T all 27 terms are 1. For β ≠ T, at least one of the three matrix coordinates has a nonzero coefficient in this linear form. Its sum is 1 + ζ + ζ² = 0. The off-diagonal entry appears with multiplier 2, which is invertible in this field. Hence every invertible β has coefficient zero, although F(0) = 1. The missing information sits at the rank-one frequency T.

How does the proof rule out such a discrepancy? At a real place selected using the Witt-index inequality, choose a compactly supported test function η whose Fourier transform vanishes on singular Hermitian matrices. Suppose a continuous automorphic function F has zero full-rank coefficients for all g. Integrate its unipotent translates against η. The β-coefficient of this convolution factors into the β-coefficient of F and the transform of η at the associated local frequency. For invertible β the first factor is zero. For singular β the associated local matrix is singular too, so the second factor is zero. All Fourier coefficients of the convolution now vanish, so Fourier uniqueness on the compact Hermitian quotient makes the convolution zero. Density and continuity give the same vanishing with a group translation on either side of the unipotent argument.

Removing a possible pole and computing the value

At this real place, first take the Gaussian Fock vector (the constant polynomial 1). The local signature condition gives a choice of η and of the two translations for which a compact-group average defines an operator T with nonzero scalar c(0) on the theta mean of this vector. On the corresponding regularized Eisenstein family the scalar is c(z−s₀). Meanwhile, the convolution argument shows that T kills every automorphic discrepancy with zero full-rank coefficients. On a discrepancy with eigenvalue c(0), this forces the discrepancy itself to vanish.

To see where holomorphy enters, write the continued Eisenstein family as A(z)/d(z) with holomorphic numerator and polynomial denominator. Factor d(z) = (z−s₀)kd₁(z) with d₁(s₀) ≠ 0. The full-rank coefficient identities ensure that while a power remains in the denominator, the regularized numerator at the point has zero full-rank coefficients. Its eigenvalue forces that value to vanish, so one can divide the numerator by z−s₀ holomorphically and repeat. After k divisions, the difference between the resulting numerator at s₀ and d₁(s₀)I is killed by T and has eigenvalue c(0). It is zero. Division by d₁ now gives the required value.

What does a full-rank Whittaker factor count at a good finite place?

The open-cell integral compares a Fourier coefficient of the Eisenstein series with the mean of tuples of vectors having Gram matrix T. At a good finite place v, this comparison has a concrete arithmetic content. Count the tuples whose Gram matrix agrees with T modulo increasing powers of a uniformizer. Once the measures are fixed, the normalized count gives the local Whittaker value at z₀ = (M−n)/2, where M is the dimension of the Hermitian space and n is the number of vectors.

Write q for the size of the residue field of Fv. At the places treated here, 2 is a unit, the local quadratic algebra is unramified, the forms J and T are integral with unit determinant, and the scalar character ψv has conductor the valuation ring. The integral lattice is trace-self-dual. Set ε = −1 when the quadratic algebra is the unramified field, and ε = +1 when it splits. The Schwartz function is the characteristic function of the integral M × n matrix lattice. A nonzero rational det T gives this unit condition at almost all places.

Count one Gram fibre. Let Nk be the number of distinct matrices X modulo ϖk satisfying X∗JX ≡ T. Here ∗ is conjugate transpose. There are q2kMn possible input matrices and qkn² Hermitian targets. The density compares the proportion of matrices in this fibre with the proportion one would obtain if every target occurred equally often.

αk(J,T) = Nk · qkn²/q2kMn = ∏j=0n−1 (1 − (ε/q)M−j),   k ≥ 1,   n ≤ M.

At level one a change of basis reduces the unimodular target to the identity. Solutions are orthonormal frames over the residue algebra. Choose one vector of norm one, then choose the next in its orthogonal complement. In dimension r, the norm-one count is q2r−1(1−(ε/q)r). The successive dimensions M, …, M−n+1 give the product above after normalization.

Why does the density stay constant at deeper levels?

Lift a solution modulo ϖk by writing its next representative as X+ϖkY. For k ≥ 1 the quadratic term in Y disappears modulo ϖk+1. The correction must solve the linear equation Y∗JX+X∗JY = H in the residue algebra, with H Hermitian. It is solvable for every H. For instance, since 2 and T are invertible here, take Y = ½XT−1H. The linear map has a domain with q2Mn elements and a codomain with qn² elements. Every fibre has q2Mn−n² elements. Thus Nk+1 gains exactly the factor cancelled by the next density normalization.

A Gram fibre over nine elements. Take ℚ(i) over ℚ at the inert prime 3, J = I₃ and T = I₂. Then q = 3 and ε = −1. In 𝔽₉ the norm of a+bi is a²+b² in 𝔽₃. There are 252 choices for a norm-one column of length three. For each, its two-dimensional orthogonal complement has 24 norm-one columns. This gives 6,048 frames among 9⁶ matrices at the first level. The normalized density is 6,048/3⁸ = 224/243 = (1+3−3)(1−3−2). Each frame has 3⁸ lifts to level two.

Which integral gives this number? Use the self-dual Haar measure on the matrix space for its Weil pairing and the self-dual Haar measure on the Hermitian matrices for their trace pairing. Write ⟨T,b⟩ for half the quadratic-algebra trace of tr(Tb). The source integrates the following expression in b. Inside it the character has positive Gram phase, and the Fourier projection contributes the negative target phase. The height is h(b) = vol(L+bL)/vol(L) for the standard column lattice L. The auxiliary Haar measure in this ratio cancels.

Wv(z) = ∫ h(b)−(z−z₀) ψv(−⟨T,b⟩) (∫integral X ψv(⟨b,X∗JX⟩) dX) db,   Re z > n².

At a good place the Hermitian integral lattice has volume one. Grouping by its cosets rewrites the integral as a sum. The cosets appear in increasing finite sets indexed by a level k. With t = εMq−(2z+n), their sums of absolute values have a geometric majorant because qn²|t| < 1 in the stated half-plane. Each positive-level sum is the same polynomial in t.

How do congruence counts determine a polynomial?

At each positive level the finite Fourier sum is a polynomial Pk(t) whose terms are weighted by the level character at the negative target, and by a nonnegative lattice-index exponent of t. Evaluate it at t = (ε/q)m for each auxiliary rank m ≥ n. Finite Fourier orthogonality and the Gaussian sums identify that evaluation with the density of T for the identity form in dimension m. The counting formula just proved gives ∏j(1−(ε/q)m−j). This equals the evaluation of ∏j(1−t(εq)j) at the same point. Those points have distinct absolute values, so the two polynomials agree everywhere. The auxiliary rank varies only in this interpolation step.

From places to the global coefficient. The pure adelic datum is standard outside a finite set. Apply the strict-rank theorem with the extra range assumption n+2 ≤ M or anisotropy of J, and with an integrability hypothesis on a right half-plane. The congruence counts, the Whittaker integral and the density-to-mean identity all enter separately. For the example with M = 3 and n = 2 the positive-definite identity form over ℚ(i) is anisotropic over that field.

What replaces the good-place formula at an exceptional finite place?

The good-place count assumes a particular test function, the indicator of the full matrix lattice. A test supported on just one residue class can change the answer even at an unramified prime. The local argument works at every finite place and gives an entire function of the complex parameter z. Its value at s₀ = (M−n)/2 is the density of the chosen test at the target Gram matrix. The global application has n < M.

Fix the local quadratic algebra Ev = Fv ⊗F E, the local component ψv of the adelic additive character, a nondegenerate Hermitian form J of rank M, and a Hermitian target T of size n whose determinant is invertible in Ev. This allows determinants of nonzero valuation. A test Φ is a locally constant, compactly supported function of the M × n matrix X. Use the self-dual measures μ on the matrix space and ν on the Hermitian space for their respective pairings. For a Haar measure λ on Evn and two compact open additive subgroups L₁, L₂, put r(b) = λ(L₁+bL₂)/λ(L₁). It is at least one. Write ⟨b,S⟩ for half the field-algebra trace of the matrix trace of bS. The opposite signs single out the fibre X∗JX = T.

u(b) = ∫ Φ(X) ψv(⟨b,X∗JX−T⟩) dμ(X),   Wv(z) = ∫ r(b)−(z−s₀) u(b) dν(b)   for Re z sufficiently large.

Why can one compact ball determine an entire function? On a shell R < ‖b‖ ≤ 2R, change variables by b ↦ (1+x)∗b(1+x), with x in a small additive matrix ball of radius C/R. These changes preserve the shell, its Haar measure, the lattice index and the integral containing the positive Gram phase. The negative target phase acquires a term linear in x and a term quadratic in x. The latter has norm bounded by a constant times R(C/R)², so the character is trivial on it for large R. Invertibility of T lets one choose C so that at every b in the shell the linear term gives a nontrivial character of the x-ball. Its Haar integral is zero. Averaging the change of variables therefore kills the shell integral for every z, with one cutoff valid for all z. At a singular target the linear term can lose this oscillation, and the stated density hypothesis covers only the regular set.

Choose a ball B₀ beyond that cutoff and double its radius successively. Adding any of the resulting shells leaves the integral over B₀ unchanged. On B₀ the index and its logarithm are bounded, so one can differentiate the compact integral with respect to z. This gives an entire Wv, with no poles. A separate absolute estimate identifies it with the original integral on a right half-plane. For radii growing by a fixed local dilation, the jth outer shell has r(b) ≥ 2j and volume at most a constant times κj. Thus the integral of the absolute value has a geometric majorant when Re z is large. The statement requires existence of a real threshold depending on the data.

How does the test enter the value? Let g be the supplied continuous density of the pushforward of Φ dμ by X ↦ X∗JX on the open set of invertible targets. At z = s₀ the lattice weight is one. Integrating over a large additive ball Λ in b retains those X whose Gram matrix belongs to T+Λ⊥. Indeed, the average of the phase on Λ is one when the difference annihilates Λ and zero otherwise. The annihilator shrinks into the regular set around T, and self-duality gives ν(Λ)ν(Λ⊥) = 1. The integral is therefore an average of g near T. By continuity it approaches g(T). Every sufficiently large ball already gives Wv(s₀).

∫Λ u(b) dν(b) = (1/ν(Λ⊥)) ∫T+Λ⊥ g(S) dν(S)   ⟶   g(T) = Wv(s₀).
Compute the entire factor for one residue class at 3

Take E = ℚ(i), F = ℚ and the inert prime 3. Let J be the two-dimensional identity, n = 1, T = 1 and L₁ = L₂ = 𝒪Eᵥ. Use a character of conductor ℤ₃. The standard integral lattices have self-dual volume one here. Let Φ be the indicator of X ≡ (1,0) modulo 3. There are four scalar coordinates over ℤ₃, so this class has mass 1/81. Its Gram value N(X₁)+N(X₂) belongs to 1+3ℤ₃. For each lift to the next power of 3, the derivative in the real coordinate of X₁ is 2 modulo 3. For each choice of the other three digits, exactly one digit of this coordinate gives the required next Gram digit. Thus the mass is uniform on 1+3ℤ₃, a set of volume 1/3, and the density there is 1/27.

Integration of the character on this coset, including the negative target phase, gives u(b) = (1/81) · 𝟙3⁻¹ℤ₃(b). On ℤ₃ the lattice index is one. On the shell 3⁻¹ℤ₃ ∖ ℤ₃, of volume two, its value is nine because the residue field of Ev has nine elements. In this example the original integral has compact support and converges at every z.

W₃(z) = (1 + 2 · 9−(z−1/2))/81,   W₃(1/2) = 1/27.

Now keep J = I₂ and T = 1, and restore the full-lattice test. There are 24 norm-one columns modulo 3. At every such column at least one scalar derivative of the norm is nonzero modulo 3, so each residue class contributes the same density 1/27. Summing the 24 contributions gives 24/27 = 8/9, the good-place answer in these same dimensions.

Which domain reaches the global coefficient? The local proof uses no rank inequality to construct the entire function once a density is given. The global theorem supplies these densities from the normalized Gram mean when n < M and either n+2 ≤ M or J is anisotropic. It chooses a finite set S outside which the forms, measures, lattices and test meet the good-place conditions. On Re z > 0 multiply the archimedean function, the finitely many entire factors Wv for v ∈ S, and the convergent good-place product. Farther right this equals the adelic integral for the full-rank Fourier coefficient. The point s₀ lies inside the global half-plane by the strict rank inequality. Substituting the local density values gives the normalized Gram mean there. The resulting global continuation is holomorphic on Re z > 0.

Why is the archimedean Whittaker factor entire at a nonsingular target?

At infinity the Fourier variable ranges over Hermitian matrices. For a target with nonzero determinant, integration by parts trades oscillation in this variable for extra decay. Repeating this operation reaches every complex parameter. The value at s₀ = (M−n)/2 recovers the density of the test on the target Gram fibre, as in the finite-place calculation.

Start at one real place. A frame identifies the Hermitian form with J = diag(1p,−1q), with p+q = M. The character on ℝ is u ↦ exp(2πiℓu) for a real ℓ ≠ 0. Set t = 2πℓ and c = 2π|ℓ|. In these coordinates the test on a complex M × n matrix X is a polynomial P in the entries of X and their conjugates, multiplied by exp(−c∑|Xᵢⱼ|²). Define A(Y) by integrating this test against the positive phase exp(it tr(YX∗JX)). The Whittaker coefficient uses the negative phase at the target B. Write D(Y) = det(I+Y²) and w = z−s₀. The integration measure here is Lebesgue measure in the n² real coordinates yᵢⱼ = Re Yᵢⱼ + Im Yᵢⱼ.

W(w) = ∫ D(Y)−w A(Y) exp(−it tr(BY)) dY   for Re w sufficiently large.

One determinant derivative moves the convergence line. Put s = sign(ℓ). Gaussian integration gives A as a polynomial in the entries of (I−isY)−1 and (I+isY)−1, multiplied by the determinants of those inverses to powers p and q respectively. Let Δ be the determinant of the matrix of first derivatives in Hermitian coordinates. Integration by parts shows that the negative Fourier transform of Δf is (it)ndet(B) times that of f, whenever the derivatives are integrable. As det(B) ≠ 0, one can divide by this scalar.

For the decay estimate, diagonalize Y with real eigenvalues λj. Cauchy's derivative estimate uses a radius proportional to √((1+|λi|)(1+|λj|)) in matrix entry (i,j). Each determinant term differentiates once in every row and column. The product of the reciprocal radii thus supplies a factor proportional to ∏j(1+|λj|)−1 ≤ D(Y)−1/2. After N determinants, differentiating the weight D−w leaves that weight times a polynomial in w of degree at most nN with coefficient functions of Y. At integer weights 0 through nN one can absorb the weight into the two determinant powers. Polynomial interpolation transfers the same decay bound to the coefficient functions. On compact parameter sets the differentiated amplitude is bounded by a constant times D(Y)−Re w−(M+N)/2.

Where does the determinant come from in two rows?

Write the diagonal entries of the Hermitian integration variable as x,y and its upper-right entry as u+iv. For a Hermitian target with diagonal a,b and upper-right entry c+id, the trace pairing is ax + by + 2cu + 2dv. Its negative Fourier phase is the exponential of this expression times −it. In these unscaled entry coordinates the determinant derivative is ∂x∂y − (∂u² + ∂v²)/4. Applying it to the phase gives (it)²(ab − c² − d²) times the same phase. Integration by parts twice transfers the derivative to the amplitude with positive sign.

For diagonal entries 2 and 3 and upper-right entry 1 + i, the multiplier is −4t², which we may divide out. For the matrix with every entry equal to one it is zero, although the target itself is nonzero. This is why the hypothesis concerns the determinant. In the derivative estimate the two permutations also have the same decay. The mixed diagonal derivative costs one inverse radius for each diagonal entry, while two off-diagonal derivatives each cost the inverse geometric mean of those radii.

Two complex Gaussian variables and one real Fourier variable

Take n = 1, M = 2, signature (1,1), ℓ = 1, and P = 1 in the one-place Lebesgue model. Then s₀ = 1/2. The Gram value is |x₁|²−|x₂|². In radial coordinates u = |x₁|² and v = |x₂|² the measure is π² exp(−2π(u+v)) du dv. Integrating along u−v = B gives g(B) = (π/4) exp(−2π|B|). For B ≠ 0 this equals W(0). Differentiating the scalar Fourier transform of 1/(a²+y²) with respect to a at a = 1 gives W(1) = (π/8)(1+2π|B|)exp(−2π|B|). At w = −1 the weighted amplitude is the constant 1/4. Its second derivative vanishes, and −1 belongs to U₂, so the continued value is zero. At the singular target B = 0, the phase is constant. As real w decreases to −1/2 the positive integral tends to infinity, since its limiting tail is proportional to 1/|y|. This is where the invertibility hypothesis matters.

Why does a product of local Gram densities give a global mean?

At one finite place a density measures how often a tuple has a prescribed Gram matrix. A rational tuple must satisfy the same equations at every place. To bring these two descriptions together the proof averages over all adelic isometries of a single rational Hermitian space. Let E/F be the CM extension, J the nondegenerate Hermitian form on EM, and T a rational nonsingular Hermitian matrix of size n. The theorem assumes n < M, with either n+2 ≤ M or J anisotropic over E. Anisotropic means that a rational vector of norm zero must itself be zero. The test Φ has a Schwartz factor at infinity and locally constant, compactly supported factors at finite places. Almost all finite factors are the characteristic function of the standard lattice. At every place the two Hermitian matrices come from these same rational forms, and each local additive character comes from one global character.

Let H = U(J), and choose a fundamental domain 𝒟 for its rational points in its adelic group. For each h sum Φ(h−1X) over the rational solutions of X∗JX = T. Replacing h by γh for a rational isometry γ permutes these solutions by X ↦ γ−1X. The sum therefore defines a function on the quotient. Integrate it over 𝒟 using Haar measure and divide by vol(𝒟). Equivalently one can first add the measures obtained by moving each rational tuple under h ↦ h−1X, normalizing their sum by the same volume, then integrate Φ. Countability of the rational tuples and integrability justify this equivalence.

vol(𝒟)−1 ∫𝒟 ∑X rational, X∗JX=T Φ(h−1X) dh = g∞(T) ∏v finite gv(T).
Why can grouping the terms change their weights?

A finite group makes the Haar weights visible. Take H to be the six permutations of three letters and put Γ = K = {id,(12)}. A function constant on ΓhK has just two values. The class of the identity contains two permutations. The class of (13) contains the remaining four. Indeed the size of ΓhK is |Γ||K|/|Γ ∩ hKh−1|, and the two intersection sizes are 2 and 1. If the function takes values 2 and 5, the normalized Haar average is (2·2 + 4·5)/6 = 4. Giving both classes weight ½ would give 3½. The same issue arises when a quotient integral is grouped into classes, whose weights come from their volumes. The definition above keeps that weighting by integrating on a fundamental domain.

What fixes the measure on one Gram fibre?

A global product uses the local integral at a specified target T. An identity averaged over T leaves open what happens at an individual target of measure zero. The extra condition that fixes the answer is continuity of the fibre integrals on the nonsingular targets.

Regular Gram-fibre theorem. Work at a completion R of the base field F of the CM extension E/F. Let V be the space of n-tuples of vectors for the scalar extension to R ⊗F E of a nonsingular Hermitian form J on EM. The Gram map G sends a tuple to its matrix of pairings in the space H of Hermitian n × n matrices. Let B be the open set where the determinant is invertible and fix additive Haar measures μ on V and ν on H. There is a unique family of measures mT carried by G−1{T} for T ∈ B, set equal to zero outside B, with the following two properties.

∫G−1(B) φ dμ = ∫B (∫ φ dmT) dν(T)   for every nonnegative measurable φ.

For every real continuous φ compactly supported inside G−1(B), the inner integral is finite and depends continuously on T ∈ B. An empty fibre carries the zero measure. The integration formula concerns the part of the source lying over B.

How one open set of targets acquires its measures

Fix a nonsingular target T₀. The local congruence-section theorem supplies a subgroup L of changes of basis for the tuple such that h ↦ h·T₀ is a homeomorphism onto an open neighborhood of T₀. Here the target action is congruence, and G(h·z) = h·G(z). A tuple above this neighborhood therefore has unique coordinates (h, z) with z in the reference fibre G−1{T₀}. Recover h from the target and act by h−1 on the tuple to recover z.

Write χV(h) and χH(h) for the factors by which pushing forward μ and ν under h multiplies them. Pull μ back to the product coordinates and multiply by the density χV(h). Translating the group coordinate now preserves the result. Applying the same correction χH(h) to the target measure gives a left Haar measure λ on L. The corrected source measure is λ times a measure m₀ on the reference fibre. Indeed, for each relatively compact measurable fibre set A, the masses of rectangles U × A give a locally finite left-invariant measure in U. Haar uniqueness makes it a constant times λ. A fixed compact neighborhood K of the identity gives that constant as the mass of K × A divided by λ(K). This defines m₀, and exhaustion gives the product identity. Undoing the corrections gives mh·T₀ = [χH(h)/χV(h)] h∗m₀. For a compactly supported continuous test, continuity follows by integration on the fixed reference fibre. Near any fixed h, the translated test supports meet the fibre in a common compact set. Sutherland, Theorem 13.3 on Haar measure[8].

How do the entries of a Hermitian matrix give local coordinates?

Let R be a completion of the totally real field F, and K = R ⊗F E for the CM extension E/F. At a real place K = ℂ. At a finite place it is a quadratic local field or the product R × R with the two factors interchanged. Write * for transpose followed by conjugation. Fix an invertible Hermitian matrix S of size n. We seek a continuous choice of q near the identity that solves q*S q = T as T varies near S.

First choose coordinates in which the centre is diagonal. Even an invertible matrix can have a zero first diagonal entry, as does the two-by-two matrix with ones off the diagonal and zeros on it. A nonsingular Hermitian form of positive dimension has a vector of nonzero length. Indeed, if every length vanished, expanding the lengths of v + w and v + αw, with α an invertible scalar whose conjugate is −α, would force both the sum and the difference of a pairing and its conjugate to vanish. Every pairing would be zero. A vector of nonzero length splits off an orthogonal line. To do this, subtract from any vector its projection onto that line, dividing by the length. The orthogonal complement is nonsingular, so repeating gives S = b*D b with b invertible and D = diag(d₁,…,dₙ), each dᵢ in R×. At a finite place this means nonzero in the local field. The length may have positive valuation.

Triangular coordinates near D. Write the first row of a nearby Hermitian matrix as (p, r), and let C be its lower-right block. If p ≠ 0, direct multiplication gives

(prr∗C)=N1∗diag(p,C−r∗r/p)N1,   N1=(1r/p0I).

The next pivot is the first diagonal entry of the smaller matrix C − r*r/p. At D the successive pivots are exactly the nonzero dᵢ. All these computations are continuous where the earlier pivots are nonzero, so every pivot stays nonzero on an open neighborhood of D. If N′ is the triangular matrix for the smaller block, the full triangular matrix is diag(1,N′)N₁, with N₁ the first upper triangular factor in the displayed identity. Recursion uniquely recovers the pivots pᵢ and an upper triangular matrix N with diagonal entries one. The inverse map sends these coordinates to N* diag(p₁,…,pₙ) N. Both directions are continuous. At size zero there is one empty matrix and no pivot to choose.

How does a chart select one change of basis?

Choose an open subgroup U ⊂ R× on which squaring maps homeomorphically onto an open subgroup U². For real R one may use the positive numbers. Restrict the triangular chart to pᵢ ∈ dᵢU². This is open and contains D. Each ratio pᵢ/dᵢ now has a unique square root uᵢ in U, depending continuously on the pivot. With A = diag(u₁,…,uₙ)N, multiplication gives

A*D A = N* diag(d₁u₁²,…,dₙuₙ²) N.

These matrices A form a subgroup L because triangular multiplication multiplies diagonal entries, and inversion inverts them. In the original basis take Q = b−1L b. Then q = b−1A b satisfies q*S q = b* (A*D A) b. Thus q ↦ q*S q is a homeomorphism from Q onto an open neighborhood of S. Its inverse is the required section, with value 1 at S. Congruence here is a right action on forms. In the fibre integration argument one uses the left action in which h sends a tuple X to Xh−1 and its Gram matrix T to (h−1)*T h−1. Inversion in Q relates the two parametrizations.

Which square root does the chart take above 2?

At any finite place the derivative of u ↦ u² at 1 is 2. The local field has characteristic zero, so this derivative is invertible there, also when 2 has positive valuation. The inverse function theorem gives a continuous inverse on a sufficiently small neighborhood. A small closed ball about 1 of radius less than one is open in the ultrametric topology and forms a subgroup. The chart can use such a ball inside the inverse-function neighborhood. Glöckner, generalized implicit function theorem 5.2[30].

One can see the permitted size directly. Normalize the valuation by ord(π) = 1 for a uniformizer π, set e = ord(2), and take an integer k > e. For u = 1 + πkz, its square is 1 + 2πk(z + αz²), with α = πk/2 in the maximal ideal. The difference of z + αz² at z and z′ is (z − z′)(1 + α(z + z′)). The second factor is a unit. The map therefore preserves distances and is injective modulo every πj. Each residue ring is finite, so the map is also surjective there. The unique solutions for successive precisions are compatible, and completeness gives a unique solution in the local integers 𝒪. Thus (1 + πk𝒪)² = 1 + 2πk𝒪.

For R = ℚ₂ and n = 1, centre the chart at S = 1 and take U = 1 + 4ℤ₂. Its square image is 1 + 8ℤ₂. The target 9 has square roots 3 and −3 in ℚ₂. The section takes −3 because −3 ≡ 1 modulo 4. At the centre it takes 1.

Why do two choices agree at every regular target?

Take two such neighborhoods and a nonnegative continuous test supported compactly over their overlap. Write u(T) and v(T) for its two fibre integrals. On every compact target set K inside the overlap, both integrate to the same quantity, the source integral of the test over G−1(K). If u(T) exceeded v(T) at one point, continuity would give a compact neighborhood on which their difference stays bounded below by a positive number. That neighborhood has positive Haar measure. Its two integrals would differ. Thus u = v throughout the overlap. These tests determine a locally finite measure there: compact subsets can be bounded by continuous cutoffs in arbitrarily small open neighborhoods. Fibre support then gives equality of the two measures at each target.

Choose the measure from any chart containing T. To check the integration formula for the resulting family, take a countable subcover B₁, B₂, …, which exists by second countability. Give each target to the first chart containing it. The measurable pieces Bj ∖ ⋃i<j Bi are disjoint, so their integration formulas add without counting overlaps twice. For continuity near a chosen target, multiply the test by a continuous cutoff in the target that equals one near that point and is supported inside one chart. This leaves the nearby fibre integrals unchanged and gives continuity by the local construction.

One exceptional value. For the complex line with G(z) = |z|², use area on ℂ and length ds on ℝ. In polar coordinates area is ½ ds dθ, so each circle s > 0 has fibre mass π. Doubling just the measure at s = 1 would preserve the integration formula because {1} has length zero. Take a continuous test equal to one near the unit circle and supported in a compact annulus. Its fibre integral would jump from π to 2π at 1. This is precisely the ambiguity that continuity removes. The chart for a scalar length at a finite place uses the same uniqueness argument.

One example checks the direction of the transport factor. For G(z) = ‖z‖² on ℂ² and r > 0, dilation z ↦ rz multiplies the length by r². Its pushforward on the four real source coordinates is r−4 times volume, and on the real target it is r−2 times length measure. The mass transported from the fibre at s to the fibre at r²s therefore acquires the ratio r². Directly, the real ball of radius √s has volume proportional to s². Differentiating with respect to s gives a fibre mass proportional to s, as predicted.

What remains after the first vector is fixed?

Suppose the ambient Hermitian space represents the first target length t ∈ F×. Split off a rational vector of that length. In the resulting coordinates the ambient form is ⟨t⟩ ⊕ J, with J a nonsingular form of dimension r. The prescribed Gram matrix is ⟨t⟩ ⊕ T, with T nonsingular of size n. Thus there are n columns still to choose. Work at a completion R of F with K = R ⊗F E. Use coordinate Haar measures throughout, from one additive Haar measure on R and one F-basis of E.

Let e be the first coordinate vector. A first column y with length t can be written hye for a unitary isometry hy. When K is a field, Witt’s extension theorem extends the isometry between the two lines of length t. At a split place a vector is a pair consisting of a vector u and a linear functional ℓ with ℓ(u) = t. Complete u to a basis with the other vectors in ker ℓ. A change between two such bases carries both the vector and, by its inverse dual, the functional. This gives the required isometry there as well. The remaining columns are orthogonal to y. Applying hy−1 puts these columns into the fixed complement. There they have the form (0,Xⱼ), where the smaller tuple X has Gram matrix T for J. Where does the factor for each remaining column come from?

Allow the target to move, so that we can use the defining integration formula for the regular fibre measures. Write its upper-left entry as x, its first row after that entry as b, and its lower-right Hermitian block as B. Near x = t the local square-root branch gives x = a²t, with a = 1 at the centre. In the frame carried by hy the first vector is ae, and each remaining vector is (cⱼ,Xⱼ). Computing their inner products gives

Here S is the full moving target and * is conjugate transpose. The determinant identity follows by subtracting the first row times the appropriate multiple from each lower row. Thus, as long as x is invertible, the smaller Gram matrix is nonsingular exactly when S is. For fixed x and b, passing between the two lower-right blocks is a translation, which preserves their additive Haar measure.

The first row changes volume. Normalize |·|v by the rule that multiplication by u scales the volume of a set in R by |u|v. A coordinate of K has two R-coordinates, so pushing its measure forward by z ↦ at z multiplies the measure by |at|v−2. Indeed, the mass assigned to a target set is the volume of its inverse image. There is one such factor for each of the n entries of b. The first-vector measure also varies with a. Under y ↦ ay, source volumes scale by |a|v2(r+1) and its scalar length by |a|v². Hence the measure at x is |a|v2r times the image of the measure at t.

Integrating first over the column coordinates, or first over the entries of the moving target, now gives the same integral. For a continuous compactly supported test the resulting fibre integrals are continuous on this regular neighborhood. In the moving frames the unitary section can be chosen with image in a compact set when y ranges over a compact part of the orbit. For fixed y the smaller regular fibre family gives continuity in the target coordinates under the integral. Compact control of the frames bounds these integrals by a common integrable function of y. Dominated convergence then gives continuity of the outer integral. By pointwise uniqueness, the two measures therefore agree at the specified block target. There a = 1, b = 0, and the complement target is T. The only remaining factor is cv(t)n with cv(t) = |t|v−2. Axler, Theorem 3.31 on dominated convergence[31].

Why is the global normalization one?

Over F = ℚ take E = ℚ(i), the ambient form diag(2,1) and two columns. At the real place fix the first column (1,0) and take the second to be (1 + i,1). Its pairing with the first column is b = 2 + 2i, and its length is 5. Subtracting |b|²/2 = 4 leaves the complement length 1. The full Gram determinant is 2·5 − 8 = 2. Multiplication by 2 in the complex b-coordinate multiplies area by 4, so pushing the original area forward gives the factor ¼. At the place 2, |2|₂ = ½ gives the factor 4. Every other finite place gives one. These two columns in dimension two illustrate the local coordinates and the product of the scalar factors. The global induction below requires at least one extra ambient dimension.

For every rational length t ∈ F×, the product formula gives ∏v|t|v = 1. Hence the product of the local factors cv(t)n is one as well. At almost all finite places the standard lattice test also separates into the standard tests for the first vector and the complement. This latter assertion uses integral isometries at good places. The global induction uses the local recursion in the strict range n + 1 ≤ r, with the full binary space anisotropic when r = 1. The local measure identity itself needs the represented nonzero line and the indicated regular targets. Sutherland, Theorem 13.21 on the product formula[32].

|I(a) − w P(a)| ≤ C adM   for every integer a ≥ 1.

Where does the exponent come from? For the indicator of the original lattice the weighted difference between the averaged theta function and the Eisenstein series is bounded after reduction to a Siegel domain. The dilation replaces the real upper-half-plane variable x+i by (x+i)/a². Its imaginary part is a−2 at each of the d real places. The product of the local weights (Im τ)M/2 is therefore a−dM. In these coordinates let Ω denote the image of the fixed unit-radius box. Write τ(x) for multiplication by exp(x) at every real place and by 1 at the finite places. Replacing the representative permutes the summands.

Compute the volume of a shell. Rational isometries act transitively on isotropic lines. Write P for the adelic stabilizer of Ee. Unfolding the sum over lines gives an integral over (Γ ∩ P) ∖ G. Its integral costs at most a fixed constant times exp(−2d(s+1)j) times the largest test bound on these pairs. Count the scalars left in each shell. Put x = j + log r. If τ(−x)λu lies in Ω, pairing it with v gives τ(−x)λ. All these pairings lie in a fixed compact set, since the pairs and Ω range over compact sets. Clearing the finite denominators puts λ in one lattice in E of real dimension 2d. Which lattice points does an adelic box count?

The sum over isotropic lines leaves a rational scalar to count in each shell. We prove a bound for M coordinates over E and then use it with M = 1. Let E/F be a CM quadratic extension and d = [F∶ℚ]. Choose an F-basis of E. It writes an adelic vector in (𝔸F ⊗F E)M as 2M adelic coordinates over F. At each finite place v require every coordinate to belong to N−1𝒪Fᵥ, where N is a fixed positive integer. At each of the d real places take the absolute values of the 2M coordinates. The box BN(R) consists of vectors satisfying the finite conditions whose real absolute values sum to at most R. This sum is the ℓ¹ norm on ℝν with ν = 2dM.

BN(R) = {‖u‖₁ ≤ R} × ∏v finite (N−1𝒪Fᵥ)2M.

The finite factor is compact and open. Away from the primes dividing N, its factors are the usual integral lattices. Every finite adèle has a denominator at only finitely many places, and powers of the rational primes below them clear those denominators. Thus the open finite factors, as N varies, cover any compact family. Take a finite subcover, use a common multiple of its denominators, and bound the continuous real norm on the same family. Every compact Ω is consequently contained in some BN(r) with r > 0. Sutherland, The ring of adeles, Propositions 25.5–25.6 and Definition 25.7[33].

For a rational vector, each of its 2M coefficients c lies in F. The finite condition says exactly that Nc is integral at every finite place, hence lies in 𝒪F. The allowed rational vectors therefore form the additive subgroup ΛN = (N−1𝒪F)2M in the chosen coordinates. Taking differences preserves every finite condition. The real embeddings identify this subgroup with a lattice, so its intersection with a bounded real ball is finite. Sutherland, §14.2, the integer ring in its real embedding space[34].

How many translates of a small ball cover the rational points?

Let PN(R) count the points of ΛN in the closed real ball of radius R, including zero. For 0 < r₀ ≤ R, choose a maximal collection of these points whose pairwise distances are at least r₀. The open balls of radius r₀/2 about the chosen points are disjoint and fit inside the ball of radius R+r₀/2. Dilation by a positive scalar t multiplies volume in ℝν by tν. The number of centres is therefore at most (1+2R/r₀)ν ≤ (3R/r₀)ν.

Every lattice point in the large ball lies within distance r₀ of a centre, since otherwise it could be added to the collection. Subtracting that centre sends the point into ΛN in the small ball. Each centre therefore accounts for at most PN(r₀) points. Using the coefficient 5 in the subsequent shell estimate gives the comparison

PN(R) ≤ (5R/r₀)ν PN(r₀),   0 < r₀ ≤ R.

Fix Ω ⊂ BN(r) as above. Choose 0 < r₀ ≤ 1 strictly smaller than the real sizes of all nonzero points in BN(1). This is possible because the list is finite, and a nonzero rational coordinate stays nonzero under a real embedding. If the list is empty, take r₀ = 1. Thus PN(r₀) = 1. For an explicit choice take r₀ = min(1, d/(2N)). Indeed, any nonzero coefficient c has |NormF/ℚ(Nc)| ≥ 1 because it is the absolute value of a nonzero integer. The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives ∑σ|σ(c)| ≥ d/N.

The dilation τ(x) multiplies real coordinates by exp(x) and fixes finite coordinates. Let AΩ(x) count X ∈ EM with X ≠ 0 and τ(−x)X ∈ Ω. The tested vector then has real size exp(−x)‖X‖₁ ≤ r, so X belongs to the box of radius exp(x)r. Put x₀ = log(r₀/r). Below x₀ the new radius is smaller than r₀ and the count is zero. At and above the threshold apply the two-radius comparison with R = exp(x)r. It bounds even the count including zero, and gives

AΩ(x) = 0   for x < x₀,   AΩ(x) ≤ C exp(νx)   for x ≥ x₀,   C = (5r/r₀)ν.

For example, take F = ℚ, E = ℚ(i), the basis (1,i), M = 1 and Ω = B₂(1). The lattice is ½ℤ[i] with size |a|+|b| on a+bi. Taking r₀ = ¼ gives ν = 2 and x₀ = −log 4. At the threshold the actual nonzero count is still zero, while the displayed upper bound is 25. At x = −log 2 the closed radius reaches ½ and admits exactly the four points ±½, ±i/2.

In the shell integral, pairing a tested vector with its transverse dual recovers a scalar in E. The pair and the tested vector vary in compact sets, so the image of their continuous pairing is one fixed compact Ω. Here the dimension in the count is ν = 2d, one scalar over E, and the variable is x = j + log rtest for shell index j and test radius rtest. Keep the hyperbolic plane with basis e,e′ and let W be its Hermitian orthogonal complement of dimension s = M−2. Let P be the stabilizer of the line Ee in the adelic unitary group. Reduce the four coordinates. The additive quotient 𝔸F/F has compact representatives. Indeed, the Chinese remainder theorem clears the nonintegral finite residues by subtracting a field element, and an algebraic integer then moves the infinite coordinates into a bounded lattice parallelepiped. The same argument works for E and in each of the s horizontal coordinates. Denote the resulting compact sets by Cz and Cb. For the scalar choose a fixed compact set ω of idèles such that every a belongs to E×τ(j)ω for some integer j. To see this, the norm-one idèle classes form a compact group. The idèle modulus of τ(x) is e2dx. Removing the real logarithmic height leaves a norm-one class. Its representatives can be taken in a compact set by lifting a finite cover by relatively compact open neighborhoods. Absorb the fractional part of the height in ω. Finally put g in a fundamental domain 𝒟W for its rational isometries. After the rational scalar and isometry have been reduced, subtract a rational horizontal vector. This changes the central coordinate by the cross term in the unipotent group law, so subtract a rational central element last. The resulting shells cover modulo rational elements of P. Summing over possible overlaps gives an upper bound. Borel, Some finiteness properties of adele groups over number fields, Theorem 5.8 and its idèle example, p. 22[35]

Why the complementary quotient has finite volume. Borel’s finite-volume theorem applies to a connected linear group over a number field whose characters defined over that field are all trivial. Over E, U(W) becomes GLs. Its algebraic characters are determinant powers. Indeed, on the diagonal torus a character is a monomial whose exponents must be equal by permutation symmetry, and a character is trivial on each elementary unipotent subgroup. Conjugation over F takes the determinant to its inverse. A power descends only when its exponent is zero. Thus 𝒟W has finite volume for any Haar measure on U(W)(𝔸F). The same argument supplies the finite volume of the complement of dimension M−1 on a nonzero norm fibre. Borel, Theorem 5.6(i), p. 21[35]

In these coordinates a left Haar measure on P is the product of the two additive measures, a Haar measure on U(W), and χ(a) d×a. Here χ is the pushforward multiplier of conjugation on the two additive coordinates. Left translation in the unipotent group translates the centre by a quantity depending on the horizontal variable and preserves product measure by integration in the centre first. The isometries preserve additive measure. The scalar multiplier in the additive variables is exactly canceled by transforming the density χ(a) in the multiplicative variable. On τ(j)ω one has χ(τ(j)c) = e−2d(s+1)jχ(c). Multiplicative Haar measure is unchanged by translation. The mass of this shell is consequently bounded by

vol(Cb) vol(Cz) vol(𝒟W) vol×(ω) supω χ · exp(−2d(s+1)j).

Every factor before the exponential is finite and independent of j. The bound grows as j tends to −∞. The compact support of the original indicator and the discreteness of rational scalars supply the lower cutoff in the geometric sum.

At a split place one can choose a different pivot in each component. Almost everywhere the original integral column and functional already work together with scalar 1.

Use the inverse Hermitian matrix to write the functional as ⟨z,·⟩, and replace z by z − ½⟨z,z⟩v. This continuous operation leaves the pairing with v equal to 1 and makes the second vector isotropic. The resulting pairs lie in a compact set and all have the same invertible two-by-two Gram matrix as (e,e′). The compact representative theorem on this regular fibre supplies a compact family of isometries k carrying the reference pair onto them. Then hke = ae, hence hk ∈ P. Taking inverses of the compact family gives C.

If bj bounds f(pc) there for p in shell j, the result is at most μ(C′) ∑j bj ν(Sj). This gives the constant μ(C′)/m in the isotropic-line integral bound.

How can a primitive column and its dual witness both be kept bounded?

Let E/F be the chosen CM quadratic extension and put K = 𝔸F ⊗F E. A column y with M entries in K is primitive here if there is a row z₀ with z₀·y = ∑i (z₀)iyᵢ = 1. This is ordinary row-by-column multiplication. In the isotropic-line argument the Hermitian form supplies such a row. If y = g−1e and h(f,e) = 1, then z₀ = (g−1f)∗J takes value one on y, where J is the matrix of the form. We want one compact set Ω, chosen before y, that contains both a rescaled column and a row witnessing its primitivity. Rows and columns are identified with their ordered lists of M coordinates for membership in Ω.

For every primitive y, there are a ∈ K× and z with ay ∈ Ω,   z ∈ Ω,   z·(ay) = 1.

At a complex component pick a coordinate yᵣ of largest modulus. It is nonzero because the local dot product can equal one. Take a = yᵣ−1 and take z to be the coordinate row with 1 in position r and zeros elsewhere. Every entry of ay has modulus at most one, entry r is exactly one, and z·(ay) = 1. At infinity there are finitely many complex components, and each can choose its own r. Both tuples now belong to a finite product of closed unit discs.

At a finite place where the quadratic algebra is a field, use the same largest-coordinate rule with the multiplicative size |Norm(x)| in the base local field. The base valuation ring is compact because its residue classes modulo each uniformizer power form a finite cover by balls of shrinking radius, and it is complete. To see compactness of the norm ball directly in coordinates, write x = u+wθ with θ² = Δ. The norm is u²−Δw², nonzero on the compact sphere max(|u|,|w|) = 1 because Δ is nonsquare. Its absolute value has a positive minimum there. Dividing by a coordinate of maximal absolute value and using homogeneity of degree two bounds max(|u|,|w|) wherever |Norm(x)| ≤ 1. The ball is therefore closed and bounded in the two-dimensional local field coordinates, hence compact. At a split place the algebra is a product of two fields. Choose a maximum separately on each side, giving one invertible pair of scalars and one pair of coordinate rows. The witness may select different positions in the two factors.

For example, over ℚ(i) at the split prime 5, take k ≥ 1. Write a local two-entry column as y = ((5−k,0),(0,5k)). Each single entry has a zero component. The scalar pair (5k,5−k) sends y to ((1,0),(0,1)). The row with these same two entries evaluates to (1,1), the multiplicative identity. The freedom to replace the row already matters at a complex place. For real R ≥ 1 take y = (R,0) and z₀ = (R−1,R²). After rescaling by 1/R, transporting the old row gives (1,R³). Choosing the new row (1,0) bounds both tuples for the whole sequence.

Why do the local scalings form a single idèle?

The local compact sets must fit the restricted product topology. Fix an F-basis of E and let Λv consist of tuples whose coordinates in that basis lie in the integer ring of Fᵥ. Away from a fixed finite set of places the local compact set can be chosen to be exactly Λv. To see this, first use a basis 1,θ with θ² = Δ ∈ F×. Exclude the places over 2, those where Δ is not a unit, and the finitely many denominator primes of the change of coordinates to the chosen basis. At a remaining place where Δ is nonsquare its reduction is nonsquare too. Indeed, an odd-residue-characteristic square root of a unit modulo the uniformizer lifts digit by digit because the derivative 2x at that root is a unit. Thus

|u²−Δw²|v = max(|u|v,|w|v)².

For unequal sizes the largest term gives the value. For equal nonzero sizes, cancellation would give a square root of Δ in the residue field on dividing by w². Hence the local construction produces integral coordinates in the basis 1,θ. In the split case let s² = Δ. The two components of u+wθ are u±sw. Both s and 2 are units, so taking their half-sum and their difference divided by 2s recovers integral coordinates from integral components. The fixed change of basis preserves integrality away from its denominator primes. These conditions leave only finitely many exceptional places.

Fix this finite set S independently of y. Use the compact archimedean box from the first step, the local compact sets constructed there at the finite places in S, and Λv everywhere else. Their product is a compact subset Ω of KM. Indeed it lies in one restricted-product chart with the ordinary product topology, where each local lattice is compact and the product of compact sets is compact. Andrew Sutherland, Number Theory I, Proposition 25.6 and Definition 25.7[36].

Now take an actual witness z₀ for y. Their components both lie in Λv at almost every finite place. Wherever this holds outside S, choose aᵥ = 1 and keep zᵥ = (z₀)v. At the finitely many other places use the local construction to choose aᵥ and zᵥ. Thus aᵥ and aᵥ−1 both equal one at almost all finite places. They assemble to mutually inverse elements of K, so a is an idèle. The rows zᵥ assemble to an adelic row because they are integral almost everywhere. In every component zᵥ·(aᵥyᵥ) = 1. Equality of adèles can be tested in all components, giving the global identity, with ay,z in the fixed Ω.

One example explains why the input row must itself be adelic. Take a rank-one column over ℚ(i) whose component at each rational prime p is p, and whose complex component is one. The column is integral at all finite places and each local entry is invertible in the local algebra. Yet the only possible dual has component 1/p at every p. It fails the restricted-product integrality condition, so this column has no adelic witness.

For the shell estimate, y is isotropic, and ay remains isotropic. The two compactly bounded inputs ay and z now feed the continuous construction of a hyperbolic partner. Its image on Ω × Ω gives the compact family of pairs to which the adelic Gram-fibre lifting argument is applied. The row normalization by itself requires only the displayed primitivity identity. If M = 0 that identity is impossible, so there is no primitive input in that rank.

How can a compact family of frames be lifted to isometries?

At a real place of the base field, a Hermitian space is a complex vector space V with a nonsingular form h, conjugate-linear in its first variable. For an ordered tuple of columns X = (x₁,…,xₙ), its Gram matrix T has entries h(xᵢ,xⱼ). Suppose det T ≠ 0. Any linear relation on the columns would give a vector in the kernel of T, so the columns are independent. If Y has the same Gram matrix, the map xᵢ ↦ yᵢ is an isometry of the column spans. Witt’s extension theorem gives an isometry of all of V extending that map. The shell estimate needs more. Given any compact set Ω of tuples, one compact set C in the unitary group must supply a lift g with gX = Y for every Y ∈ Ω of Gram matrix T. Sprehn and Wahl, Forms over fields and Witt’s lemma, Theorem 3.4[37].

First diagonalize T by one fixed change of columns in both tuples. Indeed, a nonzero Hermitian form has a vector with nonzero value on the diagonal, by the polarization identity. Split off its line by orthogonal projection and repeat on the nonsingular complement. The new columns are mutually orthogonal with real squared lengths bᵢ ≠ 0, which may have either sign. Undoing the common column change at the end preserves the equation gX = Y.

Move one column and keep the earlier columns fixed. Suppose the next column is currently x and must be sent to y, with h(x,x) = h(y,y) = b ≠ 0. Set t = h(y,x). For at least one choice of λ = ±1 we have |b − λt| ≥ |b|, since the mean of |b−t|² and |b+t|² is b²+|t|². With u = x−λy and δ = b−λt, define

A(z) = z − u h(u,z)/δ,   B(z) = z − (1−λ)y h(y,z)/b.

Here h(u,x) = δ, so A(x) = λy. To check that A is an isometry, expand h(Az,Aw). The coefficient of h(z,u)h(u,w) in the difference from h(z,w) is [h(u,u)−2 Re δ]/|δ|², which vanishes because h(u,u) = 2b−2λ Re t. The second map acts by λ on the line of y and fixes its orthogonal complement. Thus BA is an isometry sending x to y. Each previously matched column is orthogonal to both and stays fixed.

Keep the lifts in a compact set. The subset of Ω on which the Gram matrix equals T is closed in Ω, hence compact. Start there with the identity matrix. At the first column retain both closed subsets where the corresponding sign satisfies |δ| ≥ |b₁|. They cover the compact set, and on each the displayed matrix depends continuously on Y. At the next column use its image under the current matrix as x and repeat within each subset. After n columns there are at most 2n compact subsets. On each, the product of the successive matrices is a continuous function of Y. The union of their compact images is the required C. At a tie either sign supplies a lift.

In the shell argument the two initial vectors e, f are isotropic, with h(e,f) = 1. Their Gram matrix has determinant −1. The column change (e+f, e−f) gives squared lengths 2 and −2, so both steps have a denominator of absolute value at least 2. For instance, the pairs (a e, a−1f) for 1 ≤ a ≤ 2 lift to the compact family diag(a, a−1) on their plane, extended by the identity on its orthogonal complement. The one-vector orbit mean uses the same real-place assertion for a line of nonzero norm. The next argument explains how the integral choices at finite places enter the compact family of adelic representatives.

Theorems used. Witt’s extension theorem for a Hermitian space

Why can the same columns be used at every place?

Fix a CM extension E/F with conjugation and an invertible Hermitian matrix J of size M. Let X be an ordered tuple of n rational columns in EM. When their Gram matrix is nonsingular, the columns are independent and form a frame for their span, which may be smaller than the ambient space. Stack them as a matrix and write T = X∗JX, where ∗ means conjugate transpose. Assume det T ≠ 0. Given an adelic tuple Y with this same matrix of pairings at every place, we seek one adelic isometry carrying X to Y. The first change of basis takes place among the n columns. It can be chosen over E before taking any completions.

Consider the pairing h on the space of column coefficients, with matrix T. For n > 0 there is a vector w of nonzero length h(w,w). To see this, suppose every length vanished. Expanding the length of u+v gives h(u,v)+h(v,u) = 0. Choose a nonzero θ with conjugate −θ by taking the difference of an element of E outside F and its conjugate. Expanding the length of u+θv then gives θ(h(u,v)−h(v,u)) = 0. Together the two identities force every pairing to vanish, contradicting nonsingularity. The nonzero length β is fixed by conjugation and therefore belongs to F. For every z, subtract w h(w,z)/β to obtain a vector orthogonal to w. The orthogonal complement is nonsingular because a vector in its radical would pair to zero with the whole space. Repeating the argument gives an invertible rational matrix S of new columns. The identity serves for the empty tuple. Thus

S∗TS = diag(β₁,…,βₙ),   βⱼ ∈ F×.

For example, over ℚ(i) take two columns e, f of lengths 0 and 2 with h(e,f) = 1+i. The Gram determinant is −2. Choose f first and then e−f(1−i)/2. Their lengths are 2 and −1, and their pairing is zero. The division by 2 is valid in every completion. At places above 2 its inverse lies outside the valuation ring, which matters when we ask whether a local isometry preserves an integral lattice.

The tuples XS and YS have the same diagonal Gram matrix. A unitary map g acts on the left, so g(XS) = YS implies gX = Y on multiplying both sides on the right by S−1. The same rational S and its inverse have integral entries outside finitely many places. We can therefore use this one diagonal model in the local tests that follow.

Which denominator is a unit at a finite place?

Let E/F be a CM quadratic extension, with conjugation z ↦ z̄. Let X be a rational frame of n columns in an M-dimensional nonsingular Hermitian space. Assume its n-by-n Gram matrix has nonzero determinant. The columns are then a basis of their span, with n ≤ M. Suppose an adelic frame Y has the same Gram matrix. We want an isometry carrying X to Y that preserves the coordinate lattice at almost every finite place. Fix a common rational change of columns that makes the Gram matrix diagonal, with nonzero entries β₁,…,βₙ in F. Consider one pair of columns of equal squared length β. The real-place construction divides by δ = β − λ̄t, where t = h(y,x) and λλ̄ = 1. To keep this division integral, we need δ to be a unit.

Here are four possible values of λ, fixed once for the extension. Choose a nonzero θ with θ̄ = −θ by subtracting the conjugate of any element of E outside F. Then d = θ² lies in F× and 1, θ is an F-basis of E. Take s ∈ F× with s² ≠ d. Put P = (s²+d)/(s²−d) and Q = 2s/(s²−d). Expanding the squares gives P²−dQ² = 1, so α = P+Qθ has norm one and Q ≠ 0. Our choices are 1, −1, α and −α.

At a finite place v, write 𝒪v for the integers of Fᵥ and Rᵥ for the ring of integers of E ⊗F Fᵥ, a product of two valuation rings at a split place. For the moment suppose 2, d, Q and β are units of 𝒪v and P is integral. Then θ is an integral unit. Each t ∈ Rᵥ can be written a+bθ with a = (t+t̄)/2 and b = (t−t̄)/(2θ) in 𝒪v. Both quotients are integral and fixed by conjugation. For λ = p+qθ, multiply δ by its conjugate to obtain a scalar in the base ring,

Nλ = δδ̄ = (β−pa+qbd)² − d(qa−pb)².

Suppose all four norms vanish in the residue field. Taking differences gives N−1−N1 = 4βa and N−α−Nα = 4β(Pa−Qbd). The first forces a ≡ 0, and the second then forces b ≡ 0 because Qd is a unit. But now N1 ≡ β² ≠ 0. Thus at least one norm is a unit in 𝒪v. For its phase, δ−1 = δ̄/Nλ belongs to Rᵥ.

Why two signs can fail. At an inert place the residue algebra is a field. If β−t and β+t both vanished there, their sum 2β would vanish. At a split place each sign can fail in a different component. For example, 5 splits in ℚ(i). In the residue algebra 𝔽₅ × 𝔽₅, conjugation swaps the factors and i = (2,−2). Take β = 1 and t = (1,−1). The choices λ = 1 and −1 give δ = (0,2) and (2,0). With θ = i and s = 1, we have α = i. For λ = i both components of δ equal 3 modulo 5, so its norm equals 4 modulo 5 and division is integral.

An integral isometry at almost every finite place

We can now specify a finite set S outside which every step works. Include all places above 2 and all ramified places. Include the places where any diagonal entry βᵢ, d or Q fails to be a unit, or P fails to be integral. Also include any place where the form matrix J, its inverse, the rational frame, or the common change of columns and its inverse have a nonintegral entry. Each fixed number-field entry has finitely many denominator primes, and each nonzero diagonal entry, as well as d and Q, is a unit away from finitely many primes. Finally include the finitely many places where the given adelic frame has a nonintegral entry. For a compact family of frames this last set can be chosen uniformly. The open sets of tuples integral outside a given finite set cover the family, so finitely many suffice, and we take the union of their exceptional sets. Sutherland, The ring of adeles, strong approximation, §25.3, Definition 25.7[33].

Fix v outside S. Write h(z,w) = z*Jw, where * is conjugate transpose. For one pair of integral columns x, y with common squared length β, choose λ by the four-norm test and put u = x−λy. For any column w and scalar c, let Tw,c(z) = z−wc h(w,z). The two maps we need are

A = Tu, 1/δ,   B = Ty, (1−λ̄)/β,   x ⟼ Ax = λy ⟼ BAx = y.

Indeed h(u,x) = δ, and B multiplies y by λ̄. To see that the maps preserve the lattice in both directions, write Lz = w h(w,z). This operator is self-adjoint for h and L² = h(w,w)L. Multiplying (1−c̄L)(1−cL) therefore gives the identity whenever c+c̄ = cc̄ h(w,w). This equality holds for A because h(u,u) = δ+δ̄, and for B because (1−λ̄)(1−λ) = 2−λ−λ̄. Thus each map is unitary with inverse Tw,c̄. Every coefficient of the maps and their inverses is integral since w, J and c are integral.

Start with the identity. If g has matched some columns, use x = gXᵢ and y = Yᵢ for the next pair of diagonalized columns. Every earlier matched column is perpendicular to both x and y, so A and B fix it. Replacing g by BAg matches one more column and preserves the lattice. After the last column, undo the common column change to get gᵥX = Yᵥ for the original frames. At each v outside S, gᵥ belongs to the unitary stabilizer of RᵥM, where M is the ambient dimension. The places above 2 enter S because the norm differences divide by 4. The adelic orbit argument supplies the transformations at the remaining places and assembles the local maps.

Which local inverses form an adelic inverse?

A finite adèle of F is a tuple (aᵥ) in the completions Fᵥ with aᵥ in the valuation ring 𝒪ᵥ outside a finite set. Its inverse is an adèle precisely when every aᵥ is nonzero and almost every aᵥ is a unit of 𝒪ᵥ. Indeed the only possible inverse has components 1/aᵥ. At a place where aᵥ is integral, its inverse is integral exactly when its valuation is zero. At the finitely many archimedean places one just needs a nonzero component. As an example over ℚ, take aₚ = p at every finite prime and a∞ = 1. This is an adèle with every component nonzero. Its componentwise inverse has negative valuation at every prime. In contrast, a fixed nonzero rational number and its inverse have a nonzero valuation at only finitely many primes. Sutherland, The idele group, Definition 26.2[38].

Apply this criterion to a denominator in a unitary change of frame. At a finite place put Aᵥ = Fᵥ ⊗F E. This is a quadratic field or a product of two copies of Fᵥ. In both cases the norm of δ is N(δ) = δδ. A nonzero norm gives the explicit inverse δ/N(δ). In a split algebra the norm tests both components. For example, (0,1) is a nonzero element with zero norm. Each of the four candidate phases gives a scalar norm fⱼ. Why do they generate the unit ideal over the full ring of base adèles? For t = a+bθ, their two differences are 4βa and 4β(Pa−Qbd). The scalars 4β and Qd are nonzero elements of F and therefore have adelic inverses. Hence the ideal generated by the four norms contains a and b. For the phase +1 we have f₁ = (β−a)²−db², so β²−f₁ belongs to the ideal generated by a and b. Adding f₁ shows that the ideal of the four norms contains β². Dividing by β² shows that a linear combination of the norms with adelic coefficients equals one. Evaluating this identity at an exceptional place produces at least one nonzero fⱼ. This suffices in the local field even at a ramified or dyadic place. For instance, over ℚ₂(i) take β = t = 1 and the phases ±1, ±i. Their denominators are 0, 2 and 1±i. None is an integral unit, yet 2 is invertible in the field. Where all the coefficients and norms are integral, at least one fⱼ must be an integral unit, since otherwise the sum would lie in the maximal ideal.

Select an admissible index at each place. Both the numerator δ and the inverse of the selected norm are then integral at almost every finite place. Consequently the entries of the elementary unitary corrections, and of their inverses, are adèles in the chosen coordinates. Different places may use different indices. The four indicator functions of the chosen sets take values in {0,1}, hence are integral everywhere. Multiplying each candidate by its indicator and adding realizes the local choices as a single adelic coefficient. This construction applies at each of the finitely many column steps. Each new correction fixes the already matched columns because they are orthogonal to both vectors used in that correction.

How does a pointwise lift give a single compact family?

Write G for the adelic unitary group preserving J. By the column construction and the rational change of basis, every adelic tuple Y of Gram matrix T equals gX for some g ∈ G. Conversely, an isometry preserves all pairings, so the orbit of X is exactly the fibre Z of the Gram map at T. Without the nonsingularity hypothesis, equality of Gram matrices can leave several orbits. In a hyperbolic plane the zero vector and a nonzero isotropic vector both have Gram matrix (0). Every invertible linear map fixes zero.

For the shell bound we need one compact family of such g as Y varies in a given compact set Ω. We first check the topology needed to pass from points to compact sets. In any basis of E over F, an adelic coefficient is a pair of base adèles. Conjugation is linear in these coordinates and multiplication is polynomial. The tuple space is therefore locally compact and Hausdorff, and the entries of the Gram matrix are continuous. The fibre Z is closed. Give an invertible matrix the topology of the pair (g,g−1). In the product of the two matrix spaces, the equations gh = hg = I and g∗Jg = J define a closed set. This gives G local compactness, the Hausdorff property and a countable basis, inherited from the finite powers of the adèle ring. The action is continuous by matrix multiplication.

Why the adelic orbit map is open. Given any neighborhood W of the identity in G, choose a compact neighborhood K with K−1K ⊂ W. The translates of the interior of K cover G, and second countability gives a countable subcover. Transitivity then covers Z by countably many translates of the compact, hence closed, set KX. By the Baire category theorem at least one of these closed translates has nonempty interior in Z. Translating back, choose kX in the interior of KX with k ∈ K. Then k−1 int(KX) is a neighborhood of X inside K−1KX ⊂ WX. Translating this inclusion to each group element proves that g ↦ gX is open onto Z. The Stacks Project, Lemma 5.13.3, Baire category theorem[39].

Take a relatively compact open neighborhood of each group element. Their images under this open map cover Z, so finitely many images cover Ω ∩ Z. The union of the closures of those finitely many neighborhoods is a compact family of adelic isometries giving all the required lifts.

This compactness controls all places together. To see its force, consider the open sets of matrices for which both the matrix and its inverse have integral coordinates outside a prescribed finite set of places. They cover G as the finite set varies. A compact set of representatives meets the requirement for one common finite set, by taking the union from a finite subcover. In coordinates one can enlarge that set to include the finitely many primes in the multiplication table of the chosen rational basis. Applied to the hyperbolic pair, the compact family transports the fixed pair to each of the pairs used in the shell comparison.

Why does a compact set have finite mean on a nonzero norm fibre?

Fix t ∈ F× and a compact adelic set Ω. An unrepresented norm contributes zero. If ⟨e,e⟩ = t for a rational e, the line Ee is nondegenerate. Its orthogonal complement has dimension M−1. The stabilizer G1 of the vector e is the adelic unitary group of this complement. Witt’s extension theorem identifies every rational vector of norm t with γ−1e for some γ ∈ Γ. Two choices give the same vector precisely when they differ by left multiplication by an element of Γ1 = Γ ∩ G1. Thus the classes are Γ1γ in Γ1 ∖ Γ. Unfolding replaces the sum integrated over Γ ∖ G by the integral of f(h) = 𝟙Ω(h−1e) over Γ1 ∖ G, before division by V.

The compact representative theorem supplies a compact set C of isometries such that every norm-t vector in Ω has the form ce with c ∈ C. It uses adelic Witt extension and compact lifting on the closed orbit. Consequently, whenever f(h) = 1, we have h−1e = ce and hc fixes e. Thus the support lies in G1C−1. The compact-cover integral bound for a function ≤ 1 bounds its unfolded integral by a fixed constant times the volume of Γ1 ∖ G1. Finite arithmetic quotient volume in the smaller dimension proves integrability on this fibre.

Finally, the continuous norm maps Ω into a compact adelic set, which meets the closed discrete diagonal copy of F in finitely many points. Add the finite means for those nonzero norms. Enclose Ω in one box and apply the isotropic bound to its nonzero vectors of norm zero. This gives the finite reference mean used in the large-radius packing estimate. Including the origin in that reference box adds exactly one.

Use the height to choose the radius. After reduction write yw = Im τw and Y = minw yw. There are fixed t, κ > 0 such that Y ≥ t and every yw ≤ Y/κ. The finite test φ is locally constant and compactly supported, so it is bounded and its support has a common denominator N. Positive definiteness of the Gaussian majorant bounds the absolute weight of a vector of maximum coordinate size s by a constant times exp(−cYs²) for some c > 0. For √Y s ≤ 1 use the ball of radius 1/√Y. For 2j−1 < √Y s ≤ 2j use the ball of radius 2j/√Y and weight exp(−c4j−1). The ball bound costs at most a constant times 4jkY−k/2, since Y ≥ t. Subtract the common term. The zero vector contributes φ(0) to the theta average. The Eisenstein expansion begins with the same term. For each denominator ideal 𝔞 there are at most N(𝔞) classes, since they lie in 𝔞−1/𝒪F. Their total is bounded using ∑𝔞≠0 N(𝔞)1−M, which converges for M ≥ 3.
