Where do the finitely many cusp matrices come from?

Let F be totally real of degree d, with ring of integers 𝒪. A point of the Hilbert upper half-space has one coordinate τw = xw + iyw, with yw > 0, at each real embedding w. For a matrix in SL₂(F) with bottom row (c,b), direct multiplication by the conjugate denominator gives Im(gτ)w = yw/|w(c)τw+w(b)|². We need one row whose denominator is small at every embedding.

Embed 𝒪² in ℝ2d using all its real embeddings. At each place, apply to a pair (a,b) of real coordinates the determinant-one map (a,b) ↦ (√y · a, (xa+b)/√y). The product map preserves the covolume of the lattice for every τ. Choose a cube [−R,R]2d of volume greater than 22d times this covolume. Minkowski’s convex body theorem supplies a nonzero lattice point in it. Adding the squares of the two coordinates at each place gives a pair (c,b) ∈ 𝒪², independent of the place, with

|w(c)τw + w(b)|² ≤ 2R²yw   at every w.

Complete that row. Its two entries generate a nonzero integral ideal I. The class group is finite, so fix an integral ideal J in each class. For the class of I there is a scalar λ with λI = J. Hence |N(λ)| = N(J)/N(I) ≤ N(J), uniformly bounded by a constant B over the fixed finite list. Put (p,q) = λ(c,b). From pJ−1 + qJ−1 = 𝒪 choose a,b′ ∈ J−1 with aq−b′p = 1. This gives a determinant-one matrix g with top row in J−1 and bottom row in J. Choose one such matrix r for each class that occurs. Every entry of r−1g is a difference of two products in J J−1 = 𝒪. Thus g = rk with k ∈ SL₂(𝒪) and r in a fixed finite set. Multiplying (p,q) by a unit preserves the ideal, so the same construction works for every unit multiple. Why can two spheres of different lengths have the same mass coefficient?

Fix a CM extension E/F with conjugation, and an anisotropic Hermitian plane with nonsingular matrix J. Write Q(x) = x*Jx, where * means conjugate transpose. For β ∈ F×, the rational sphere consists of x ∈ E² with Q(x) = β. Average its rational points over the adelic unitary quotient to obtain a measure Θβ. The first mass formula for this length supplies a nonnegative number κ such that, on product tests, Θβ integrates as κ times the product of the local Gram-fibre integrals. A separate choice of κ for each β would leave an unknown weight inside the sum over lengths. A rational change of variables makes the same κ work throughout that sum.

Build the change of variables from two points. Suppose Q(x) = β and Q(x′) = β′, both nonzero. If x*J = (r₀,r₁), put y = (−r₁,r₀)t and take the two columns of Pₓ to be x and y. Pₓ*JPₓ = β diag(1, det J),   γ = Pₓ′Pₓ−1,   γ*Jγ = λJ,   λ = β′/β.

In particular γx = x′. Its entries belong to E and its multiplier λ belongs to F. This one matrix bijects all rational points of the first sphere with those of the second. On the group used in the average, put h′ = γhγ−1. It is unitary and γ(h−1x) = (h′)−1γx. Pull back the Haar measure and the fundamental domain together under this conjugation. The volume dividing the average is preserved. Reindexing the sum and changing variables gives γ∗Θβ = Θβ′ because the normalized theta measure is independent of these auxiliary choices.

Compute what happens on a fibre. At a place v, write dX for ambient additive Haar measure and db for Haar measure on the scalar length coordinate. The Gram-fibre measures mᵥ(b) recover the ambient integral by integrating over b on the regular locus. Define the positive factors aᵥ and bᵥ by γ∗dX = aᵥ dX and (multiplication by λ)∗db = bᵥ db. Since Q(γX) = λQ(X), the changed family must reconstruct aᵥ dX using bᵥ db. Uniqueness of the normalized fibre measures fixes the quotient, including its direction. Combine all infinite places in F∞.

γ∗mᵥ(β) = (aᵥ/bᵥ) mᵥ(β′),   (a∞/b∞) ∏v finite (aᵥ/bᵥ) = 1.

For the first product formula the proof expresses γ as a linear map in F-coordinates. For the second, scalar congruence on a one-by-one Hermitian matrix acts by λ². Outside finitely many places the factors are one and γ and its inverse preserve the standard lattice. On a product test enlarge its finite set of places to include these exceptions. All local changes of measure then cancel in the product, leaving exactly the original κ in the formula for Θβ′.

Over ℚ(i)/ℚ take J = I₂, x = (1,0)t and x′ = (1,i)t. Their lengths are 1 and 2. The frame gives γ with rows (1,i), (i,1). Multiplication gives γ*γ = 2I₂ and detℚ(i)γ = 2. At infinity its factor on vectors is therefore 1/4, and on lengths it is 1/2. The fibre factor is (1/4)/(1/2) = 1/2. At 2 the absolute values are |4|₂ = 1/4 and |2|₂ = 1/2, giving pushforward factors 4 and 2 and fibre factor 2. At every odd prime the factors are one. Thus the product of the fibre factors is (1/2)·2 = 1, although the real fibre measure alone changes. This computes the transport of a mass formula without evaluating either sphere’s individual mass.

Which lengths reach the counting theorem? Start with the coefficient supplied for a fixed β ≠ 0. If the infinite fibre measure or any finite fibre measure is zero, its factorization forces Θβ = 0. The local finiteness and summability already supplied let one write the zero factorization with coefficient 1 directly. Otherwise the binary representation theorem gives a rational vector of length β from the nonzero infinite fibre measure. Now consider every β′ ≠ 0. A represented β′ receives the same κ by the preceding argument. For an unrepresented β′ the rational sum is empty, and the contrapositive of that representation theorem gives zero infinite fibre measure. Apply the individual mass formula for β′ to obtain its finiteness and summability conditions. Its zero factorization now holds with the chosen κ as well. For example, length −1 is empty over the reals in the positive definite plane above. The degree-one Gram matrix at β = 0 is singular, and anisotropy leaves only the zero rational vector there. The counting theorem uses precisely the nonzero lengths. Having a common κ on all of them permits the positive-volume comparison that gives κ = 1.

Why does the infinite fibre detect a rational point in this plane?

For a proposed nonzero length t, compare J with diag(t, t det J). Their determinants differ by t², the norm of t from E to F. At an indefinite real place both planes have one positive and one negative direction. At a definite place representing the sign of t makes their signatures agree there too. With all signatures equal, Landherr’s classification gives a rational isometry of the two Hermitian forms. The image of the first basis vector then has length t. Consequently a missing rational length has the wrong sign at some definite real place. The infinite fibre is empty there and its supported measure vanishes. The archive obtains the classification result used here from a quadratic Hasse norm theorem.

gv(s) = 0 for s ∉ 𝒪,   |gv(s) − 1| ≤ 3/q for s ∈ 𝒪,   |gv(s) − 1| ≤ 1/q² for s ∈ 𝒪×.

The factor ½ occurs because the field trace doubles a scalar from the base field. The local Gram-fibre integration formula identifies gv on nonzero lengths with the continuous density of the pushforward of volume on 𝒪⁴ by Q. In particular, if the ratio of the inverse-image volume to target volume is constant on all sufficiently small target balls about s, it equals the fibre mass there. Choose a vector on which Q is nonzero and take it as the first vector of a basis over the local field. For each choice of the other three coordinates the equation Q = 0 has at most two roots in the first. Singletons have Haar measure zero, so Fubini gives zero volume. An invertible linear change of basis preserves null sets. Thus integrating the regular density gives the entire volume vol(𝒪⁴) = 1.

How is a measure on a single length defined?

Even when a vector of length s exists, the set of all vectors of that length has zero four-dimensional volume. We can still assign it a three-dimensional measure. At a good finite place, choose a primitive residue class C = a + π𝒪⁴. Since B is invertible modulo π, some coordinate of B a is a unit. Keep the other three coordinates y as parameters and use the length in place of that coordinate. For any s in I = Q(a) + π𝒪 and any compatible y, there is exactly one remaining coordinate in its residue class. Indeed, given a solution modulo πk, changing its next digit changes the next length digit by multiplication by that unit. Every required digit has a unique lift, and completeness gives the coordinate. Call this vector x(s,y).

For each fixed y this correspondence preserves one-dimensional Haar measure. It gives a bijection of the residue balls at every precision, and corresponding balls have the same volume. Integration in the length and the three free coordinates now gives, for a locally constant test function φ on C,

∫C φ(x) dx = ∫I (∫y ≡ afree mod π φ(x(s,y)) dy) ds.

The inner integral defines the contribution of this class to the length-s fibre. For φ = 1 it equals q−3 throughout I. For example, over ℚ₃ take the sum of four squares and the class (1,0,0,0) modulo 3. Each of the last three coordinates ranges over 3ℤ₃. The contribution is 1/27 at every length congruent to 1. Integrated over that target ball it gives (1/27)(1/3) = 1/81, precisely the volume of the source class.

Every nonzero integral vector has a unique expression πjz with j ≥ 0 and z primitive. On this shell four-dimensional volume scales by q−4j and length by π2j, so the fibre measure scales by q−2j. At a fixed nonzero integral s only 2j ≤ ord(s) can occur. The shell sum for φ = 1 thus defines a locally constant density near s. It agrees pointwise with the continuous regular Gram-fibre mass used in the product formula by uniqueness on regular fibres. Both integrate to the same volume on every sufficiently small target ball, and every such ball has positive measure.

Why is the error smaller at a unit length?

First count primitive vectors, meaning that some coordinate is a unit. For a residue value a, let N(a) be the number of solutions of the reduced equation Q(x̄) = a in the four-dimensional residue space. Delete the zero vector if a = 0, and write N×(a) for the resulting count. Every remaining solution has nonzero gradient Bx̄ because B is invertible modulo π. Suppose a solution modulo πk is lifted to x + πky. The next digit of the length is determined by the nonzero linear functional y ↦ (Bx̄)·y. Exactly q³ choices give any prescribed next digit. A target ball modulo πk has volume q−k. Its primitive preimage consists of N×(a) q3(k−1) balls of volume q−4k. The ratio is independent of k and equals N×(a)/q³.

Residue count. For a nonsingular quadratic form in four variables over a field of odd cardinality q, one has |N(a) − q³| ≤ q if a ≠ 0, and |N(0) − q³| ≤ q². For a unit length, every solution is primitive. Dividing the first bound by q³ proves the unit estimate. For any integral length the primitive density P(s) therefore satisfies |P(s) − 1| ≤ 1/q + 1/q³, where the last summand allows for deleting the origin.

Choose a nontrivial additive character ψ of the residue field and write G(u) = ∑x ψ(uQ(x)). Character orthogonality gives qN(a) = q⁴ + ∑u≠0 ψ(−ua)G(u). Indeed summing ψ(ut) over u gives q for t = 0 and zero otherwise, since translation by an element with character different from one preserves that sum.

Over a field of odd characteristic, completing squares diagonalizes the nonsingular form with four nonzero coefficients. If χ is the quadratic character extended by χ(0) = 0, the equation y² = z has 1 + χ(z) solutions. In each of the four one-variable character sums, changing u from 1 to a nonzero value consequently multiplies the sum by χ(u). The four factors give χ(u)⁴ = 1, so G(u) = G(1). Its modulus is q². To check this, square its modulus and replace the first argument in the double sum by x + y. The sum over x of ψ(xtBy) vanishes unless y = 0, when it contributes q⁴. Finally ∑u≠0 ψ(−ua) equals −1 for a ≠ 0 and q − 1 for a = 0. Dividing by q gives the two count estimates.

What do vectors divisible by the prime contribute?

Write k = ordv(s) for a nonzero integral length. If k is 0 or 1, every vector of length s is primitive, since Q(πy) = π²Q(y). If k ≥ 2, the nonprimitive part lies in π𝒪⁴. Passing from y to πy multiplies source volume by q−4. The matching target ball is scaled by π², which multiplies target volume by q−2. Taking the ratio gives the recurrence

gv(s) = P(s) + q−2gv(s/π²)   (k ≥ 2).

Each application lowers the valuation by two. To verify the uniform error, put w = 1/q ≤ ½ and assume the lower-valuation density differs from one by at most 3w. The primitive bound and the recurrence give an absolute error at most w + w³ + w²(1 + 3w) = w + w² + 4w³ ≤ 3w. The two base valuations already obey this bound. This proves it for every nonzero integral length.

For example, take the positive Hermitian form |x₁|² + |x₂|² over ℚ(i) at 3. The scalar form in four coordinates is a sum of four squares. Modulo 3, each nonzero coordinate contributes 1. To represent 1 there must be one or four nonzero coordinates, giving 4·2 + 2⁴ = 24 solutions. To represent 0 with a primitive vector requires three nonzero coordinates, giving 4·2³ = 32. Thus g₃(1) = 24/27 = 8/9 and g₃(3) = 32/27. At length 9 the vectors divisible by 3 first contribute, giving g₃(9) = 32/27 + (1/9)(8/9) = 104/81.

The reason for keeping both error bounds appears in the average over lengths. At units the error is already at most q−2. The larger bound 3/q occurs only on the nonunits, which have local measure 1/q. Their contribution to the mean absolute error on 𝒪 is at most 3/q². In the global argument, divisibility of a rational length by several primes is counted by the norm of their product ideal.

How does a general Schwartz test reach every regular fibre?

The density at infinity serves a separate purpose. Here the tuple has any number n of columns, the rational form J is nonsingular, and source and target carry additive Haar measures μ and ν. When n > M, the rank of a Gram matrix is at most M, so every fibre at an invertible target is empty.

Fix a regular target and choose a neighbourhood O in which congruence carries any one target to every other by continuously varying invertible matrices. Right multiplication LS by hS transports mS₀ to mS up to a positive continuous factor. It is the target pushforward Haar multiplier divided by the source pushforward Haar multiplier. Near the fixed target the inverse maps are bounded, so ‖x‖ ≤ B‖LSx‖ with one B. Schwartz decay of order D+1 now gives |Φ(LSx)| ≤ CW(x) uniformly nearby. Dominated convergence on the single reference fibre proves continuity for the integrals of both Φ and |Φ|.

To recover the density identity, multiply Φ by continuous compactly supported cutoffs between zero and one, eventually equal to one at each point. For each cutoff use the compact-test disintegration. On a compact set K of regular targets, continuity bounds ∫ |Φ| dmS by one constant. Dominated convergence applies on each fibre, on K, and on the source, where |Φ| is integrable. Thus the integral over the preimage of K equals the integral of the fibre densities over K. The global formula uses this theorem first with its coordinate measures, then with source and target measures multiplied by positive scalars a and a′. The density in the second use acquires exactly a/a′.

For the Whittaker integral the two Fourier measures are self-dual. If the measure on matrices is cv times its coordinate measure and the measure on Hermitian targets is ev times its coordinate measure, the density is multiplied by cv/ev. This follows already by integrating over a compact target set. The source integral gains cv, while integration against the new target measure supplies ev. The reference scalar measures give the valuation ring volume one at each finite place and the ring of integers covolume one at infinity. With the chosen global additive character, both families of self-dual scaling constants have product one and equal one at almost every finite place.

gv(T) = (cv/ev) ∫ Φv(X) dmv,T(X),   (c∞/e∞) ∏v finite (cv/ev) = 1.

The coordinate-measure identity, initially tested on nonnegative measurable products, applies to the integrable complex-valued product Φ. Why can we integrate the paired kernels in either order?

The Siegel–Weil theorem on these data supplies integrability in h. Its regular Eisenstein value bounds the absolute value of the normalized target mean by a power of the doubled height. The height at (g,g) is at most a constant times a power of the height at g. Multiplying the mean by ν(Y) therefore gives a polynomial bound for ∫Y |K(g,y)|² dν(y). This step uses the rank and Witt-index assumptions of the global formula.

By rational invariance we can take the height H(x) on the quotient, absorbing a constant in the bound. At every fixed y, the kernel also grows at most polynomially in x. The same decay proves that each defining lift integral exists there. Continuity and invariance in both rational variables give measurable kernels on the quotients.

Change the order. Put F(x,x′,y) = K₁(x,y)u₁(x) K₂(x′,y)u₂(x′). For fixed x,x′, Cauchy–Schwarz in y gives ∫ |K₁(x,y)K₂(x′,y)| dν ≤ N₁(x)N₂(x′). The remaining bound separates into a function of x and a function of x′. Tonelli’s theorem applies to |F| because it is nonnegative, giving the absolute bound below. With equal kernels and equal inputs this bound also gives Θi ∈ L²(Y). We can now use Fubini for the complex integrand itself.

∫X²×Y |F| ≤ M₁M₂ < ∞.
⟨Θ₁,Θ₂⟩Y = ∫X² ⟨K₁(x,·),K₂(x′,·)⟩Y u₁(x) u₂(x′) dμ(x) dμ(x′).

The Petersson pairing here conjugates the second factor. If g₁ and g₂ represent x and x′, the mixed doubling identity makes the inner pairing the normalized doubled theta mean times ν(Y) and χB(det g₂). Substitution accounts for the single target-volume factor in the norm formula. The absolute bound above exchanges integrations over the two source copies and the target. Try the two orders on an infinite sum. Give X = {1,2,…} counting measure and Y = {+1,−1} equal probabilities. Let K(n,y) = n yn−1, u₁(n) = 21−n and u₂(n) = (z/2)n−1 with |z| = 1. 6.13The part that stays inside the integral

For each admissible chain step and each additive measure and fundamental domain of covolume one, choose one polynomial datum φ and one finite-type test vector v. They work for every nonzero vector u of the stage multiplicity space. The order matters. These choices give a nonzero JS(s₀) already before choosing a Hecke eigenvalue. Two restrictions on the finite datum enter the support proof. Its matrix must lie in the summand selected by the split-place idempotent and be integral in the chosen frames. At every selected CM place its top square block must reduce to an invertible block triangular matrix, and the family of upper-left blocks must meet the given subgroup condition. If both a matrix and its translate have nonzero test value, these unit top blocks recover integrality of the transformation in the selected summand. Self-duality gives the conjugate summand, and the two reductions give the required level of the finite transformation. Away from the selected places this already follows from g ∈ U(S). Thus a transformation outside the level moves the support off itself.

For the Weil matrix coefficient one must still transfer this disjointness to the theta vector. A finite sum of additive characters is one on the support and zero on its translate. The corresponding sum of Heisenberg operators fixes the datum. After conjugating the coefficients, transporting by g−1, and reversing the translations, it kills the same datum. The operators commute with the polynomial Fock construction at infinity. Moving the finite sum from one entry of the Hermitian pairing to the other therefore shows W(g) = 0.

On the remaining subgroup, write g = b∞ κ with κ ∈ K. The Weil coefficient acquires the level character χK(κ). The Petersson coefficient acquires the same character before conjugation. Their product contains |χK(κ)|² = 1. The Petersson coefficient also contributes the scalar ⟨u,u⟩ and a product of real discrete-series matrix coefficients. Pushing the restricted adelic Haar measure forward along the projection to the real group gives a Haar measure m∞. Its normalization includes the finite-level volume. If Z∞ denotes the remaining Weil coefficient times the conjugate of that product of real coefficients, the result is

JS(s₀) = ⟨u,u⟩ · ∫ Z∞(b∞) dm∞.

The finite-level computation controls the entire restricted integral, including any relation between the block reductions at the selected places.

Why the real-place projection has positive mass

Fix one real place τ of a step of the iterated theta chain. Its integral pairs a Weil matrix coefficient with the conjugate of a discrete-series coefficient. Even when both vectors have norm one, the integral can vanish if the two coefficients detect different parts of the representation. Here the Fock model realizes vectors using polynomials with a Gaussian inner product. Restricting a representation to a compact subgroup breaks it into finite-dimensional types. A joint highest-weight polynomial selects a specific type for each of the two compact groups. We must show that this choice survives projection onto the component detected by the source vector. The chain chooses a polynomial Φ of the prescribed highest weights for both compact groups and a unit source vector of its prescribed highest weight. Its real-place comparison identifies the polynomial with a vector in the Fock model of the oscillator representation.

Build the projection. Let G̃ be the double cover of the real unitary group U(p,q) with Haar measure ν. Let σ be the source discrete series on this cover, v its chosen unit vector, and dσ its formal degree for ν. We use the inner product linear in its second entry. Write mv(g) = ⟨v,σ(g)v⟩. For unit v, Schur orthogonality gives ∫ |mv(g)|² dν(g) = 1/dσ. This fixes the scalar that makes the projector send v to itself in σ. For any unitary representation π of the cover define the operator

Pvx = dσ ∫G̃ mv(g) π(g)x dν(g).

The chain’s gap condition ensures absolute integrability of the kernel. The estimate used here requires every pair of source parameters in opposite signature blocks to differ in absolute value by at least 120(p+q)min(p,q)3/2. In polar coordinates the discrete-series decay then pays for the growth of Haar measure. The joint-vector theorem additionally uses the admissible pair of parameters, their matching compact weights and the chain’s further gap and Casimir conditions.

Schur orthogonality gives Pvx = ⟨v,x⟩v in σ itself. In any π, inversion gives Pv* = Pv. Convolving the same kernel on both sides of a translate gives Pvπ(g)Pv = mv(g)Pv. At the identity mv(1) = 1, proving idempotence. Its range is the closed span of the vectors T v for continuous intertwiners T from σ to π. In the Fock representation let η be the normalized joint polynomial vector. Testing the integral operator against η and using η − Pvη ⟂ Pvη gives

∫G̃ ⟨η,π(g)η⟩ mv(g) dν(g) = ⟨η,Pvη⟩/dσ = ‖Pvη‖²/dσ.

The Fock coefficient has absolute value at most one by unitarity, so the same integrability estimate justifies this pairing.

6.16Summing the split local integral one lattice at a time

At a split place, the unitary group can be written as GLa over the local field. A matrix takes the standard lattice to a new lattice, and two matrices give the same lattice exactly when they differ on the right by its stabilizer K. Give K Haar volume one. Choose a uniformizer ϖ, an element of valuation one, and write q for the residue-field size. The elementary divisors of a lattice give a unique weakly decreasing tuple of integers d = (d₁,…,da). Two integers extracted from it enter the kernel. The signed sum D = ∑dᵢ gives the determinant valuation and the twist zD, with |z| = 1. The sum k = ∑|dᵢ| measures the total displacement. For d = (1,−1), the twist is one although the displacement is two. With X = q−(a/2+s), the spherical section gives zDXk on every lattice in the cell.

Let v be the spherical vector and write its matrix coefficient as c(g) = λ(π(g)v). By the Hecke eigenvector equation, summing π(g)v over this cell gives a scalar hd times v. Applying λ gives hdc(1). Thus all the information from the representations in this part of the sum fits into a single scalar per tuple. Write Ad = zDhdc(1). If |c(g)| ≤ C, then |Ad| ≤ C |Sd| by the triangle inequality.

In the first cell, the sublattices of index 3 correspond to the four lines in the two-dimensional residue space. Multiplication by ϖ identifies the second cell with the first. The coefficient of X is therefore 8.

At displacement two the tuples (1,1) and (−1,−1) give one lattice each. The other three are (2,0), (1,−1) and (0,−2), all equivalent by central scaling for the purpose of counting. A lattice of type (2,0) is the kernel of a surjection onto the quotient of the local integer ring by (ϖ²). There are 9² − 3² primitive pairs of coefficients for such a map. Two maps have the same kernel precisely when a unit of the quotient relates them, and there are 9 − 3 such units. Each of the three cells has 72/6 = 12 elements. The counting series begins 1 + 8X + 38X². For the constant coefficient 1 of the trivial representation, the two Satake parameters here are √3 and 1/√3. Thus the product below becomes (1 − X²)(1 − 3X²)/[(1 − 3X)²(1 − X)²]. Its coefficients bound the absolute sum at this one place. (ThF)(g) = ∑xK ∈ G/K h(x)F(gx),   (T1DF)(1) = ∑xK ⊂ D F(x).

The second formula sets h equal to the indicator of D. Thus two functions with the same normalized Hecke values at the identity have the same sum on every double class.

Work over ℚ₃(i), i² = −1, with its anti-diagonal unitary group in rank two. Take d = diag(3,1/3) and D = KdK. Write u(c) for the upper unitriangular matrix with upper entry c. Unitarity gives c + σ(c) = 0, so c ranges over iℚ₃. The triangular labels are dau(c)K. At fixed a, two labels agree exactly when their corners differ by an element of iℤ₃. Throughout D, the least valuation of any matrix entry is −1, since left or right multiplication by an integral matrix with integral inverse preserves that minimum. On our triangular representative it is min(a,−a,a + v(c)), with v(0) = +∞. The following possibilities exhaust this test.

Direct multiplication gives u(c) = l diag(c,−1/c)J l. Both diagonal entries of diag(c,−1/c)d are units and this matrix preserves the form, so the middle factor belongs to Kd−1K = D. Why do these labels count each coset once?

The sum runs over cosets gKn. With n = m + 2, write Gm for the smaller unitary group and U for the upper block triangular unitary matrices with identity diagonal blocks of sizes 1, m, 1. Fix a representative g₀ for each smaller coset. Given an integer a, the block diagonal matrix M = diag(ϖa, g₀, ϖ−a) is unitary. The Hermitian form pairs the first coordinate with the last, so the two outer factors cancel; the middle block preserves its own form. The labels and their map are

ℤ × (Gm/Km) × (U/(U ∩ Kn))   →   Gn/Kn,   (a, g₀Km, [u]) ↦ MuKn.

Changing u by an integral factor on the right leaves its image unchanged. Changing the chosen representative for the middle coset can change the radical coordinate. We keep that choice fixed throughout the count.

Recover the labels from a unitary matrix

Existence. Triangularize g on the right by an integral unitary change to obtain g = Bk, with B upper triangular. The local Iwasawa theorem does this by integral unitary row operations on g−1 followed by inversion. A pivot of largest absolute value makes the required ratios integral. Orthogonality for the anti-diagonal form supplies the vanishing entries in the paired half once the first ⌊n/2⌋ columns are reduced.

Take the three diagonal blocks of B to form M′. Block triangular multiplication preserves diagonal blocks, and the unitary inverse exchanges the outer coordinates and takes their conjugates. Thus M′ is unitary and B = M′u′ with u′ ∈ U. If the first entry is x, the last is 1/σ(x). Take a = v(x) and let g₀ represent the coset of the middle block. In h = M−1M′ the two outer entries are units and the middle block belongs to Km. Hence h ∈ Kn. Conjugation by a block diagonal matrix preserves U. The identity g = M(hu′h−1)(hk) now has the desired form.

Uniqueness. Suppose MuKn = M′u′Kn for two sets of labels. Put h = M−1M′. The quotient (Mu)−1M′u′ factors as h times a member of U. Its diagonal blocks are those of h, and it belongs to the integral group. The outside entries of h are ϖa′−a and ϖa−a′. Both must be integral. This forces a = a′. Its middle block g₀−1g′₀ is integral and unitary, so the two middle cosets coincide. With our fixed representatives M = M′. Cancellation leaves u−1u′ ∈ U ∩ Kn, exactly the last equivalence relation in the displayed map.

How the length of one matrix determines the two levels

Length counts independent denominators in the lattice generated by the standard rows and the rows of the given matrix. Fix the signed outer valuation a, a middle unitary block g of size m and length h, and one unipotent representative with row r, paired column b and upper corner c. In three blocks their product has the form

G = diag(ϖa, g, ϖ−a) · [(1, r, c), (0, I, b), (0, 0, 1)],

where the three parenthesized triples are block rows. The middle lattice supplies integral matrices U,V,C with gC integral, (U + Vg)C = I and v(det C) = h. We use the additive valuation v(ϖ) = 1. For any scalar or row x, let d(x) be the least integer k ≥ 0 for which ϖkx is integral in every coordinate. This includes d(0) = 0. Put

α = max(a,0),   R = d(rC),   S = d(c − r · (CVg)b),   t = max(0,R − α).

The length of G is |a| + h + max(2t, S − 2α). Thus a budget of j above |a| + h allows R ≤ α + ⌊j/2⌋ and S ≤ 2α + j, simultaneously. For a ≥ 0 the allowable levels are e = a + ⌊j/2⌋ and f = 2a + j. For a < 0, the base length still includes −a but the two levels are just ⌊j/2⌋ and j.

Derive the length by eliminating rows

In the sum of the two row lattices, combine the middle rows of the identity using U and the middle rows of G using V. These mixed rows form the block (0, C−1, Vgb). Multiplying this block on the left by C and subtracting the standard middle rows leaves pure last coordinates (CVg)b. Likewise, subtracting gC times the mixed rows from the middle rows of G leaves (gCU)b. The original last rows also give the scalars 1 and ϖ−a. The pure last coordinates just listed span the fractional ideal generated by y = ϖ−α−t. Indeed the row and column identity says that a power of ϖ clears rC exactly when it clears both columns (CVg)b and (gCU)b. The largest denominator among those columns, 1 and ϖ−a thus needs α + t powers, and some generator attains that value.

Build a triangular block matrix P with these mixed middle rows and last row (0,0,y). For a ≥ 0 keep the first standard row in P and subtract ϖa times it from the first row of G. For a < 0 keep the first row of G and subtract the first standard row from ϖ−a times the retained row. Either way the extra row is (0,ϖαr,ϖαc). The pivot in the first column of P is 1 in the first case and ϖa in the second. The other diagonal blocks are C−1 and y, so −v(det P) = max(−a,0) + h + α + t = |a| + h + t.

In the basis of rows of P, the coordinates of the extra row are

ρ = (0, ϖαrC, ϖα(c − r · (CVg)b)/y).

The middle term already contributes ϖαr · (CVg)b in the last column, explaining the subtraction. The largest denominator exponent in ρ is t′ = max(t, S − 2α − t). If t′ is zero, the extra row already belongs to the lattice of P. Otherwise replace a row of P whose coefficient in ρ has valuation −t′ with the extra row. The new determinant is the old determinant times that coefficient. The old row is recovered by dividing by this same coefficient, since its inverse and the ratios of every other coefficient to it are integral. This gives a basis of the full enlarged lattice. Its length is |a| + h + t + t′, the formula above.

Why one row controls both final-column denominators

Eliminating the middle rows produced two columns, w = (CVg)b and z = (gCU)b. We want the least power of the uniformizer ϖ that clears both. Write d(x) for the least k ≥ 0 such that ϖkx has integral coordinates. The proof gives a test for every scalar λ in the local field, including scalars that conjugation moves.

λrC is integral   ⇔   λw and λz are integral.   d(rC) = max(d(w), d(z)).

Let J reverse the coordinates and let σ be the valuation-preserving field involution. Write x♯ for reversal, conjugation and transposition, turning a row into a column or a column into a row. Then b = −r♯. The middle block is unitary for J, so g−1 = Jσ(g)TJ and (xg)♯ = g−1x♯ for a row x. Reversal permutes the valuations and σ preserves them. Thus λx is integral exactly when λx♯ is integral. The middle lattice supplies integral U,V,C,gC with (U + Vg)C = I. These square matrices over a field also satisfy C(U + Vg) = I.

Set rC = rC. Expand r = rCU + (rCV)g and take the negative adjoint. This gives b = x + g−1y, where x = −(rCU)♯ and y = −(rCV)♯. If λrC is integral, so are λx and λy. Substitution in the two columns gives

w = (I − CU)x + CVy,   z = (gC)Ux + (I − (gC)V)y.

All four coefficient matrices are integral. For the converse, I = CVg + CU gives b = w + g−1z. Taking the negative adjoint again yields rC = −w♯C − z♯(gC). Integrality of λw and λz therefore implies integrality of λrC. Taking λ = ϖk gives the maximum in the test above. In the length calculation the last column also contains 1 and ϖ−a. Its largest denominator exponent is consequently max(0,a,d(rC)). If the row exponent exceeds max(0,a), lowering it by one forces at least one of the two column tests to fail. This is where the proof finds an entry attaining the bound.

Either column can supply the largest denominator

Over ℚ₃(i) with i² = −1 and σ(i) = −i, take the matrices below. Each pair of parentheses denotes one row.

g = [(1, i/3), (0, 1)],   C = diag(1,3),   U = [(1,0), (i,0)],   V = [(0,0), (−i,0)].

The upper-right entry of g has trace zero, so σ(g)TJg = J. Multiplication gives U + Vg = diag(1,1/3) and gC = [(1,i),(0,3)]. Both CVg and gCU have zero first row. Their last rows are (−3i,1) and (3i,0). For r = (1/3,i/9) the paired column is b = (i/9,−1/3)T. The last entries of w,z are 1/3 − 1/3 = 0 and −1/3. Change just the second row coordinate to i/3. Now the last entries are 1 − 1/3 = 2/3 and −1. In both cases d(rC) = 1. For the first choice of r, only z detects that power of 3. For the second, only w does. Both examples admit upper corner zero because r · b = 0.

Counting the rows and lifting each one

The row count has to answer two questions. How many row classes pass the lattice test? For each such row, is there a corner with the required denominator that makes the matrix unitary? Fix the middle unitary block g of size m and length h. The lattice calculation supplies integral matrices U,V,C with gC integral, (U + Vg)C = I and v(det C) = h. Here v is additive with v(ϖ) = 1. At row level e, set A = ϖeC. The admissible rows form Λ = {r ∈ Lm : rA ∈ 𝒪m}, and two rows have the same class when their difference is integral.

Write A = P diag(ϖd₁,…,ϖdₘ) Q with P,Q and their inverses integral. The diagonal matrix is integral because it equals P−1AQ−1, so every dᵢ ≥ 0. Changing r to rP preserves the integral row lattice and removes P from the calculation. Multiplying on the right by Q preserves integrality in both directions. The ith coordinate can now range over ϖ−dᵢ𝒪/𝒪. This quotient has (q²)dᵢ elements, since each digit ranges over the extension residue field. Multiplying the coordinate counts and taking determinants gives

[Λ : 𝒪m] = (q²)∑ dᵢ = (q²)v(det A) = q2(h+me).

Raising the row level by one allows one additional residue-field digit in each of the m coordinates. The factor (q²)h is already present at level zero.

How to choose the corner

For a representative r ∈ Λ, form its paired column b by bᵢ = −σ(rm+1−i), using indices 1 through m. Put b₁ = CVg b and b₂ = CU b, where these subscripts now label two whole vectors. They add to b since C(U + Vg) = I. The lattice duality calculation gives ϖeb₁ and ϖeg b₂ integral. To see where g enters, expand r = (rC)U + ((rC)V)g. Negating, conjugating and reversing coordinates sends this to b = x + g−1y with ϖex and ϖey integral, by unitarity of g. Thus b₁ = (I − CU)x + CVy and g b₂ = gCUx + (I − gCV)y. Both expressions have integral matrix coefficients.

Write ⟨x,y⟩ = ∑ᵢ σ(xᵢ)ym+1−i for the Hermitian form and Tr(z) = z + σ(z). Choose an integral τ with Tr(τ) = 1. For example, τ = σ(z)/(σ(z) − z) works whenever z is integral and its difference from its conjugate is a unit. Put

s = ⟨b₁,b₁⟩ − ⟨b₂,b₂⟩,   c = r · b₁ + τs.

The two norms make s fixed by σ. Since r · b₁ = −⟨b,b₁⟩, the trace of c is −⟨b,b₁⟩ − ⟨b₁,b⟩ + s = −⟨b,b⟩ = r · b. This is precisely the unitary relation on the upper-right entry of the unipotent matrix with row r and column b. Its corrected corner is c − r · b₁ = τs. Multiplying a Hermitian norm by ϖ2e scales each of its two arguments by ϖe. For the second norm use ⟨b₂,b₂⟩ = ⟨gb₂,gb₂⟩. Both scaled norms are integral. Consequently the corrected corner passes the test at every f ≥ 2e. The ball count takes e = max(a,0) + ⌊j/2⌋ and f = 2 max(a,0) + j, so every row in its index actually lifts.

A row that uses both denominator powers. Over ℚ₂(ω) with ω² + ω + 1 = 0, take m = 1, g = C = U = 1 and V = 0. With a = 1 and j = 0 the levels are e = 1, f = 2. The four row classes in ½𝒪/𝒪 are represented by 0, 1/2, ω/2 and (1 + ω)/2. Choose r = 1/2. Then b = −1/2, b₁ = 0, b₂ = b, and s = −1/4. Taking τ = −ω gives Tr(τ) = 1 and c = ω/4. Indeed 4c is integral and Tr(c) = −1/4. At the hypothetical smaller level f = 1, any lift of this row would need 2c integral while Tr(2c) = −1/2. The trace of an integral element is integral, so this particular row cannot lift at that level.

Why one more corner digit gives q choices

Fix an admissible row in a unitary cell. Its paired column is then fixed, and the upper-right entry c satisfies c + σ(c) = row · column. Two lifts of the same row therefore differ in the corner by an element of trace zero. Subtracting their corrected corner conditions cancels the row–column term and says that ϖf times this difference is integral. For the valuation ring 𝒪, put T = {u ∈ 𝒪 : σ(u) = −u}. After choosing one lift, all the allowable differences form ϖ−fT. An integral change of corner contributes an element of T, so the fiber over this row class has size [ϖ−fT : T].

The residue field 𝒪/ϖ𝒪 has q² elements. To compute the number of its digits available in a trace-zero corner, choose x ∈ 𝒪 such that Δ = σ(x) − x is a unit. Its existence is part of the unramified involution hypotheses. Every y ∈ 𝒪 has two integral trace-zero coordinates

u = σ(x)y − xσ(y),   w = σ(y) − y,   y = (u + xw)/Δ.

Conversely, start from any u,w ∈ T and use the last formula for y. Since σ(Δ) = −Δ, one gets σ(y) = (u + σ(x)w)/Δ, which recovers w and then u. Thus this is an additive isomorphism T × T ≃ 𝒪. It commutes with multiplication by ϖ because σ fixes ϖ. Reducing both sides modulo ϖ gives [T : ϖT]² = |𝒪/ϖ𝒪| = q². In particular every corner digit has q choices. This proof works even in residue characteristic two because its only scalar division is by the unit Δ.

Multiplication by ϖf identifies the original quotient with T/ϖfT. Each successive quotient ϖiT/ϖi+1T is isomorphic to T/ϖT, so there are precisely qf corner classes, including one when f = 0. The counting theorem inserts this as the second factor, alongside the separate row-lattice index. It uses f = 2 max(a,0) + j in the ball of excess length j.

Four corners at level two. Take L = ℚ₂(ω), where ω² + ω + 1 = 0. This polynomial is irreducible and separable modulo 2, giving the unramified quadratic extension with 𝒪 = ℤ₂[ω], ϖ = 2 and q = 2. Here σ(ω) = −1 − ω. The trace of a + bω is 2a − b, so T = ℤ₂η with η = 1 + 2ω. Taking x = ω gives Δ = −η, a unit. With row zero the column and its correction vanish. At f = 2 the corners have representatives 0, η/4, η/2 and 3η/4. Each has integral quadruple and trace zero. Two representatives agree modulo T precisely when their numerators in units of η agree modulo 4. This checks the local index even in residue characteristic two. In the global chain every dyadic place outside the exceptional set must split. This inert dyadic example therefore illustrates the local counting lemma only.

∑j≥0 djXH+j = c XHJm(X),   Jm(X) = (1 − X)(1 + qX)/(1 − y²).

Taking |X| in the same shell calculation proves absolute convergence. It authorizes regrouping individual cosets by length.

A cell in rank three. Set m = 1, q = 3, a = h = 0. The first four balls contain 1, 3, 81 and 243 cosets. The shells therefore contain 1, 2, 78 and 162. At X = 1/27, y = 1/3, their infinite weighted sum is (26/27)(10/9)/(8/9) = 65/54. The value 65/54 accounts for the diagonal label a = 0 alone. To obtain the local Euler factor, the sum over diagonal valuations weights each cell by its spherical coefficient and includes every a ∈ ℤ.

For a ≥ 0 the middle piece sums to 1/(1 − yβ). For a < 0 it starts at y/β and sums to (y/β)/(1 − y/β). Bringing these to a common denominator gives numerator 1 − y². This cancels the same denominator in Jm. Write Zn for the full normalized spherical sum and α′ for the tail of the parameter list. Summing the third piece over g₀Km now gives the smaller rank sum, with X replaced by q²X.

Zm+2(X,y;β,α′) = [(1 − X)(1 + qX)/((1 − yβ)(1 − y/β))] · Zm(q²X,y;α′).

The hypotheses on |yβ| and |y/β| guarantee both sums converge. In ranks zero and one the whole unitary group is integral, so the normalized sum is 1.

7The arithmetic balance

A bound for a centered prime sum can survive a surprisingly large error in a single arithmetic measurement. The proof takes measurements at many places and along a chain, then divides by their total weight. This chapter follows that division and accounts for each power of the scale that it costs.

7.1An identity before an estimate

Write H for the finite abelian group used to label the translations, E = (ℤ/2ℤ)² × H, and Φ for the subgroup whose first coordinate is zero. The character χC equals +1 on Φ and −1 on its complement. The index 0 in a sum over additive characters denotes the character identically equal to one. The map ℓ assigns a complex number to each character. At this stage it is input data. Its identification with logarithmic derivatives belongs to the arithmetic realization.

Choose a > 0, a translation τ ∈ H, weights wρ > 0 for ρ ∈ Φ, and an integer cutoff N ≥ a/wρ for every such ρ. The host data distinguish a prime d and a finite set S containing 2 and the auxiliary parameter q1, with d outside S. Outside S and d inertia is trivial. At primes of S, both inertia and the specified Frobenius element lie in Φ. At d, the inertia elements are exactly zero and the involution τ₀ = ((1,0),0). Inertia here records the local symmetries invisible on the residue field. Frobenius describes raising residues to the residue-field size.

Write A for the weighted prime-power count at one sample and one chain stage. To assign a weight to g outside Φ, pair it with ρ = ((1,1),0) + g + ((0,0),τ) inside Φ. At n = pi the weight is (a/n − wρ)+, where the subscript means the positive part. At an unramified prime the character sum is 2 if g equals the ith Frobenius power and zero otherwise. Its contribution is therefore twice log p times the weight when that power lies outside Φ. At a prime of S the Frobenius coset lies inside Φ and contributes zero. At d the inertia subgroup has order two, so averaging replaces 2 by 1 at each matching element outside Φ. Each such weight contributes log d times its value. These three calculations identify the count with the finite character expansion.

For v = wρ the identity (a/n − v)+ = v(a/(v n) − 1)+ changes the scale to y = a/v. Terms beyond the cutoff vanish. Write Gψ(y) for the centered ramp. For a nontrivial ψ it sums the von Mangoldt weight, multiplied by the local character value and y/n − 1, over 1 ≤ n ≤ y, then adds y ℓ(ψ). For the trivial character it uses the centered zeta ramp. Substitution gives the following main term, where γ is Euler’s constant.

M = a log a − (1 + γ)a − (a/|Φ|) ∑ρ ∈ Φ log wρ + a ℓ(χC).

The trivial character gives the first three terms. For the other characters the centering contributes −a ℓ(ψ). Summing the conjugate phases over the complementary half of E kills the nonconstant characters except χC, whose sum is −|Φ|. This accounts for the plus sign. The pairing of the two halves permutes the weight indices, giving precisely the average of their logarithms. The remainder A − M is the same character average with centered ramps in the summands. This proves the analytic identity at fixed host data. Identifying the degrees, periods, heights and covolumes of the geometric construction with this particular M is an additional theorem.

At one translation the lattice calculation uses the sum over all sampled indices t and stages j. Its total amplitude was denoted by A = ∑t at. Here the object being summed is the count At,j just computed, and its main term is Mt,j. The two identifications together make the geometric residual exactly ∑t,j (At,j − Re Mt,j). This equality is what allows the character average to use the geometric bound.

7.2Which characters survive?

Let A0 be a subgroup of H. For ψ a character of E, put Sψ = ∑u ∈ A₀ ψ(0, −u). Translation by any v ∈ A0 permutes this sum and multiplies it by ψ(0, −v). Thus the sum vanishes whenever one of these multipliers differs from one. Otherwise it equals |A0|. For e1(τ) = ((1,0),τ) and s ∈ A0, the corresponding shifted sum acquires the phase ψ(e1(τ)). Summing over s ∈ T2 ⊆ A0 and averaging over subgroup translations therefore contributes a density δ2/2 with δ2 = |T2|/|H|. The two in the denominator comes from |Φ| = 2|H|.

For example, take H = ℤ/4ℤ and A0 = {0, 2}. On H the four characters are ψj(h) = exp(2πijh/4) for j = 0, 1, 2, 3. Averaging ψj over A0 gives (1 + (−1)j)/2. The odd indices cancel and the even ones survive with value 1. If T2 contains one element, its contribution occupies one of the eight positions in Φ. The factor 1/8 comes from that count, independently of which surviving character is evaluated.

At a scale x ≥ 3, fix a loss ε > 0, a real sampling weight c with |c| ≤ 1, and a finite sample T ⊆ H. The survivors form the annihilator Ψ of A0. A further selection K ⊆ Ψ retains characters used in the target. These characters satisfy ψ(τ₀) = 1, and the selection includes the trivial character. Among retained characters, a character trivial on all of H receives weight 1. The others receive c. Call these weights ωψ. For retained characters nontrivial on H, the sum over T of ψ(0,τ) differs from c|T| in norm by at most M0x−1+ε|T|, where M0 also bounds |Ψ|. The constants bounding ℓ on retained nontrivial and discarded characters are respectively K0 and CE log x. The sum of norms of the discarded centered ramps is denoted Σ. Orthogonality by itself leaves this last error to be paid.

How much does moving the weight change one ramp?

Fix one measurement, with amplitude a > 0. As its weight w varies, both the scale a/w and the multiplier in front of the centered ramp change. Write Fψ(w) = wGψ(a/w). For all positive w, w′ and every character ψ, the variation satisfies

|Fψ(w) − Fψ(w′)| ≤ (3a/min(w, w′)) |w − w′|.

Assume w ≤ w′, and set Δ = w′ − w. At index n, multiplying the original ramp by w gives (a/n − w)+. Raising the weight by Δ shortens this ramp by at most Δ, even if it crosses zero. Both ramps vanish for n > a/w. Thus we can compare their sums over the same finite set.

For a nontrivial ψ, the coefficient of this ramp is Λ(n) times a local character value of absolute value at most one. At a ramified prime this value is an average of roots of unity. The centering contributes w(a/w)ℓ(ψ) = aℓ(ψ) at either weight, so it cancels. By the triangle inequality the absolute change is at most Δ ∑n≤a/w Λ(n), hence at most 3(a/w)Δ by the following estimate.

Why is the von Mangoldt sum at most three times the cutoff?

Put Ψ(y) = ∑1≤n≤y Λ(n). For an integer m ≥ 1, each prime power pj in (m,2m] contributes log p to Ψ(2m) − Ψ(m). It also contributes one to the exponent of p in the central binomial coefficient. Indeed, counting multiples in (2m)!/(m!)² gives the exponent as the sum over j ≥ 1 of ⌊2m/pj⌋ − 2⌊m/pj⌋. Every summand is zero or one, and every power in that interval contributes one. Therefore Ψ(2m) − Ψ(m) ≤ log binom(2m,m) ≤ 2m log 2. The last inequality follows by summing all binomial coefficients of degree 2m.

If y > 1, choose the integer k with 2k−1 < y ≤ 2k. Adding the estimates at m = 1, 2, …, 2k−1 along the powers of two gives Ψ(y) ≤ (2k+1 − 2) log 2 < (4 log 2)y < 3y. For 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 the sum vanishes.

Theorems used. Legendre’s formula for a factorial

For the trivial character the zeta centering leaves −a log(a/w) + (1 + γ)a. Let D be the uncentered ramp sum at w minus its value at w′. Since every coefficient is Λ(n) ≥ 0, the preceding argument gives 0 ≤ D ≤ 3(a/w)Δ. The centered difference is D − a log(w′/w). The quantity subtracted belongs to the same interval, since log(1 + Δ/w) ≤ Δ/w. The distance between two numbers in that interval is at most its length. This proves the stated constant for ζ as well. Interchanging the weights treats w′ < w.

For example, take a = 12 and change w from 3 to 4. In the zeta sum the term at 2 drops by log 2 and the term at 3 drops by log 3, reaching zero. All other terms have zero change. Thus D = log 6. The centered difference is log 6 − 12 log(4/3), about −1.66. The sign change comes from the logarithmic correction.

The cost per measurement

At a thick index the target weight is b, the actual weight lies in [b, b + η + 1], and |a/b − x| ≤ 1. The smaller weight in the denominator of the variation bound is therefore b. Substituting the two upper bounds gives

|Fψ(w) − Fψ(b)| ≤ 3(a/b)(w − b) ≤ 3(x + 1)(η + 1).

There are f = |Φ| possible positions, each with 2f characters in the Fourier sum, and the sum is divided by f. Adding these two contributions produces the 2b/x per measurement used in the averaged inequality.

8Supplying the arithmetic hypotheses

The arithmetic estimate uses many fields and many primes. To control their total contribution, the proof bounds the lengths of cohomology groups on carefully chosen intervals. This is where one must keep track of which parameters have already been fixed when a field or window is chosen.

8.1From Galois representations to window data

Over a CM field E, the row hypothesis applies to a regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representation of positive rank a. A CM field is a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real field. In this setting a polarization relates a representation to a twist of its conjugate dual. For each allowed ℓ-adic coefficient realization, the conclusion gives a representation of the absolute Galois group on an a-dimensional ℓ-adic vector space, a weight and Hodge–Tate weight data. Its hypotheses include continuity, semisimplicity and prescribed local compatibility. The local theory uses both places above ℓ and places away from ℓ. The window construction uses this row directly and to obtain its open-image input, together with the base-change theorem.

The separate chapter on the two theta lifts explains the Galois input. For the derivative estimate used on the geometric side, see the factorial gain and the mixed-coordinate correction. The estimate on cohomology below has different indices and quantifiers.

8.2What the good arithmetic window controls

One can first think of a degree-one cohomology class as a way of assigning a value to each symmetry. A cocycle satisfies c(gh) = c(g) + g·c(h). Two choices give the same class if they differ by g ↦ g·a − a. For the group of order two acting trivially on ℤ/4, the choice at its generator must double to zero. The two possibilities 0 and 2 give exactly two classes. In the arithmetic problem the group is a Galois group, the action includes a twist and one retains classes whose restrictions vanish at the specified places. This is the reason a kernel of a restriction map occurs below.

We measure a finite ℤℓ-module by its length. Filter it until each successive quotient has order ℓ. If there are d quotients, its order is ℓd. Both ℤ/ℓ² and (ℤ/ℓ)² have length two, although they require different numbers of generators. Later the tower estimate uses both quantities. Over a coefficient ring with residue field of size ℓf, each quotient instead contributes f to the base-ℓ logarithm of the order.

Fix a number field E and a rational prime ℓ. The coefficient module here is the discrete quotient ℚℓ/ℤℓ. A Tate twist changes the scalar by which Galois acts. If the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character is χcyc, the action on this quotient uses χcyc−j for the integer j in the window sum. With this action the cocycle rule above becomes c(gh) = c(g) + χcyc(g)−jc(h). Vanishing on restriction means the restricted cocycle becomes a coboundary.

Let S consist of the finite places above ℓ. Take the Galois group of the maximal extension unramified at every finite place outside S. One chooses a place of the algebraic closure above each member and restricts to the corresponding decomposition group. Write hℓ,j for the ℤℓ-module length of the subgroup of locally trivial degree-one classes. The related degree-two group has coefficients ℤℓ(j + 1). Thus the locally trivial subgroup within degree one is the intersection of the kernels of those local restriction maps.

Given t and B, the cohomological estimate requires finiteness of every hℓ,j for 1 ≤ j < t, for all allowed choices of closure and local data. For every finite set P of rational primes it also requires

∑ℓ ∈ P (log ℓ) ∑1 ≤ j < t hℓ,j ≤ B.

The field varies with a primitive character ψ, the height in a cyclotomic tower, and two auxiliary primes q,d. In a cyclotomic field containing the relevant roots of unity, the subgroup fixing E consists of the automorphisms whose exponents satisfy four conditions. These are congruence to ±1 modulo 2e+2, ψ(a) = 1, and two quadratic-symbol conditions at q and d. For a fixed ψ and 0 < ε < 1/52, choose any integer function e(x) satisfying x2+8ε ≤ 2e(x) ≤ 2x2+8ε for all x ≥ 1. The cohomological window theorem gives J ≥ 1 and a threshold X0. For every X beyond it and every admissible pair (q,d) at scale X1/J, there is Y ≥ X1/J with Y² ≤ X. Throughout [Y,Y²], every such field satisfies the length bound for t = ⌊x401⌋ and B = exp(xε/2). An admissible pair must obey the prime, congruence, divisibility and logarithmic size conditions of the prime-pair theorem.

8.3Splitting the obstruction by the action of conjugation

There is a different estimate for each of three parts of the cohomological sum. To see where they come from, fix a CM field in the construction, a twist index j and an odd prime ℓ. Complex conjugation on the CM field induces a linear involution c on the degree-one cohomology. Its action preserves the locally trivial subgroup. Put s = (−1)j. Because 2 is a unit in ℤℓ, every locally trivial class v has a decomposition

v = ½(v + scv) + ½(v − scv).

Applying c to the first summand multiplies it by s, and applying it to the second multiplies it by −s. Both still lie in the subgroup. A vector in both eigenspaces satisfies 2sv = 0, hence vanishes. The sum is direct, so the full module length equals the sum of its two eigenspace lengths. Here “plus” means eigenvalue (−1)j; for odd j this is the −1 eigenspace. At ℓ = 2 the projectors involve a forbidden division, and the full module is estimated separately.

On the joint window there are bounds B2 on the sum of full lengths at ℓ = 2, and B+ and B− on the logarithmically weighted odd-prime sums of the two corresponding lengths. Each comes with finiteness for its twists and primes. Length additivity gives finiteness of the full group at odd primes as well. For any finite prime set, split off 2 if present, and add the two odd-prime inequalities term by term. This proves the bound B2 log 2 + B+ + B−. It explains why the factor log 2 appears only on the first term.

Their product proves the required exp(xε/2). This comparison is uniform over fields obeying the conductor bound.

The tower estimate uses a bound on degree-two cohomology, Poitou–Tate duality, local finiteness, local Tate duality and the Ferrero–Washington theorem. The plus contribution also uses separate representation counts. The following argument explains how the number of generators of a tower module controls the choice of the common interval.

8.5What Ferrero–Washington supplies in this proof

A generator bound limits how many independent ℓ-adic directions can contribute to the growth of a cohomology group. The argument starts with the ideal class groups of the number fields in the finite layers of a cyclotomic tower, passes to a single module for the infinite tower, and then recovers the length at any chosen finite layer as a quotient of that module. The class group of a number field is the group of its nonzero fractional ideals modulo principal ideals.

Write Cl(L) for the ideal class group of a number field L, written additively. The number of independent characters of order ℓ depends on Cl(L)/ℓCl(L). For an abelian extension K/ℚ containing a primitive ℓth root of unity, or a primitive fourth root of unity at ℓ = 2, the cyclotomic rank bound of Ferrero and Washington gives a single integer r such that

|Cl(K(μℓⁿ))/ℓCl(K(μℓⁿ))| ≤ ℓr   for every n ≥ 0.

Here μℓⁿ denotes the roots of unity of order dividing ℓn. The constant can depend on ℓ and K. The following construction gives one such bound.

First work in the full cyclotomic fields L = ℚ(μfℓⁿ) for fixed f > 1 prime to ℓ. Let C = Cl(L), let J be complex conjugation, and write E = (1 − J)C. The character comparison below supplies a bound B0 for the index of ℓC + (1 − γ)C, for its chosen Galois element γ. It also supplies N and n0, independent of n, such that in the integral group ring (γ − 1)N belongs to the ideal generated by θ, 1 + J and ℓ for n ≥ n0. Here θ is the integral half-sum, whose coefficients use one representative from each pair of opposite residues. The integral annihilator on ideal classes gives θ(1 − J)C = 0. Take the smoothing integer 2fℓ + 1.

Put T = 1 − γ. Multiply the relation by 1 − J. The θ term kills the class group, the 1 + J term disappears because J² = 1, and the last term has image inside ℓE. Hence TN kills V = E/ℓE. Each quotient TaV/Ta+1V is an image of V/TV. The map 1 − J in turn sends C/(ℓC + TC) onto V/TV. Multiplying the at most N quotient sizes gives |V| ≤ B0N. On the finite group E, the kernel and cokernel of multiplication by ℓ have the same order, so the same bound holds for |E[ℓ]|.

At odd ℓ a reflection inequality bounds |C/(ℓC + E)| by ℓ times the number of ℓ-torsion elements on which conjugation acts by −1. Each such element x lies in E, since (1 − J)(((ℓ + 1)/2)x) = x, with the integer scalar (ℓ + 1)/2. The remaining factor |(ℓC + E)/ℓC| is at most |E/ℓE|. The resulting bound is ℓB02N. At ℓ = 2 put C− = ker(1 + J). The separate sign estimate gives [C−∶E] ≤ (2φ(4f))N, where φ is Euler’s totient. On C[2], the map 1 − J has image in E[2] and kernel in C−[2]. The latter has order at most [C−∶E] |E[2]|. Squaring gives the uniform allowance ([C−∶E] |E[2]|)².

To transfer either bound, denoted by B, to the abelian field K, use its inclusion in a cyclotomic field. The embedding lemma chooses f,D before n. For every K′ = K(μℓⁿ) it produces a full cyclotomic field L of conductor fℓm, with m ≥ n0 and [L∶K′] ≤ Dℓn₀. Restrict the unramified ℤ/ℓ-characters from K′ to L. The size of the restriction kernel is bounded by the subgroup index [L∶K′], and the Artin character comparison bounds its image by the number of class-group characters of L. Thus |Cl(K′)/ℓCl(K′)| ≤ Dℓn₀B. The written proof chooses this integer itself for r, since it is at most ℓr. The arithmetic inputs to this derivation include the group-ring relation, the uniform ambiguous-class index, Stickelberger annihilation, reflection and the sign estimate at 2. Their statements have the pinned suppliers above.

8.6Which part of the class group has a uniform bound?

Fix a prime ℓ and a number field F containing a primitive ℓth root of unity. In a layer K = F(μℓn), assume K is totally complex and Gal(K/F) is generated by τ. Write C = Cl(𝒪K) additively. The first input to the uniform class-rank estimate controls the largest quotient of C killed by ℓ on which τ acts trivially. The term coinvariants describes this last condition. Define BF to be the number of continuous characters GF → 𝔽ℓ unramified at every finite place away from ℓ. Ramification above ℓ is allowed. Kummer theory makes this number finite, independently of the layer.

Q = C/(ℓC + (1 − τ)C),   [C ∶ ℓC + (1 − τ)C] = |Q| ≤ BF.

Why can the base field bound this index? A character of Q is determined by its composite with C ↠ Q. That composite is fixed by τ and therefore by its powers. As Q is a finite 𝔽ℓ-vector space, it has as many characters as elements. By the Hilbert class field comparison, pulling class characters back to U = GK identifies the invariant ones with a finite space E of characters on U. They vanish on all finite inertia in U and are invariant under conjugation by G = GF. The total-complexity hypothesis on K supplies the archimedean hypothesis for this identification, including at ℓ = 2.

Intersect the kernels of all characters in E inside U, and call the intersection N. It is open since E is finite and U is open. Since G is profinite and N is normal by conjugation invariance, G/N is a finite group. Every commutator gug−1u−1 belongs to N, so U/N is central in G/N. The quotient G/U is cyclic. Each element of G/N is therefore a power of one lift times a central element, so G/N is abelian. Every character in E factors through U/N, and every character of U/N satisfies the same invariance and inertia conditions.

For any finite abelian ℓ-primary or mixed-order group D, |Hom(D,𝔽ℓ)| equals |D[ℓ]|. The inclusion of the subgroups killed by ℓ in U/N and G/N now bounds the number of characters of the first group by that of the second. Pullback from G/N to G is injective. Every inertia group away from ℓ fixes the cyclotomic layer and hence lies in U. All its elements lie in N by the definition of E. The pulled-back characters are consequently among the BF allowed characters. This proves the index bound. The distinction between counting and extending is visible for 3ℤ/9 ⊂ ℤ/9. Each group has three 𝔽₃-valued characters, and all three characters of ℤ/9 restrict to zero on 3ℤ/9.

Where does the exponent come from? For conductor M = fℓn with (f,ℓ) = 1, put a = 1 for odd ℓ and a = 2 for ℓ = 2. Take the fixed base F = ℚ(μfℓa) and varying K = ℚ(μM), n ≥ 2. In the units modulo M, γ = 1 + fℓa generates the kernel of reduction to conductor fℓa. Its subgroup has index φ(fℓa), where φ is Euler’s totient. The archive acts on ideal classes by the inverse automorphism, so it uses the relative generator τ corresponding to γ−1. This provides one BF for all these layers.

Suppose now f > 1, write J for complex conjugation, and let Θ be the integral Stickelberger element used in this calculation, with auxiliary integer c = 2fℓ + 1. Two further results enter. Integral Stickelberger annihilation makes Θ(1 − J) act as zero on C. Separately, nonvanishing of the twisted, projected Θ in characteristic ℓ supplies a depth n₀ and one exponent N such that (γ − 1)N belongs to the group-ring ideal (Θ, 1 + J, ℓ) for every n ≥ n₀. The tested characters satisfy χ(−1) = −1, a condition which in characteristic two reads χ(−1) = 1. These two inputs give the first inequality below, and the ambiguous-class estimate gives the second.

|(1 − J)C ∩ C[ℓ]| ≤ |Q|N ≤ BFN.

At odd primes reflection then bounds |C/ℓC| by ℓ(BFN)². At 2 the proof inserts the bound from real-unit signatures and obtains ((2φ(4f))NBFN)². These are the eventual cyclic-layer estimates used to bound the original abelian tower.

How does the minus class count control the plus classes?

Let K be a CM field containing a primitive ℓth root of unity ζ, with ℓ an odd prime. Write C = Cl(K) additively, let J be complex conjugation, and put E = (1 − J)C. The tower estimate bounds the number of elements in E[ℓ], where brackets denote the subgroup killed by ℓ. To see which classes still need to be counted, first divide C/ℓC by the image of E. In the resulting vector space Q = C/(ℓC + E), each class coincides with its conjugate. In fact Q identifies with the plus eigenspace of C/ℓC by sending a representative x to (x + Jx)/2. The division takes place in 𝔽ℓ.

Odd-prime reflection. Let C[ℓ]− consist of the classes y with ℓy = 0 and Jy = −y. Then

|Q| ≤ ℓ · |C[ℓ]−|.

Count the linear maps χ from Q to 𝔽ℓ. Choosing their values on a basis shows that there are |Q| of them. By Artin reciprocity each gives a character of the absolute Galois group of K unramified at every finite prime. These characters satisfy χ(c⁻¹gc) = χ(g), where c is any lift of J to the algebraic closure. Indeed the Artin map carries conjugate primes to conjugate Frobenius elements and χ has the same value on a class and its conjugate.

Fix ζ for the rest of the argument. For each character choose a nonzero β satisfying g(β)/β = ζχ(g). For a nonzero χ, let L/K be the cyclic extension fixed by its kernel. A generator acts by a scalar ζχ(g) of norm one, so Hilbert’s Theorem 90 gives such a β in that extension. For the zero character take β = 1. Then a = βℓ lies in K×. At every finite prime the extension is unramified. Its normalized integer valuation therefore restricts to the normalized valuation on K. Evaluating βℓ gives ℓ ∣ ord𝔭(a) at every prime 𝔭. The fractional ideal (a) is consequently the ℓth power of a unique fractional ideal 𝔞.

Send χ to the class [𝔞]. A different choice of β differs by a factor from K×, so 𝔞 changes only by a principal ideal. Products of radicals give sums of characters, making this a homomorphism. Its image is killed by ℓ. To find its sign, apply g to βc(β). The factor from β is ζχ(g). The factor from c(β) is c(ζχ(c⁻¹gc)) = ζ−χ(g), because conjugation inverts ζ. Their product is 1, so d = βc(β) lies in K× and a · J(a) = dℓ. Taking the unique ideal ℓth root gives 𝔞J(𝔞) = (d), hence J[𝔞] = −[𝔞]. This is where a plus character produces a minus ideal class.

Where does the extra factor ℓ come from?

Suppose [𝔞] = 0. Taking a generator b of 𝔞 gives a = u bℓ with u a unit of K. The relation a · J(a) = dℓ implies that u · J(u) is an ℓth power in K. Also u/J(u) is an algebraic integer with absolute value one at every complex embedding. By Kronecker’s theorem it is a root of unity. Thus u² = (u/J(u)) · u · J(u) is represented by a root of unity modulo ℓth powers. Since ℓ is odd, raising this equality to the power (ℓ + 1)/2 shows that u itself has that property.

Finally, the class of a modulo ℓth powers determines χ. If two such classes coincide, the quotient of the two radicals, after division by an element of K×, is an ℓth root of unity and therefore belongs to K. The two characters agree. The kernel thus injects into the image of the roots of unity in K×/(K×)ℓ. The roots of unity in a number field form a finite group. Under a complex embedding they are contained in the cyclic group of roots of Xm − 1, where m is their number, so they form a cyclic group themselves. Its quotient by ℓth powers has at most ℓ elements. Multiplying this kernel bound by the size of the minus subgroup containing the image proves the reflection inequality.

Why is the bound squared in the tower?

If y belongs to C[ℓ]−, then (1 − J)((ℓ + 1)y/2) = (ℓ + 1)y = y. Here (ℓ + 1)/2 is an ordinary integer. Thus each such y belongs to E[ℓ]. The map C/ℓC → Q has kernel E/(E ∩ ℓC). This kernel is a quotient of E/ℓE, which has size |E[ℓ]| by counting the kernel and image of multiplication by ℓ on the finite group E. Hence

|C/ℓC| = |E/(E ∩ ℓC)| · |Q| ≤ ℓ · |E[ℓ]|².

The two copies of |E[ℓ]| have different origins. One counts what was lost in forming the quotient Q. The other bounds the possible images of characters of Q under reflection. For a check of this multiplication, take ℓ = 3 and the abstract group C = ℤ/9 ⊕ (ℤ/3)², with J negating the first coordinate and fixing the other two. Here E is the entire first factor, |E[3]| = 3, and |Q| = 9. Multiplication by 3 on C has image of size 3, so |C/3C| = 81/3 = 27, exactly 3 · 3². For n ≥ 1 in the cyclotomic tower, the layer K = ℚ(μfℓⁿ) contains the primitive ℓth root ζfℓⁿfℓⁿ⁻¹. The uniform bound |E[ℓ]| ≤ BFN now gives ℓBF2N.

Fixed classes and coinvariants in two dimensions

Let C = 𝔽₃² and τ(x,y) = (x + y, y), an automorphism of order three. Its fixed vectors form the first coordinate line. Since (1 − τ)(x,y) = (−y,0), this entire line maps to zero in Q. The second coordinate induces Q ≃ 𝔽₃. Both groups have three elements, but the projection kills every fixed vector. The three invariant characters are exactly (x,y) ↦ by, one for each b ∈ 𝔽₃.

For an arithmetic check of the two indices, take ℓ = 3, f = 2 and n = 2. The units mod 18 form a group of order six. The powers of γ = 7 are 1, 7, 13, so their subgroup has index two and the relative class action uses 13. The field ℚ(μ₁₈) = ℚ(μ₉) has absolute discriminant 3⁹. Its Minkowski bound is (4/π)³(6!/6⁶)√(3⁹) < 4.47. The prime 2 has order six mod 9, so the prime above it has norm 64. The sole prime above 3 is generated by 1 − ζ₉. Every class thus has a principal representative of norm at most four. Here the class-group index |Q| is one. Over the base ℚ(μ₃), Kummer theory also gives BF = 9. Its Eisenstein integers are principal, so every cube class unramified away from 3 has a representative which is a unit times a power of 1 − ζ₃. Conversely these representatives are units away from 3, where the cube-root polynomial has separable reduction. The six roots of unity supply three classes modulo cubes and the exponent at the sole prime above 3 supplies three more choices, giving 3 · 3.

Why a Stickelberger coefficient survives reduction modulo ℓ

The class-group argument needs one depth at which every allowed character leaves a nonzero coefficient. Fix a prime ℓ, an integer f ≥ 1 coprime to ℓ and an odd integer c > 1 coprime to fℓ. In the selected cyclotomic tower f > 1 and c = 2fℓ + 1. At level n put M = fℓn. For a residue s modulo M, let ⟨s⟩ be its representative between 0 and M−1. Each unit supplies a basis element [s] of the group ring. The integral relation uses just one unit from each pair {s,−s}.

g(s) = ⌊c⟨c−1s⟩/M⌋ − (c−1)/2,   Θ = ∑s unit, 2⟨s⟩<M g(s)[s].

For odd ℓ let W be the group of (ℓ−1)st roots of unity in ℤℓ. For ℓ = 2 take W = {1,−1}. At depth d ≤ n, the map πd reduces a unit modulo ℓd and then takes its coset modulo the image of W. Twisting by a character χ sends [s] to χ(s)[πd(s)]. The theorem gives one d ≥ 2 depending on ℓ, f and c. For every n ≥ d, every field k of characteristic ℓ and every character χ of the units modulo M into k× with χ(−1) = −1, the twisted image of Θ has a nonzero coefficient at depth d. The coset carrying that coefficient may vary.

Convert the coefficients into a difference. Extend χ by zero on nonunits, calling the extension Ψ. Sum g(s)Ψ(s) over all residues s above y modulo ℓd and call the result α(y). Choose one ℓ-adic root r from each pair {r,−r} in W, forming a set R. On units, both g and χ change sign under negation, so their product has the same value at both representatives. The lower-half sum defining Θ can therefore use the representatives selected by R in each quotient fibre. Reduction is injective on W at depth d ≥ 2, and on nonunit fibres α vanishes. Thus vanishing of the twisted image would imply ∑r∈R α(r−1y) = 0 for every y, with r reduced modulo ℓd. This argument chooses representatives directly, which is essential in characteristic two.

The function Ψ has additive period fℓ. Adding fℓ preserves the prime divisors shared with M. On a unit s it amounts to multiplying by 1 + fℓ/s, a unit of ℓ-power order. Its character value is 1 because in characteristic ℓ the only ℓ-power root of unity in a field is 1. Set B = cfℓ. Subtracting c from s lowers the residue ⟨c−1s⟩ by one, with wraparound at zero. The floor difference counts the integers 0 ≤ j < c congruent to s, with a correction −c at zero. Add fℓ such consecutive differences. The corrections now occur at the multiples of c. Periodicity lets Ψ weight the result, and summing over the fibres gives a formula at the chosen depth.

α(y) − α(y−B) = ∑0≤j<B, j≡y mod ℓd P(j),   P(j) = Ψ(j)(1 − c·1c∣j).

In particular P(1) = 1, because Ψ(1) = 1 and c > 1. The issue is whether different directions r and different indices j can hide that coefficient after reduction.

Sinnott’s separation argument. Write Xv for a formal translation by an additive residue v, so multiplication adds exponents. At finite level put Ar = ∑y α(y)Xry and Pr = ∑j<B P(j)Xjr. The difference equation says Pr = (1−XBr)Ar. The putative vanishing says ∑r Ar = 0. Multiplying by the product of all the differences eliminates the functions Ar.

∑r∈R Pr ∏u∈R, u≠r (1−XBu) = 0.

Write the same expression with exponents in the additive group ℤℓ before reduction. Only finitely many exponents can occur. They have the form jr + ∑u∈S Bu for 0 ≤ j < B and a subset S of R. This finite list is known before the coefficient field or character is chosen. Any two distinct ℓ-adic integers differ at some finite depth. Taking the maximum of these depths over the list and increasing it to at least two makes reduction injective on the list. Hence the displayed identity also holds with exponents in ℤℓ.

Fix one direction r₀ and take exponents modulo the additive subgroup ℤ·Br₀. Every summand except the one indexed by r₀ contains the zero factor 1−XBr₀. For every other u, the image of Bu has infinite order. Indeed, a nonzero integer relation between u and r₀ would make their ratio a rational root of unity and hence ±1, excluded by the choice of representatives. Multiplication by 1−XBu is then injective on finite sums. Any nonzero coefficient fixed by this translation would repeat at infinitely many exponents. Cancel these factors. The exponents jr₀ for 0 ≤ j < B remain distinct modulo ℤ·Br₀, so every P(j) vanishes. This contradicts P(1) = 1.

A failed shallow test at 2. Take ℓ = 2, f = 3 and c = 13. Every character here satisfies the sign condition. Indeed χ(−1)² = 1, so (χ(−1)−1)² = 0 in the characteristic-two field and χ(−1) = 1 = −1. At n = d = 2, M = 12 and the units in the lower half are 1 and 5. Since 13 ≡ 1 modulo 12, the coefficients are ⌊13/12⌋−6 = −5 and ⌊65/12⌋−6 = −1. Both represent the same coset modulo 4 after quotienting by {±1}. The trivial character gives −6 = 0 in 𝔽₂. The theorem allows this cancellation at a shallow depth.

For these same parameters d = 7 suffices. There is just one direction, which we may choose as 1, and B = 78 < 128. If all projected coefficients vanished, α would vanish everywhere. At y = 1 the difference equation instead gives α(1)−α(51) = P(1) = 1. This works for every input level n ≥ 7. As a numerical check at n = 7 and χ trivial, the units above 1 are 1 and 257 with coefficients 5 and 0. The units above 51 are 179 and 307 with coefficients 0 and 4. The two fibre sums are therefore 1 and 0 in 𝔽₂. The finite fibre calculation lets you compare cancellations at different levels.

How does a surviving coefficient bound a power of γ − 1?

The nonvanishing theorem detects a twisted sum at one fixed projection depth d, however far up the tower the source lies. The class-group bound needs an integral ideal membership with a single exponent at all those levels. The bridge between them is a polynomial in one nilpotent variable.

Read the order of vanishing in the cyclic direction. At level n let G be the units modulo fℓn. Write [g] for the basis element of its group algebra and set T = [γ]−1. Work over an algebraic closure k of 𝔽ℓ. The proof constructs a homomorphism p from G into the cyclic subgroup generated by γ. It preserves the shallow projection π, sends complex conjugation J to 1, and γ has order dividing ℓn. Consequently Tℓn = [γℓn]−1 = 0. For an odd character χ the twist Φ formed with p is a polynomial in T, since every [p(g)] is a nonnegative power of 1+T. The map induced by π takes Φ to the known nonzero twist and sends Tℓd to zero.

Choose a polynomial representing Φ and factor out its lowest nonzero power, writing Φ = Tru(T) with u(0) ≠ 0. The polynomial u(T) has an inverse. After division by its constant term it is one plus a nilpotent, whose inverse is a finite geometric sum. If r ≥ ℓd, the image of Φ in the shallow quotient would vanish. Thus Φ divides the required power, with multiplier Tℓd−ru(T)−1.

A detectable coefficient which has no inverse

In the group algebra of a cyclic group of order eight over 𝔽₂, write T = [γ]−1. The elements 1, T, …, T⁷ form a basis and T⁸ = 0. Project to the cyclic group of order four, where T⁴ = 0. The element Φ = T³(1+T) has nonzero image T³. It has no inverse in the original ring, but it divides T⁴. Multiplying Φ by T(1+T)⁷ gives T⁴ because (1+T)⁸ = 1. This is a check of the polynomial step.

Recover the untwisted relation. The part discarded by p has exponent dividing φ(fℓe) = ℓam with ℓ ∤ m. Here e is 1 at odd ℓ and 2 at ℓ = 2. Raising g/p(g) to ℓa defines a homomorphism b with image D of order prime to ℓ. In the algebra k[G]/(Θ,1+[J]), split the action of D into characters. For an eigenvector v ≠ 0 of character ψ, take χ satisfying χ(g)ℓa = ψ(b(g)), using inverse Frobenius in k. As [J] acts by −1 and p(J)=1, this χ satisfies χ(J)=−1, precisely the required sign.

Taking the ℓa-th power of the coefficient sum for Θ raises each term to that power in characteristic ℓ. On an eigenvector the one-term identity is [g]ℓav = [p(g)]ℓaψ(b(g))v. Thus the result on v equals the ℓa-th power of the cyclic twist Φ acting on v. Since Θ itself is zero in this quotient, that power of Φ kills v. Raising its divisibility relation to the same power shows that Tℓd+a kills v. Character orthogonality recovers the identity. Summing the character projectors before normalization gives |D| times 1, and |D| is invertible in k. Hence this power of T is itself zero in the quotient.

Lift back to ℤ. Put N = ℓd+a. Write the relation over k as TN = uΘ + v(1+[J]). Choose an 𝔽ℓ-linear map k → 𝔽ℓ fixing 1. Apply it to every coefficient of the equation. Linearity suffices because the factors Θ and 1+[J] have integral coefficients. Lift the two multipliers from 𝔽ℓ to ℤ. Every coefficient of the remaining difference is divisible by ℓ, giving the third generator of the ideal. Both d and a were fixed before the source level n.

([γ]−1)N ∈ (Θ, 1+[J], ℓ) ⊂ ℤ[G]   for every n ≥ d.

To use this relation, put V = (1−J)Cl(L)/ℓ(1−J)Cl(L). The integral class annihilator makes Θ act by zero there, (1+J)(1−J) = 0, and reduction kills ℓ. Hence the operator T = [γ]−1 satisfies TNV = 0. Multiplication by Ta maps V/TV onto each successive quotient TaV/Ta+1V. A bound B for the first quotient thus gives |V| ≤ BN. This is where the uniform exponent enters the class-group estimate.

In the dyadic example, f = 3 gives φ(3·4) = 4 and a = 2. Taking the sufficient depth d = 7 from the difference calculation gives N = 2⁹ = 512 for every n ≥ 7. The calculation modulo 8 tests a single character at a smaller depth. The exponent 512 uses a depth that works for every allowed character in every later layer.
